4. R3 — Booleans have exactly three spellings
6. R5 — Multi-value flags are repeatable, never comma-split
7. R6 — Every listable object has a list and a detail command
8. R7 — Anything that names an object completes it
9. R8 — Four wording templates, one implementation

docs.title: Client link test
docs.summary: Two tools measure one client's link to OLR: LibreSpeed, which runs in that client's browser, and iperf3, which runs a client on it. Both answer "how fast can this phone or laptop talk to the router", which is a different question from the Speedtest by Ookla tool beside them: that one measures the router's own uplink and never involves the client at all.
docs.html:
Two tools measure one client's link to OLR: LibreSpeed, which runs in that client's browser, and iperf3, which runs a client on it. Both answer "how fast can this phone or laptop talk to the router", which is a different question from the Speedtest by Ookla tool beside them: that one measures the router's own uplink and never involves the client at all.

Neither of these measures LAN-to-WAN forwarding, NAT, or another client's link.

LibreSpeed (browser, default)

Open Tools, then LibreSpeed, on the client. The test runs in that client's browser against this router, so nothing has to be installed on either end.

The page is LibreSpeed 6.3.1 (internal/tools/librespeed/, LGPLv3, unmodified). olrd serves it at /link-test/ and answers the four requests the LibreSpeed worker makes:

RequestAnswer
GET /link-test/download?ckSize=NN MiB of a fixed random block, flushed per MiB
POST /link-test/upload200 once the body is read and discarded
GET /link-test/pingan empty reply, for latency and jitter
GET /link-test/ipthe address the router saw the request come from

/link-test/ is deliberately not part of /api. The upload test posts raw bytes, and the API refuses a non-JSON body on purpose, so these endpoints sit outside it. What authorizes them is a viewer cookie: the tools page calls POST /api/tools/link-test/session — inside the API, behind the same password or token as everything else — and olrd answers with an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict session cookie scoped to /link-test/, forgotten by the daemon after two hours. This is the pattern the client inspection page already uses to embed mitmweb. Reopening the page mints a new cookie; a browser that never signed in to this router gets an explanation, not a bandwidth source.

The surface is framed only by this router's own page (X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'), because the tool page embeds it. That page is the tool: the frame sits under the Tools heading with no introduction, no second title and no link out, so the test itself is everything the operator has to read.

Telemetry is off and no result is stored: there is no database behind this page, so the privacy dialog LibreSpeed can show would be a false promise.

The random block is generated once at startup and repeated. That is what keeps the router's CPU out of the measurement, and it is safe because the point of the randomness is only that no step between the router and the browser can compress the payload and report a speed the wire never carried.

What limits the number

The measurement ends in the browser, so it is capped by the slowest of: the client's Wi-Fi, the switch, the router's NIC, the router's HTTP path, and the client's own JavaScript and CPU. A browser test rarely passes about 1 Gbps even on a faster link, and a phone on Wi-Fi usually reports the Wi-Fi rate rather than the wire. Read it as "at least this fast, and stable or not", not as a wire-rate certificate.

iperf3 (sustained, wired)

Open Tools, then iperf3. OLR starts a temporary iperf3 server on a chosen, currently configured LAN IPv4 address (TCP 5201) and shows the client commands. Install iperf3 on the router and the other client; the other client's terminal displays the results.

This is the honest option for a wired link faster than a browser can measure. The server stops after two minutes, on request, or when olrd shuts down normally. A process killed ungracefully can leave a child behind; check for iperf3 -s if the port is unexpectedly busy.

The address is checked against OLR's configured networks and the kernel's current interface addresses. OLR does not modify firewall rules. If the OLR firewall is enabled, temporarily allow TCP 5201 from the test client and remove that opening afterward. Only start a session on a trusted LAN: other clients able to reach that address and port can use the server while it runs.

The measurement terminates on the router. It measures that client's link and OLR's local TCP receive/send path, not forwarding between two interfaces, NAT, or internet speed. Wi-Fi, switches, the client and other traffic can limit the result before the router's NIC does.

If TCP 5201 is already held by an iperf3 process and the selected LAN address is reachable, Tools displays the external server and the client commands without starting or stopping it. The session lifetime is controlled by that service, not OLR. A different port holder is reported by process name/PID/unit where available; OLR never kills or reconfigures an existing process.

Picking between them

Use LibreSpeed for the everyday question — "is this room's Wi-Fi fine?" — because it needs nothing installed and runs on the client that is asking. Use iperf3 when the answer has to be a wire rate: gigabit or faster Ethernet, a sustained multi-stream load, or a before/after comparison of a cable or a switch port.

docs.title: Client QoS
docs.originalTitle: Client QoS: priority and speed limits
docs.summary: Implementation: Linux HTB/fq_codel queues enforce policies automatically, without an enable switch. Downloads are shaped on managed LAN egress; uploads redirect LAN ingress to owned IFBs. Ethernet MAC classifiers cover both address families and NAT without changing gateway routing marks. Optional link rates apply per LAN interface; without rates, priority only orders local contention.
docs.html:
Implementation: Linux HTB/fq_codel queues enforce policies automatically, without an enable switch. Downloads are shaped on managed LAN egress; uploads redirect LAN ingress to owned IFBs. Ethernet MAC classifiers cover both address families and NAT without changing gateway routing marks. Optional link rates apply per LAN interface; without rates, priority only orders local contention.

Legacy enabled is ignored. API zero clears a limit. Pending policies lack an unambiguous managed LAN interface; client IP changes do not affect classification. Startup and ten-second reconciliation restore intent and detect drift. No-op applies retain queues. Editing rebuilds queues and may discard queued packets. Errors explicitly distinguish saved intent from successful kernel application.

Foreign roots/ingress filters are refused; unconfigured zero-handle kernel roots (including default multi-queue NIC roots) may be replaced. Root handle 4f4c:, ingress preference 20290, and IFBs with olr:qos:<interface> aliases identify ownership. Removing the last policy removes owned roots/redirect filters but retains empty ingress attachments and IFBs. nftables flowtables are refused. Proprietary acceleration must be disabled by the operator. Unset aggregate rates use a 100 Gbit/s technical ceiling.

Run privileged traffic verification with OLR_QOS_INTEGRATION=1 go test ./internal/qos -run TestKernelTraffic -v as root, with ip, tc, nft and iperf3 installed. It tests real IPv4 NAT/IPv6 traffic in both directions and reset in isolated network namespaces. Restricted workspaces run unit tests only.

1. What the operator sees

The client detail page exposes exactly two policies for traffic crossing this router:

  • Network priority: High, Normal (the default), or Low. Priority decides who gets served first when the managed link is busy. It is not a reserved minimum speed, and Low must be allowed to use spare capacity.
  • Speed limit: optional maximum download and upload rates in Mbps, set independently. An unset direction is unlimited by this client policy; API zero clears the limit. The two limits are ceilings, not targets or promises of available bandwidth.

Show the saved policy and its effective status separately. A policy is not "active" just because its configuration was stored. If client placement or a kernel facility is missing, explain which one prevents enforcement. Defaults are Normal and unlimited; no policy changes any packet until a client policy is configured.

A single-client edit must not rewrite the entire client inventory. The policy belongs to qos and refers to the canonical client MAC owned by clients. It does not become an identity field in clients, nor does it depend on DHCP: a client may have a static address. Its detail page is an entry point to the QoS API, not the owner of the policy.

2. Link setup (not another per-client policy)

The router needs configured upload and download shaping rates, based on measured throughput rather than the physical Ethernet port speed. Otherwise priority cannot reliably control the bottleneck in an ISP modem or upstream network. Aggregate rates remain available through configuration/API for advanced use; the web UI exposes only per-client controls, with no Gateway rate form. The Overview page's browser-local utilization limits are display preferences; they must not silently become router configuration or imply that QoS is on.

Shape on the managed LAN interface where Ethernet identities remain available. This also limits routed LAN-to-LAN traffic. Aggregate rates are independent per LAN; a shared whole-WAN ceiling across several LANs is not implemented. Since downloads have already crossed the ISP link, download shaping manages the subsequent queue and TCP feedback; it cannot prevent bytes from having arrived at the router. Report both directions independently.

3. Kernel ownership and classification

qos owns only its qdiscs, filters, IFB and classifier rules. It must inspect existing root qdiscs before writing, refuse a foreign owner, and remove only objects it can identify as its own. The kernel state is observed fresh for plan/drift/status; a daemon restart restores stored intent without replacing a correct running queue. Adding, editing or clearing a policy may interrupt queued packets; aggregate rate changes also rebuild queues. Report partial failures rather than claiming a transaction.

Use Linux tc for shaping and queueing. A classful hierarchy (for example HTB with fq_codel leaves) can express per-client ceilings and High/Normal/Low scheduling while allowing unused capacity to be borrowed. CAKE is useful for whole-link SQM but by itself is not a drop-in implementation of arbitrary per-client ceilings. Do not promise per-application classification: the two controls here classify clients. Existing gateway fwmarks select exits; QoS must neither overwrite those bits nor mistake an exit mark for a priority.

Resolve each MAC's managed LAN interface through clients at apply time and reconcile placement changes. Ambiguous or unknown placement leaves the policy pending. Classifiers match MACs, so address changes need no rule rewrite. Cover both directions and both address families in tests. Locally switched traffic that does not traverse this router is outside scope. Detect hardware/software flow offload that bypasses the queue and do not report an unenforced policy as active.

4. Acceptance checks

  1. With no client policies, existing traffic and foreign qdiscs are untouched. With measured rates configured, filling the managed queue no longer makes a high-priority flow wait behind a low-priority bulk transfer; an idle low-priority client can use spare capacity.
  2. An upload/download limit caps only that client in that direction, including after its address changes. Removing a limit restores unrestricted use up to the managed link rate; changing a name, icon or group preserves the policy.
  3. A reboot restores the policy. A no-op daemon restart does not drop a queue. Clearing policies removes only olr-owned state.
  4. Missing kernel support, an occupied qdisc, unknown LAN placement or a partial apply is visible in status and does not yield a false success in the UI. Verify IPv4, IPv6, NAT, gateway exits and VPN egress separately.
  5. The API and CLI expose the same two per-client concepts as the detail page. The UI labels Mbps consistently and validates positive, bounded numbers.

Implementation should be exercised in Linux network namespaces with traffic and latency measurements, not just a mock of the tc calls. A Go unit test on another OS cannot establish that the policies actually shape packets.

docs.title: Configuration safety
docs.summary: The global apply lock covers reading intent, merging a PATCH or editing an object, validating cross-module references, planning and saving/applying the result. Bodies are read before taking the lock. GET and plan requests remain independent of the lock.
docs.html:
The global apply lock covers reading intent, merging a PATCH or editing an object, validating cross-module references, planning and saving/applying the result. Bodies are read before taking the lock. GET and plan requests remain independent of the lock.

The DHCP/DNS background recovery watch uses the same lock. Its initial poll is only a hint; it rechecks eligibility after acquiring the lock, then reads and applies current intent without releasing it. An intervening disable, file edit or disruptive change is therefore not overridden by a stale recovery decision. Cancelled lock waits and failed eligibility reads do not consume restart attempts.

Config GET responses include a strong ETag. Send it as If-Match when replacing a fetched document or array. A concurrent change returns 412 before anything is written. Reload and review the draft; do not silently retry it against the new version. This is optional for older clients. The browser attaches the revision to the fetched config and preserves it through object spread, so a later background refresh cannot authorize an older draft.

Device identity edits use PUT /api/devices/devices/{mac} and forgetting uses DELETE at the same path. These edit one stored identity under the lock and preserve all other devices and groups. Observed presence and DHCP/firewall policies are separate resources. Whole-inventory PUT remains available for imports, with If-Match recommended.

Firewall native rules retain their existing combined runtime/intent revision from /ruleset; /config also accepts the intent ETag for ordinary config edits. Native rule editors should continue using the combined revision to detect changes made outside olr.

Link, dial/WAN, DHCP and DNS config writes accept dry_run and confirm. Their execution plan is checked under the lock before saving intent or changing runtime state. A disruptive request without confirm=true returns 409 with the plan and no completed steps. A dry run returns 200 and writes nothing. Malformed flags return 400. The browser sends confirmation only after its confirmation dialog; the local CLI sends it explicitly, matching the existing gateway CLI contract. Use --dry-run to review CLI changes first.

POST /apply repairs previously stored intent without another confirmation. Disruptive link, uplink, DHCP, DNS, gateway, firewall and WireGuard changes save a durable recovery point before applying. Explicitly keep the change in the browser within two minutes, or use olr recovery status followed by olr recovery confirm <id>. A successful apply or reconnect never confirms automatically. olr recovery revert <id> restores immediately. While a trial is pending, unrelated configuration edits are refused, including from local CLI. Multi-request browser edits continue the same trial using the X-OLR-Recovery-ID response/request header, without extending its deadline.

Timeout restores the previous complete intent and reconciles managed network state, including retiring addresses/routes introduced by the trial. Existing IPv4 addresses and main-table default routes are captured for first-adoption recovery. The mode-0600 journal in /var/lib/open-linux-router/connectivity.json survives restart; startup reverts an unconfirmed trial immediately. Recovery failures remain visible and retry, preserving both the previous and trial intent. Physical link failure, hardware removal, external configuration changes and unavailable backends can still require console access. Recovery does not undo external package installations or changes made outside OLR.

docs.title: Content standards
docs.summary: The visual direction is a precise, calm network console. Content must support that direction: users should identify the important information before reading supporting text. This guide complements the visual guide.
docs.html:
The visual direction is a precise, calm network console. Content must support that direction: users should identify the important information before reading supporting text. This guide complements the visual guide.

Vocabulary

Two words are kept apart, in English and in Chinese:

WordMeansDoes not mean
device / 设备Network equipment olr manages: switches, access points and routers. /devices, olr devices, the device inventory.A laptop, phone or printer on the LAN.
client / 客户端A thing on the LAN, keyed by MAC: identity, presence, groups, the target of a policy. /clients, the client inventory.The equipment olr reaches over a management interface.

Both used to be called "device", which is why a page that says "device" no longer said which one. Network is a third word and always means a subnet Gateway serves (olr net, link.networks), never this inventory. Where a sentence is about hardware in general — "the device's own management interface", "connect it to the device" — leave it alone; the rule names the two inventories, not every use of the word.

Start with the user's decision

Advanced's System group includes Backup. The backup page distinguishes a credential-bearing configuration export from runtime or whole-machine backups. Selecting a restore file validates it first; replacement requires a separate explicit action showing scope, credential changes and the recovery deadline. Preserve the original JSON bytes in both directions, including uint64 values.

Disruptive network changes require a second decision after application. A global recovery notice shows the remaining confirmation time, Keep changes and Revert now. Never confirm automatically on a successful API response or page load. Keep failed recovery and lost connectivity visible; explain how to reconnect to the previous address after the countdown.

Client priority and speed limits apply automatically, without an enable switch. Use “applied” only after observing matching runtime state. Show pending device placement and apply failures explicitly. Blank means unlimited. Keep the user workflow focused on per-client priority and speed limits; do not add aggregate QoS settings to Gateway or imply they are required for client limits.

Before adding content, write down the page's primary task and what the user needs to decide next. Give each visible element a purpose in that decision. Remove repeated or unrelated information; move useful later-stage information to the stage where it is needed.

Page typePrimary questionLead withSupporting content
Directory / entryWhich capability do I need?Recognizable names and distinct imageryA short distinction only if names are ambiguous
MonitoringWhat is happening, and what needs attention?Current state, important changes, key measurementsUnits, freshness and scope beside the data
ConfigurationWhat am I changing?Current value and its controlNecessary constraints, consequences and apply action
Diagnostic operationWhat should I run?Target, essential options and run actionRequirements and measurement scope
Diagnostic resultWhat happened, and what next?Outcome and decisive measurementsEvidence, limitations and a relevant next action

Apply these rules to existing pages as well as new features. The page-by-page review record documents the current baseline.

Simplification preserves data and consistency

Reducing clutter does not mean reducing every data display. First remove repeated introductions, obvious instructions and duplicated labels. Then clarify grouping, ordering and state. Do not shrink metric cards, value typography or chart space to make a page appear quieter. Overview cards may reduce padding and row height to improve density while preserving values, units and mobile interaction targets. Section landing pages omit titles duplicated by navigation, retaining a visually hidden page title. Detail and operation pages keep their identifying titles.

  • Overview shows Status, Traffic, Latency and Quality cards. Traffic's title-right map icon toggles statistics and map views in place. Its pressed state identifies the active map, and its accessible label names the next view. The detailed map has its own /map address. The quality radar shows Speed, Latency, Stability, Wireless and Functionality on a 0–100 higher-is-better scale. Wireless defaults to 80 when unmeasured or stale; explain this display-only default in details and the accessible chart description. Other missing or stale axes show a dash. Draw a polygon when all five axes have display scores. Omit the card total and measured-category caption. Details show the total out of 100 using normalized weights of current scored categories and components. Missing tests never reduce the score; measured failures still count. Clicking Quality or its chart links to the assessment page at /quality. It leads with the overall score, one display grade, the count of scored categories and the measured coverage, with the reference transfer's download and upload rates beside them: the numbers a reader can check lead, and the score stands next to what produced it. Categories follow in one panel; each names the score in a fixed column and states what it measured in that category's own units — throughput, median and variation, expected responses, reachable services. Never repeat a category state as a word on every row: "partial" describes the unfinished half of the catalogue, not this connection, and the coverage bar already says how much was scored. Only a state the operator can act on, such as an outdated result, earns a label. Expanding a row lists its tests; a service test item can rerun just that service, and a category heading can rerun every test behind that category. Unmeasured categories are excluded from the total. Raw service and NAT evidence and the scoring explanation stay in collapsed Measurement details. The page always includes the reference transfer, so replace the old optional-bandwidth switch with one short line at the run action; keep freshness and the router-default-route scope visible without restating the workflow. The view has its own /quality address. Snapshot reads never start tests. Clicking the Latency title opens the /latency test page, without a separate plus button. Internet target selection remains available through the API and CLI; failure never silently switches the chosen target. Show the latest single HTTPS latency sample, with <1 ms for sub-millisecond values; keep DNS lookup simple and omit bandwidth tests. Overview's site grid contains only pinned sites, with none selected by default; Internet and DNS remain visible. Clicking the Latency title opens /latency to manage pins. The pin is a small button before the site mark; an unpinned pin is hidden until its row is hovered or the button is focused, while a coarse pointer keeps it visible. Only the pin toggles Overview visibility — the mark and name are not a control. It indicates saved state, and its accessible action names the site and whether it will be pinned or unpinned. Save immediately to router configuration, retain choices across sessions and restarts, and show a failed save explicitly. A pin change is serialized, with progress on its row. Pinning changes presentation without starting probes or changing measurements. Show all monitored sites in one table, divided into the catalog's category sections (Communication, Social, Entertainment, News, Shopping, Tools, then Custom). A category heading is a plain semibold line; rows sit indented beneath it. Each site occupies one row: pin slot, bare icon, name, 24 fixed squares for the router-local day's hours, and a right-aligned daily average. Omit the visible hour axis, router date/offset and scheduling copy, and per-row test controls. Each tooltip gives the exact date, hour range and result. Missing and future hours stay neutral, and a failed attempt uses the same neutral fill; green is below 100 ms, amber from 100 to 499 ms and red from 500 ms. A retest replaces the current hour rather than appending another sample or changing other hours. Automatic tests run at about :30; the page's Test all measures one site at a time in reading order and updates only the current hour. It names the progress position and draws the current hour's probe as a spinner that settles into its square; it does not scroll or highlight the active row. A site that fails or times out does not stop the rest. Retain history through daemon and router restarts without inventing measurements for downtime. The row's average is the mean of that day's successful samples, in the same colour bands, and is a dash when none succeeded. Prefer matching bundled theSVG marks, then favicons and bare initials; add no icon frame. The catalog cannot be added to, removed or edited here. Keep completed results visible while Test all is running. Say when a request to measure fails; reading the page never starts tests. Up and elapsed uptime lead Status above system health. Click uptime for a dialog with CPU, memory and root disk used/total values; omit the separate System card. Click system health for a dialog with DHCP, DNS and Gateway states, with links to their pages. Distinguish checking, unavailable, disabled, needs attention and OK; retain the visible fault alerts below the cards. Latency and Map have no information icons. Traffic flips to reveal its map on the back, without a Map details row; clicking the grayscale map links to the color map at /map. All three detail pages use the shared header, PageHeading, content area and footer, with Overview selected in navigation. Country colors distinguish geography, while download/upload retain their semantic colors. omit the inline direction legend and top-ten summary.
  • Overview Status shows one public-network summary using IPv4's country flag, city and ISP. Its row opens a dialog showing IPv4, IPv6 when available, ASN and ASN Organization from the IPv4 lookup, in that order; label the organization “Org”.
  • Keep download and upload limits beside their respective measurements; separate controls serve separate decisions and are not automatically redundant.
  • Overview cumulative traffic uses Download then Upload labels, each with its byte unit. Preserve unavailable states rather than displaying zero when counting is disabled or a read fails.
  • Group Overview live traffic and utilization separately from cumulative traffic, site probes. Align section starts across desktop cards while keeping each group's internal spacing suited to its content; Status remains one list.
  • Keep common configuration fields, addresses, counters and useful evidence visible. Do not move them into disclosures solely to shorten a page.
  • Reuse existing headings, Card, ListRow, StatusStrip, fields and Dialog. Do not invent a compact card, new density tier or special layout for each feature. Choose shared size variants: MetricValue sm for inline measurements, md for summaries and lg for diagnostic results; Card's sm/default spacing is separate from Heading's sm/md/lg emphasis. Unavailable latency is never a zero result.
  • Disclose lengthy technical explanations and infrequently used advanced options. Keep prerequisites and consequences beside the action they affect.
  • A page can pass review without a visible redesign. Preserve a coherent existing presentation when its content already supports the user's task.

State and data contracts

Quality assessments run on demand from the /quality page reached through the card heading or chart. The page always includes the reference transfer. A full run replaces the snapshot; rerunning one category or service test reuses the other evidence, merges the fresh result and recalculates every affected score. While a rerun is in progress, keep the last scores visible, disable the other rerun controls and say which test is updating. Measured scores do not expire; results survive daemon and router restarts. The result view labels the same reference score Excellent 90–100, Good 75–89, Fair 60–74 or Poor below 60; the label is presentation, not another calculation. Not tested, cancelled, timed-out and unscored states replace the number with a dash, and a running assessment shows progress there instead; each carries one sentence saying what happened and what to do next. Missing data is never shown as zero.

A speed test runs as one request that stays open until the measurement ends, so its page reads the run's stage on a second request rather than waiting on a spinner. The measurement is shown the way LibreSpeed's page shows its own: two dials, download and upload, on a logarithmic 0–10 Gbps scale. The direction being measured carries the rate it has reached, the other holds its last reading, and both settle on the result, with latency and jitter above them. A dial that has not measured shows a dash rather than a zero, and a service that reports only a finished result says it is measuring instead of inventing numbers it cannot see yet. The controls stay to one row — way out, test server, start — and carry no explanatory copy; controls, start button and dials sit in one card, the way the embedded LibreSpeed page is one panel.

LibreSpeed is the exception among the tools: its page frames LibreSpeed's own document unchanged, because that page is the measurement, and OLR supplies only the viewer credential and the frame around it. Every other speed test borrows that page's dials for its own result rather than shipping its own charts.

World traffic combines IPs at the same remote coordinates into one map connection. Line width represents that connection's combined upload and download relative to the busiest one; per-IP rates stay in details. Arcs are one amber hue, outside the map's country colours, and each connection has one neutral dot that travels out and back, illustrating both directions without selecting a direction based on traffic volume.

Ingress distinguishes saved repairs from applied settings. When other existing errors prevent application, say the repair was saved, list the remaining service names and problems, and explain that the running proxy stays unchanged until the final repair applies automatically. Retain this warning after refresh.

World traffic uses two-second sampling and UI refresh. Smooth map transitions communicate continuity between samples, not individual packets or exact connection lifetimes; the details ranking and rates continue to show the latest observed snapshot. World traffic ranks remote IPs over a rolling thirty-second observed window, then locates only the top forty using cached ip.sb city lookups. Details show city (or region) and country; arcs use only valid returned coordinates, omitting IPs without coordinates. State that IP locations are approximate in the details dialog, which also carries the sampling caveats and ip.sb attribution. The detailed administrative map adds country, province/state and major-city names progressively on zoom, stopping at regional detail because IP locations are approximate; it sits in a bounded panel below the page heading, with no text overlay or close button. Country fill colors distinguish geography and carry no traffic or status meaning. Traffic has no GeoIP city, region or country labels. Map labels use bundled geography and local fonts, without fetching an external basemap. Show their share of observed traffic in the details dialog, and retain unknown locations in that denominator. Never imply zero activity is a failed read, or sampled conntrack bytes equal whole-router totals. Details name short-connection and bypass limitations, warm-up, counting-disabled and unavailable states.

Distinguish loading, read failure, unknown, empty, disabled and healthy states. No response is not an empty rule set; saved configuration is not proof of a running service or end-to-end connectivity. Use neutral pending/unknown styling, an explicit error and a retry where useful. Name configuration counts as such.

Firewall monitoring retains semantic permission categories and adds incoming source as a separate dimension. Use one vertical diagram with three visual rows: external semantic categories at the top, one virtual OLR / Firewall node in the middle, and LAN/trusted and local categories at the bottom. Both outer rows show arrivals at OLR, not an external-to-LAN forwarding path. Each category shows its name and packet count; position conveys source and color conveys the Allowed/Blocked decision. Keep full source and decision text in tooltips, without repeating them on each node. Omit explanatory paragraphs and the matching-conditions disclosure below the diagram. Hide zero-traffic categories and sources. Path widths use log(1 + packet count) weights normalized separately for each side, with a 4px minimum so small categories remain visible. Retain exact packet labels and byte totals and matching conditions in tooltips. Keep unavailable counters distinct from a verified zero-traffic state.

Show QoS as saved configuration until enforcement exists. Device details group stable identity and saved settings on the left, live uplink, priority and live traffic on the right. Reuse Overview rate meters with Download and Upload labels beside narrower bars, without arrows. Total below Upload shows download then upload with the Overview arrows, added up over the same retained history the title matrix draws, so a reader can check it against the cells above it; it states no window of its own, because the matrix beside the title already is that window's picture. Unavailable history shows dashes. Services below Group lists matching configured services as icons that open their webpages, with an equally sized add action that opens Ingress and prefills the current device. Empty lists show only the add action. Devices without a reserved name/address prefill their observed host instead. A device whose source of a name is gone keeps the name it last announced: rows and lists show it as the device's name, and its page says under the title when that name was last heard. A name field offers it as the last known name rather than as what the device calls itself, and nothing is saved as the operator's name unless the operator saves it. A device that dialed in draws the same row, matched by its tunnel address, and its add action prefills that address rather than a device reference. Group is a tag that opens its edit dialog. Compact Uplink and Priority segmented selectors lead the right column, in that order. Uplink selections retain network-change confirmation and apply feedback. On desktop, pair Vendor with Uplink, MAC with Priority, IP with Download, Group with Upload and Services with Total in shared rows. Place read errors and traffic availability messages after those rows so they do not shift the corresponding values. The title's activity matrix shows one day per column, newest on the right, and six four-hour periods from top to bottom. The displayed date range adapts to the available width, with fixed square cells; dates without retained history remain explicitly missing data. Leave future periods blank and show download/upload totals immediately on hover or focus. Format the time as 10-14 4:00-8:00, followed by traffic only; omit sampled/progress wording. A device page reports identity and settings, and leaves presence to the lists and the map. It draws no Last heard and no Way in row, and the hardware address is a fact row rather than a chip beside the title. Lists, the network map and the device dialog still report when a device was last heard, never whether it is online: a DHCP lease outlives presence by hours and the kernel keeps a stale neighbour entry looking complete, so Online would be a claim this box cannot support; Last heard is the fact it can. The one exception is a device that dialed in: every configuration this router renders carries a keepalive, so three minutes without a handshake really is a broken tunnel, and that page alone says Connected; the map draws the same fact as a dot rather than a word. Its Last heard (the handshake) and Way in (the tunnel interface and subnet) stay, because the tunnel is the only thing that can answer them, and its configured name is a fact row in the same place the device page puts its MAC. That page's two actions, handing over a new setup file and editing the device, are one pair in the lower right corner, in the space the counters leave beside the taller facts column; no rule separates them from the facts they belong to. Name the file the button hands over, rather than a category of configuration: the file exists only after the click, and why it cannot be downloaded again belongs to its tooltip and to the confirm dialog that decides the loss. Speed bars open download/upload limit dialogs; keep the configuration-only caveat in those dialogs and save feedback, without a status row. Omit Notes and the QoS heading. Device activity sits at the right of the title bar, without visible explanatory text. Only the current period breathes with live combined download/upload speed: faster traffic means faster breathing; idle or unavailable rates stay steady. Rate updates smoothly change playback speed without resetting the breath. On becoming idle, complete the current breath before settling at full brightness. Historical colors continue to represent accumulated traffic. The lowest nonzero tier (below 10 MiB combined upload/download per four-hour period) uses a stronger neutral gray than zero/missing data; green starts at 10 MiB. Four green levels use the device's retained 90-day four-hour totals at or above 10 MiB, split at 25%, 50% and 75% of the greater of the maximum total and 1 GiB, independently of screen width. These divide the byte range, not the number of cells. Values equal to a boundary use the lighter tier; identical totals share a color, and a flat or single-sample history below 1 GiB follows the same minimum reference. Different devices' greens represent their own relative traffic, not comparable byte quantities. This distinguishes low traffic without implying whether a person is actively using the device. Immediate four-hour hover/focus hints show sampled download and upload or explicitly report missing/unavailable data. Partial samples are not exact four-hour totals. History belongs to the client, not to an address: every address it used, including one it has since dropped, stays part of its matrix and of the total beneath it. A peer, which has no hardware address, is the one card whose history is looked up by address, and the one kind of traffic kept without a client behind it: nothing else is stored under an address, so no total counts traffic that no screen could show. It begins accumulating after daemon startup. Sampling runs every ten seconds and the matrix refreshes every minute; the first reading establishes a baseline. History retains at most 90 days and is restored from SQLite's activity table in /var/lib/open-linux-router/runtime.db after restarts/upgrades. Silently dropped history is not an error state: when the table's address/bucket ceiling is reached the oldest periods go and the matrix simply begins later, so an operator sees a shorter left edge rather than an empty current column. Transactional checkpoints run every minute and on normal shutdown; an abrupt power loss may lose the latest minute. It is not reconstructed from cumulative counters. Changing device addresses can hide samples associated with its previous addresses.

Device Uplink offers Default (inherit interface/system routing) and named exits only. Existing explicit router-connection overrides remain accurately displayed until the user selects Default or a named exit. Use label/value pairs within each device-detail half. Keep units with their inputs and chevrons beside selected values. Lead identity rows with Vendor. Edit addresses and their fixed toggle in a dialog opened by clicking the IP. Show a Fixed tag beside reserved addresses; keep the hover hint limited to DHCP lease information and omit the hostname field. Preserve diagnostic scope: router-originated tests do not measure a downstream device's path. The Inspection switch starts and stops interception directly, without confirmation. Explain credentials, certificate trust and cleanup in the setup guide. It is the device's setting, not a session: it stays where the operator left it across reloads, daemon restarts and upgrades, so no copy may promise a countdown or a temporary window. When the proxy cannot start, the card keeps the switch on, says why beside it and offers Retry instead of showing the switch off. Device Inspection is one card, and its title names the switch in the title bar: no second "Inspection" label sits beside it. The setup gear remains available whether the switch is on or off; QR code, guide link and global retention controls belong in that dialog. The panel remains visible with Inspection off or another device active: Activity shows retained samples and Requests shows saved history. Current DNS queries appear while this device is active. Requests defaults to Saved; its Live choice opens the embedded mitmproxy viewer while active, without adding another card or duplicating its request list. Certificate installation, trust and cleanup belong in the public five-step guide, with the certificate at step two. Saved requests include complete native flows after a captured request completes or fails. Keep the unfinished-request boundary visible: in-flight content may be lost if the proxy stops. Expose history_error as an archiving failure, rather than implying a live response proves it was saved. Saved rows open request and response headers/body previews; identify binary content and truncated previews, and offer the full .mitm download. Search and pagination work independently of current inspection state. Clear saved requests requires an explicit confirmation that names this device and explains that activity and other devices are kept. Activity offers 4-hour, 24-hour, 7-day and 30-day ranges; the total reads "in selected range". Retained samples survive stopping inspection and control-daemon restarts. Sampling occurs while inspection is on; downtime is not reconstructed. Saved-request retention defaults to 30 days and 5 GiB total across all devices on the router; sampled site activity has its own 30-day/64-MiB bound. Always make the shared router scope explicit beside the storage limit and usage; never imply a per-device allowance. Global settings accept 1–365 days and 1 MiB–1 TiB. Lowering limits can remove older saved requests immediately. Sites are named by registrable domain under the public suffix list, so a multi-label suffix such as com.cn is never shown as a site. The DNS section lists Time, Record, Type and right-aligned Answer values without a visible header row and without a switch of its own: the panel's switch already opened it. An accessible search icon in the section heading reveals a compact filter that opens to the left of itself; closing clears the filter. The panel keeps its title bar fixed and expands content downward under one divider below that bar; its sections are separated by headings and spacing rather than by a rule each, and the DNS rows carry no rules. The switch keeps its place at the trailing edge as content changes. WireGuard devices keep DNS as its own card with its own Inspection switch, because their tunnel traffic cannot be inspected; there the card starts closed. Do not promise encrypted DNS blocking beyond the supported protocol and port.

Use download then upload consistently. Device names may supplement an address only when the address uniquely identifies a device. Keep long domains, IPv6 addresses and provider errors readable rather than silently truncating them.

Disclosure and hierarchy

Access groups technology tiles under “Networking”, “Add a way out” and “Add a way in”. Keep WireGuard, Tailscale, NetBird, ZeroTier, Headscale, SSH, SOCKS5, Gateway and HE Tunnel Broker in the directory. Shadowsocks, Trojan, VLESS, VMess, Hysteria, TUIC, OpenVPN and IPsec are outside the product scope. Do not label the directory as proof of legal compliance or describe removed technologies as a statutory list of prohibited products. A technology can appear in both directions; its tile goes straight to the configuration owner for that direction, and a technology OLR does not configure opens its project documentation instead. Remove System default and purpose filters from this page. Use app-style icons above names without enclosing cards. Use project logos for branded technologies, including frp's official icon. SOCKS5 and Port forwarding use reviewed original app artwork with simple flat functional shapes and no lettering; the name remains below each icon. Other unbranded entries retain a capital initial on a tinted tile. The approved HTTP and HTTPS artwork does not introduce directory entries or replace Caddy's mark. Port forwarding is a forwarding rule rather than a remote-access technology, so it is not a tile here; it lives under Advanced with the firewall whose ruleset it shares. Functions and state appear on hover/focus and in the tile's accessible name. External technologies remain explicitly “Not integrated”; broader ecosystem uses are not promises of OLR configuration support. Existing service states remain authoritative.

Tunnel Broker keeps provider details together in one saved assignment, with activation and LAN assignment as separate decisions. Saving defaults to off. Show five sections on one page with sticky step navigation; omit the repeated page introduction and back-link heading. Keep endpoint requirements and change consequences visible; disclose server comparisons and technical explanations.

Overview group headers open the group's detail page directly on desktop and mobile. The unnamed device bucket retains its in-place disclosure. Keep service icons beside the compact activity column, leaving the remaining row width for the device name. Group details lead with parent, device counts and subgroup links beside bulk uplink and priority controls in the device summary layout. Keep current-member scope, replacement behavior and the priority enforcement caveat beside the explicit apply actions; selected values are batch choices, not observed shared settings. List member devices below the summary.

Gateway's landing page is a directory of choices, not a status report. It has six groups, each naming a part of the router and each holding the ways of building that part: Internet (DHCP, PPPoE, a static address), Interfaces & routing (the interfaces, the route table, external rules), DHCP (dnsmasq, and Kea when it lands), DNS (unbound, and the resolvers OLR will offer beside it), Firewall (nftables, firewalld, ufw, port forwarding, external filtering) and Intrusion prevention (fail2ban, CrowdSec). The order runs from the two parts an operator sets up once to the three whose shipped defaults most installs keep, and closes with the two services that act on what the firewall and the daemons log. A choice OLR does not configure — firewalld, ufw, fail2ban, CrowdSec — links to the project's own site and says the setup is external, never claiming a page OLR does not have.

A tile names a choice, never a module and never a mechanism: the word on it is the one an operator would use to pick it, and the sentence that explains it is the tooltip. A choice OLR cannot configure yet keeps its tile, muted and inert, so a group shows what it will contain instead of growing a tile at a time; it is not an external setup and the tooltip says so plainly. A tile that is a link opens the one page that configures the choice, where the switches and the live answer both live — the directory itself holds no switch, no status strip and no draft, and no tile opens a dialog.

Open newly navigated pages at the top so their title and primary information are visible. Preserve section targeting for hash links and scroll for query-only changes.

Default to two content levels: the main information and necessary context. A third level needs a specific reason, such as a consequential safety condition. An explanation is optional, including under a page title. Do not fill every available subtitle or helper slot just because the component supports it.

Entry pages help selection. Operation pages explain execution. Result pages explain outcomes. Do not put protocol implementation details, setup instructions or descriptions of the next screen on every directory card.

Keep information that affects safety or interpretation visible at the decision point: disruptive network changes, authentication consequences, unavailable data, stale measurements and test scope must not disappear as part of simplification. Secondary diagnostics and raw technical evidence can be disclosed separately with clear labels.

Languages and shared terminology

The UI supports English and Simplified Chinese. Keep English source messages and their Chinese translations together through t() and web/src/lib/locales/zh-CN.ts; reuse messages rather than inventing synonyms. Use 网关 for Gateway, 出口 for Uplink / Way out, 接入 for Access, 地址池 for Address ranges and 地址预留 for Reserved addresses. Translate status and actions without changing protocol identifiers, addresses, commands, user names or API data. Keep technical backend errors verbatim so operators can diagnose them.

Language selection is browser-local, persists across reloads and synchronizes between tabs. On first visit, use Chinese for a Chinese browser preference and English otherwise; unsupported languages fall back to English. Switching languages updates the document language and visible controls without resetting forms or restarting queries. Keep the switch available before login and initial setup. New messages without a translation fall back to English. Translate complete sentences with named placeholders when values are embedded; do not assemble new sentences from translated fragments. Keep state decisions independent of copy.

Naming and writing

Use familiar tool names and concise task labels. A diagnostic that is a named upstream project takes that project's full name, which is why the tools directory reads Speedtest by Ookla, Cloudflare Speed Test, Fast.com, LibreSpeed and iperf3 rather than one "speed test" and a service picker: the service is the distinction that helps an operator select one, and each measures a different path. A shortened name would make two entries ambiguous — "Cloudflare" alone also names the tunnel on Access — so the tile carries the same name as its page. Preserve established names and their own spelling, such as Ping, NatTypeTester, Traceroute and iperf3 (all lowercase). Do not invent broad category labels for a single item.

Name a state for what it means for the user, not for how it is carried out. The IPv6 DNS card on Gateway reads IPv6 disabled, not AAAA filtered: dropping AAAA records is one way to reach that state, and the mechanism only answers the question for a reader who already knows the record type. The setting's own page may keep the mechanism's name, because there the operator is choosing it; a status that reports the outcome names the outcome. The Forwarding card follows the same rule: devices reach the internet or they do not, and which sysctl was written is not something the operator can see or act on. The card's title stays the module's own word, because the switch it reports is the one in the Gateway routing card at interfaces#forwarding.

Avoid repeating the title in a description, stating obvious click behavior or adding a generic next-step sentence. Use one short sentence when an explanation is necessary. Keep essential text readable; reducing font size is not a remedy for excessive content.

Keep the footer to the product copyright, Credits, version and the icon-only GitHub, theme and language controls. On desktop, bottom-align the visible content with 12px bottom padding. The row stays on one line, so phones keep the year alone in the copyright instead of the product name the header already carries. Describe the current and next theme, and the language in use and the one a click switches to, in their accessible labels and tooltips, and name GitHub in the accessible label and tooltip of its mark.

Capability and richness

Device icon selection supports the same theSVG library as site logos. Choosing a library logo changes only the picture, preserving the device category. Keep automatic detection available and show a clear empty result for unmatched searches.

Show the real capability set together with consistent visual weight. Keep entries compact enough to scan across the set. Richness comes from recognizable, distinct capabilities, useful data and dependable interactions. Do not inflate it with oversized panels, redundant labels, decorative badges or unavailable features.

Use a consistent ordering. Add grouping when the collection is large enough that groups reduce search effort; add search when scanning the collection becomes burdensome. Five tools need neither filters nor one category per card.

Advanced directory reference

Advanced's goals are quick selection, a current answer and a calm presentation. Its contract is:

  • Three groups with charters: System (the machine and what may reach it), Services (background work for the network), Diagnostics (measurements). Place a feature by its charter, not by which module happens to own it.
  • One tile per destination. Most tiles wear a capital initial on a 64px tinted tile: the tiles of a group share one hue, and the letter carries identity.
  • A tile that names an upstream tool or service takes that name and its mark instead — filling the tile when the mark carries its own backing (NextTrace) and on white when it is a plain glyph (the three internet speed tests). A tile that is a protocol or OLR's own measurement keeps its initial. One destination measures one thing, so the three internet speed tests are three tiles rather than one tile and a service picker.
  • The name below the tile is the whole name, nothing printed under it, and it wraps to a second line rather than being cut off at an ellipsis: two names in one row that both read "Cloudflare…" would defeat the tile. Beyond two lines the name is too long for the directory; the page may carry a longer title than the tile (Admin access opens Administrator access).
  • Function and state appear on hover/focus and in the tile's accessible name.
  • The whole tile is a keyboard-accessible link; no dialog opens on click.
  • There is no intermediate "Tools" page: a diagnostic tile opens the tool.
  • Keep explanations, requirements and results on the individual pages.

Review before shipping

  • Can the primary information be identified without reading every paragraph?
  • Does each supporting line change a decision or explain a necessary constraint?
  • Is any information repeated across title, description, badge and action?
  • Are instructions shown at the step where they are used?
  • Does simplifying preserve warnings, measurement scope and unavailable states?
  • Can users scan the capability set on desktop and find entries on a phone?
  • Do imagery, whitespace and type reinforce the same information hierarchy?

Update both guides when changing a shared presentation contract.

docs.html:
Visual specimen: ui-control-specimen.html. Open it in a browser; it restates the tokens by hand and is illustrative, not built.

This is the shared contract for the five control atoms every page has. It follows the visual guide, the semantic component contracts and the audit that motivated it. Where this document and a page disagree, this document wins; where it is silent, the visual guide applies.

The rules exist to answer four questions the same way on every screen: what state is this thing in, how do I change it, what else can I do to it, and where does that lead. A reader should learn the answer once, on the first page they open.

Principles

  1. One fact, one shape. A state is drawn in exactly one of three shapes, and the shape says what kind of thing is being reported (see §2).
  2. Tone belongs to the word, not to the page. "Running" is green wherever it appears; a page cannot decide otherwise.
  3. The dot carries tone, the word carries meaning. Colour is never the only signal, and the word is never tinted to compensate for a weak dot.
  4. The glyph is the verb. Chevron navigates, pencil edits, ellipsis offers a menu, rotating chevron expands. No glyph is reused for a second verb.
  5. One primary action per region. A page header and a dialog footer each have at most one filled button.
  6. One control per row, one per card header. A second action belongs on the page the row leads to, in the card body, or behind one menu (§6).
  7. Off is not a fault, and "I cannot see" is not a fault either. The only red things on a page are things that are broken and that this page can fix.
  8. Never invent a control from a class string at the call site. If a state, switch, button or row action needs a new look, it gets a variant.

1. The five tones

ToneMeansDot (6px / 8px)WordPill
okobserved healthy, working as askedbg-successtext-success-foregroundbg-success/10 text-success-foreground
warnworking but needs a look: drift, degraded, blocked by a dependency, never connectedbg-warningtext-warning-foregroundbg-warning/10 text-warning-foreground
faultbroken or cannot work, and something here can fix itbg-destructivetext-destructivebg-destructive/10 text-destructive
offdeliberately switched off; nothing is expectedbg-muted-foreground/40 filledtext-muted-foregroundbg-muted text-muted-foreground
unknownwe cannot see it: reading, unreadable, never checkedhollow ring: border border-muted-foreground/60, no filltext-muted-foregroundborder border-border bg-transparent text-muted-foreground

Two decisions worth stating explicitly:

  • off and unknown differ by shape, not opacity. Both are neutral, but a filled dot means "we know, and it is off" while a hollow ring means "we have no answer". At 6px an opacity difference is invisible; a ring is not.
  • A failed read is unknown, not fault, because the module is not necessarily broken and the alert carries the error. The one exception is a page's own verdict sentence (§2.3): "Status unavailable" is the top-line answer, and an operator cannot act on a page that cannot read the box, so the verdict escalates unknown to fault — one red thing, at the top, once.

Retire every other neutral: bg-muted-foreground/50, /45, /80, bg-success/70, bg-success/12, bg-warning/15, bg-destructive/12, text-muted-foreground/50, /60.

2. Three status shapes

ShapeOwnsExactly one per…Example
StatusPillthe state of the surface's subjectcard or page headerRunning beside Connection settings
StatusInlinethe state of an item in a list, stack or tablerowdot + Connected in a device row
StatusStripthe verdict for a whole module or pagepage"Handing out addresses" + detail + master switch

2.1 StatusPill

24px tall, 6px radius, 12px medium text, no dot. It is the answer to "is the thing this card is about working?", placed immediately after the card title. Do not use it for tags, values or measurements (§2.4).

2.2 StatusInline

A 6px dot plus a 13px word, on one line, vertically centred with the surrounding text. Two emphases:

  • answer (default): the state is the row's payload — foreground text, medium weight. Used in ListRow trailing, table cells, stack cards.
  • dense: the state repeats down a compact list and the list is about something else — muted word, tone only on the dot. Used only for the Overview module list.

The strip and page verdicts use the 8px dot; inline and dense use 6px. There is no third size.

2.3 StatusStrip

The existing card, with three changes:

  • tone: Tone replaces dot: string. Callers stop writing colour classes.
  • density: 'page' | 'compact'. page is the standalone card (p-4 sm:p-6); compact is the block that DNS and DHCP currently hand-copy inside their landing card (p-5, extra summary rows as children).
  • The master switch, drift row, details disclosure and children stay as they are; the switch is the only switch the strip draws, and the headline sentence names it.

2.4 Data is not status

A measurement (bytes, counts, rates, scores, addresses) is a value, never a pill. The one judgement that stays a pill is a grade — Excellent, Fair — because it is a verdict about a reading, not the reading. Not counted and Nothing yet are off/unknown statuses, not metadata.

3. Words and their tone

Tone is fixed by the word. The dictionary lives in one file (web/src/lib/state.ts) and every screen reads it.

ToneWords
okRunning, Connected, OK, Working, On, Up to date, Delegated, Advertising, Configured, IPv6 enabled, Tunnel, Via exit, Default route, Valid for {days} days
warnNeeds attention, Not yet applied, Not up to date, Behind shared NAT, Renewal overdue, Not answering, Never connected, No cable, No address, Not configured, No network, No route, No default route, Unknown exit, Bypasses the exit, Partial, LAN offline
faultNot running, Down, Expired, Not installed, Not set, Unreachable, Not found
offOff, Disabled, Not needed yet, Blocking, No IPv6, No routes, Not managed, Nothing yet, IPv6 disabled, Not in use, Direct, Loopback, Blocked
unknownChecking…, Reading…, Applying…, Waiting, Unknown, Not checked, Unavailable, Not counted, Status unknown, Asking…, Updating

Domain words stay domain words: DHCP's "Devices disconnect" and DNS's are different events and keep their own labels (features/plan/plan-preview.tsx). Only the tone is shared. Adding a word means adding a row here in the same change.

3.1 One derivation per subject

Three helpers, one per kind of subject, all returning { tone, word }:

moduleState({ enabled, running, drift, blocked, reading, unreadable })
// reading → unknown "Checking…" · unreadable → unknown "Unavailable"
// !enabled → off "Off" · blocked/drift → warn → !running → fault "Not running"
// otherwise ok "Running"

linkState({ present, up, hasAddress })      // Not found · No cable · No address · Connected
peerState({ unknown, online, lastHandshake }) // Unknown · Connected · Never connected · <elapsed>

They replace describeStatus() in routes/dhcp/index.tsx and routes/dns/index.tsx, moduleState() in routes/overview.tsx, describeState() in features/link/interface-visual.tsx and the seven-branch dot={…} expressions in routes/advanced/*.

4. Switches

One size: 44 × 24px, 18px thumb, with a 44px hit area at every breakpoint. Drop the unused size prop rather than shipping a variant nothing uses.

Three legal placements:

PlacementOwnerRule
Setting with a consequenceSwitchField (`variant="panel" \"inline"`)visible label + one-line hint; the label states the consequence, not the mechanism
Master switch for the page's subjectStatusStrip, or a card header beside a StatusPillthe switch is labelled by the subject: aria-labelledby the visible card title, or a visible Label when the title does not name it. sr-only only under the strip, whose headline already names it
Per-row switchlist rowsr-only Label naming the row's object; never a bare switch with only aria-label if a visible word could fit

Never a switch whose label appears nowhere on screen. The defect in today's cards is not the position, it is that the accessible name ("WireGuard") differs from the only visible words on the row (Connection settings, Running), so a screen-reader user and a sighted user are told different things. Point aria-labelledby at the title and the pill, and the two agree without adding a redundant label.

Busy is not disabled. busy sets aria-busy, keeps the switch's contrast, and pairs with a state word that says Applying… (unknown). disabled is reserved for "the router will refuse this" — loopback adoption, missing binary, no tunnel address.

5. Buttons

5.1 Rank

VariantUseCount per region
primarythe one action that commits: Save, Create, Add, Publish, Runat most 1
secondaryeverything alongside it: Settings, Cancel-in-a-form, Add when the page's primary is elsewhereany
quietlow-emphasis actions in dense rows, dialog Cancel, Revertany
dangerdestroys or removes data: Remove, Delete, Forget, Stop publishingany
linknavigation dressed as textany

The ranks are named for their role, not their paint: the old outline is secondary, ghost is quiet, destructive is danger, the old filled secondary is subtle, and the old default is primary. A paint name is now a lint failure rather than a habit.

5.2 Size

SizeHeightTextPaddingMobile
sm32px13pxpx-3min 44px
default36px14pxpx-3.5min 44px
lg44px14pxpx-444px
icon36px—square44px
icon-sm32px—square44px

sm must actually be smaller than default (today both are h-9). Remove icon-xs; use the standard icon sizes for page actions. Overview detail pages use normal navigation and have no floating fullscreen close controls. Icons inside buttons are 16px, never size-5.

5.3 Placement and labels

  • Page header: one primary, right-aligned, PageHeading action. Add is primary when the page's purpose is to add that object (DHCP ranges and reservations, DNS names and blocking, Gateway networks, WireGuard devices, port forwards, DDNS names, Caddy services). It is secondary only when the page already has a primary action.
  • Card header: CardAction, secondary by default, or primary when the card is the page's only object.
  • Dialog footer: destructive action first and left-aligned, then spacer, then quiet Cancel and the single primary commit. The commit verb is the object's verb — Save, Create, Publish — not "OK".
  • Destructive confirmations use danger for the confirming button; the dialog title already says what is being removed.
  • "Apply anyway" and "Take it back anyway" are not destructive. They are the primary action of a warning dialog; the warning is the Alert above them. Today five editors paint them red, which teaches that red means "continue".

5.4 Icon-only buttons

One RowAction component (§6.2) for actions inside rows and toolbars. Anything icon-only carries aria-label naming the object and the verb ("Edit Li's iPhone", "View wan1", "Change iCloud icon") plus a title with the same string. No bare +, ↑, ↓ text glyphs as icons.

6. Row actions: one control per row or header

6.1 The rule

A row or a card header shows at most one control. Not a chevron beside a pencil, not a button beside a switch. Everything else belongs on the page the row leads to, in the card body, or behind the one menu.

The row's jobWhole rowIts one controlExample
Leads to a pagelinkchevron-right 16pxWireGuard device
Opens an editor and has no pagebuttonpencil 16px in a RowActionport forward, DHCP range, DNS name
Shows a settinglink, or static when the control is the pointthat control only, with no chevroninterface row's adoption switch on its own page
Has two or more secondary actionslink or buttonmore-horizontal → RowMenutopology group
Read-only recordstaticnonegateway traffic sample
Expands in place<details>chevron-right 14px, rotates 90°technical details

Corollaries, which are what the rule actually costs:

  • Editing, removing and configuring live on the detail. A row leads to the object's page and the page owns its operations: a WireGuard device's rename, routes and removal are on the device page, not on the list. Where the object has no page, the editor is the dialog and the pencil opens it — so a row that opens a dialog still shows a pencil, and one that navigates shows a chevron.
  • A control displaces the chevron. When a row shows a switch, the row itself is still the link and no chevron is drawn. Two visible controls in one trailing slot is what made the page read as a toolbar per row.
  • A card header shows one control too. The switch when the card is about turning something on; otherwise the one action that changes it. A settings entry that would sit next to the switch becomes a line in the card body (WireGuard's connection settings, SOCKS5's link).
  • A menu is one control. Several operations may hide behind one ellipsis; they may not line up as several icons.

The one place a row expands in place rather than navigating (Disclosure) keeps its rotating 14px chevron, and the two hand-rolled disclosures in features/network-quality/network-quality.tsx should use it.

6.2 RowAction

36 × 36px (44px on phones), 8px radius, 16px icon, text-muted-foreground, hover:bg-accent/60, visible focus ring, positioned after the trailing value with 12px to the card edge. Never one row with three adjacent icon buttons (Overview's site editor has three today): one visible action plus a menu.

6.3 RowMenu

DropdownMenu under a more-horizontal RowAction: minimum 192px wide, 36px items with 16px icons, separators between action groups, destructive item last, align="end", Escape closes, focus returns to the trigger. The trigger's accessible name is "{object} options".

7. Edit

  • One entry per object, and it lives with the object. The list navigates; the page (or the dialog behind its pencil) edits. Nothing is editable from two places at once.
  • The control is the value. Editable values in a property row are the control (select, segmented control, switch, in-place input) — not a pencil beside a static value.
  • One edit entry per entity. Entity → its page → its fields; or, with no page, the row's pencil. Both patterns may not appear for the same kind of object.
  • Inline title editing stays a documented exception for device names only (device-inline-editor.tsx), because the name is the object and the list is where it is read.
  • Tags that open a dialog are buttons. The group tag becomes TagButton (24px, hover, focus, aria-haspopup="dialog"), not a Badge wrapped in a Link whose destination is a dialog.
  • A dialog's own destructive action lives in its footer, styled danger, and confirms first if it is irreversible.

8. Tokens and files

FileOwns
web/src/components/ui/status.tsxTone, StatusDot, StatusInline, StatusPill; tone → class maps
web/src/lib/state.tsWORD_TONE, moduleState, linkState, peerState
web/src/components/ui/row-action.tsxRowAction, RowMenu, RowChevron
web/src/components/ui/button.tsxranks renamed, sizes corrected
web/src/components/ui/switch.tsxbusy, no dead size
web/src/components/layout/status-strip.tsxtone, density, compact copy adopted by DNS/DHCP

Only the tone maps know Tailwind colour classes. Charts, maps and the alert component keep their own scales, because hue means something else there.

Portability across apps

These five primitives depend only on the theme tokens and cn(): no routing, no queries, no i18n beyond label props. WORD_TONE is the only product-specific file. To reuse the language in another app, copy status.tsx, row-action.tsx and the button variants, restate WORD_TONE in that product's words, and point the tokens at its palette. Keeping them in one folder is what makes that a copy rather than a refactor.

9. Migration

Each phase ships on its own and is verifiable by screenshot.

PhaseChangeFiles
P0Add status.tsx, state.ts, row-action.tsx; StatusStrip accepts tone/density; implementations emit today's classes so nothing moves4 shared files
P1Words and tones: adopt helpers, one dot size pair, hollow unknown, retint Running/Unavailable/Off, compact strip in DNS and DHCP, grade pill via StatusPill, tags out of Badgeoverview, gateway/*, link/*, dial/uplink-card, remote/*, dhcp/index, dns/index, advanced/{ddns,caddy,iptv,forwards}, nat/forward-list, gateway/exit-list, network-quality, dns/activity, group, devices
P2Buttons: ranks renamed with aliases, sm 32px, one primary rule, Apply-anyway → primary (6), Cancel → quiet (5), Remove → danger (2), Add hierarchy (10)components/ui/button.tsx + every route listed in the audit §5
P3Rows: pencil grammar for the 9 dialog rows, chevron geometry and opacity, RowMenu adoption, Overview site actions, Caddy external linkthe 9 rows + list.tsx + topology/nodes.tsx
P4Switches: visible labels on WireGuard/SOCKS5, DNS query-log into SwitchField, pool-dialog label, busy vs disabledremote.tsx, socks-card.tsx, dns/index.tsx, dhcp/pool-dialog.tsx, switch.tsx
P5Docs and guard: visual guide "Controls, lists and dialogs", semantic inventory (StatusIndicator shipped → StatusInline/StatusPill; add RowAction), page-review record, screenshotsdocs/*, web/scripts/test-control-language.mjs

Guard test

web/scripts/test-control-language.mjs (node, like test-interface-traffic.mjs) fails the build when:

  • a tone colour class appears outside the status/alert/badge/chart allowlist;
  • a size-2.5 or size-1.5 status dot appears;
  • <Switch has neither aria-label nor an id with a Label htmlFor;
  • a Button labelled Apply…/Take it back… uses variant="destructive";
  • variant="success|warning|destructive" appears on a Badge outside components/.

10. Acceptance

  • One tone per word, asserted from WORD_TONE; no page chooses a colour.
  • Dots are 6px or 8px; off is filled, unknown is a ring; fault appears once per page, in the verdict.
  • Every status has a word; every ring/dot has an accessible label.
  • One primary button per page header and per dialog footer.
  • Every interactive row's glyph matches its behaviour; no chevron opens a dialog.
  • Every switch has a visible label at card/page level and 44px targets on phones.
  • npm run lint, npm run build, npm test, make check; screenshots at 375 / 768 / 1440 in both themes for Overview, WireGuard, a Gateway stack, DNS, one dialog and one tool result.

11. Choices worth arguing about

These are deliberate, reversible, and would change what a phase looks like:

ChoiceWhat it costsThe alternative
unknown is a hollow ring, not a fourth opacityone visual idea to learnkeep neutral grey and accept that "off" and "cannot see" look identical
A failed read is unknown per module, fault at the verdicttwo rules instead of onered every module row, which is today's Overview and makes one bad read look like three outages
Row states become dot + word instead of a pillfour screens change (peer list, port forwards, exits, DDNS)keep pills in rows and accept two status shapes side by side
sm becomes 32px66 call sites shrink by 4pxleave sm at 36px and delete the name, so "small" keeps meaning "not small"
Variants are renamed primary/secondary/quiet/danger161 call sites, staged with aliaseskeep paint names (outline, ghost) that do not say the rank
"Apply anyway" becomes primarysix dialogs look less alarmingkeep red, and teach that red means "continue"

12. Non-goals

  • Not a design-system package, and not a component per text size.
  • Domain wording is untouched; the plan-impact labels stay per module.
  • Chart, map, Sankey, activity-matrix and radar colours stay domain scales.
  • The Overview hero tile, the status-strip sentence and the map's peer dot are deliberate one-offs and keep their documented behaviour.
  • No optimistic writes or apply-pipeline changes: this is presentation only.
