docs.title: IPTV multicast
docs.summary: OLR can proxy IPv4 IGMP subscriptions from named LAN networks to a separate, operator-provided IPTV upstream interface. It does not create VLAN interfaces, bridge Ethernet, relay the provider's DHCP, perform STB authentication, or proxy IPv6 MLD. The STB remains a normal client of the LAN. This works only when the provider accepts routed multicast from a proxy and the STB can obtain its service information without sharing the modem's L2 segment.
docs.html:
OLR can proxy IPv4 IGMP subscriptions from named LAN networks to a separate, operator-provided IPTV upstream interface. It does not create VLAN interfaces, bridge Ethernet, relay the provider's DHCP, perform STB authentication, or proxy IPv6 MLD. The STB remains a normal client of the LAN. This works only when the provider accepts routed multicast from a proxy and the STB can obtain its service information without sharing the modem's L2 segment.

Install igmpproxy on the router and ensure its distribution unit is not running; OLR runs a separate olr-iptv.service with a dedicated rendered file. The package intentionally does not depend on the distribution's daemon package: installing it may start a second, unconfigured service. Create the IPTV interface (or tagged VLAN) with your host network manager, olr adopt <iface>, and ensure it has an IPv4 address and a route toward the provider multicast source. OLR does not assign addresses on the IPTV upstream. IPv4 forwarding must be enabled (normally by the OLR gateway module).

The WebUI provides the same flow under Advanced → Services → IPTV multicast: select the adopted upstream interface and downstream LAN, preview, then enable. The page reports proxy service state and validation errors. Interface/VLAN creation and installing igmpproxy remain host setup outside this page.

olr iptv set --upstream iptv0 --network lan --dry-run
olr iptv set --upstream iptv0 --network lan
olr iptv status
olr iptv disable

If the multicast source addresses are outside the upstream interface's connected prefix, repeat --source 10.0.0.0/8 (with the actual provider prefix). The source list is passed as altnet to igmpproxy. OLR admits only IPv4 multicast from the chosen upstream to selected LAN interfaces when its firewall is enabled. No viewer means no joined stream, but a switch/AP without IGMP snooping may flood an active stream across its ports or wireless airtime. Test AP latency and throughput while watching TV.

Diagnostics: olr iptv status, journalctl -u olr-iptv, and ip mroute. Check for downstream IGMP membership, an upstream multicast source, then a kernel multicast route. A working proxy does not guarantee provider-specific DHCP, portal, or authentication succeeds. Dynamic changes to the underlying interface or LAN membership may require olr iptv set again to restart the proxy. Do not bridge the IPTV interface into the household LAN.

docs.title: IPv6 controls
docs.summary: DNS, address acquisition, DHCP advertisements and gateway forwarding are independent decisions. Changing one does not change the others.
docs.html:
DNS, address acquisition, DHCP advertisements and gateway forwarding are independent decisions. Changing one does not change the others.

DNS answers

Gateway → DNS and DNS → Resolving both expose Resolve IPv6 addresses (AAAA). Turning it off sets dns.filter_aaaa and returns successful empty answers (NODATA) for AAAA queries before local names, policies or upstream selection. A queries and other record types keep their usual behavior. This applies over both UDP and TCP, including queries that would otherwise use an exit's DNS server. Existing client caches remain until they expire.

The CLI equivalent is olr dns set --filter-aaaa; olr dns set --filter-aaaa=false restores AAAA answers.

Automatic interface addressing

Gateway → an interface → Automatically obtain IPv6 addresses controls link.ipv6_auto[interface]. It requires an adopted interface. An absent setting leaves the host configuration alone; it does not mean automatic addressing is enabled. An explicit off stops kernel SLAAC and the dhcpcd IPv6 client. On enables SLAAC even when this router forwards traffic, and enables dhcpcd IPv6 unless OLR already owns the uplink's prefix-delegation client.

Static IPv6 addresses, LAN advertisements, gateway forwarding and DNS are unchanged. Existing dynamic addresses may remain until their leases expire. Prefix delegation is also a separate uplink decision and continues when configured. No new DHCPv6 client is installed or started by this switch.

Settings are reapplied when the daemon starts. Original kernel settings are saved before the first change and restored when the override is removed or the interface is released. Host configuration changes are confined to OLR's existing dhcpcd block. Interfaces managed by NetworkManager, systemd-networkd or dhclient are refused rather than reporting success while another manager can overwrite the setting. Kernel writes and partial failures are reported by the existing apply flow; interface changes require its disruption confirmation.

docs.title: Latency
docs.summary: GET /api/gateway/latency returns the latest background measurements without starting network traffic. Internet and custom sites use the same metric: one HTTPS HEAD request, timed from acquiring the established connection to receiving the first response byte. DNS, TCP and TLS setup and document downloads are excluded. This is an application round trip, including server processing, not ICMP ping or a page-load measurement. There is no repeated sampling or aggregation.
docs.html:
GET /api/gateway/latency returns the latest background measurements without starting network traffic. Internet and custom sites use the same metric: one HTTPS HEAD request, timed from acquiring the established connection to receiving the first response byte. DNS, TCP and TLS setup and document downloads are excluded. This is an application round trip, including server processing, not ICMP ping or a page-load measurement. There is no repeated sampling or aggregation.

Each probe has a 15-second deadline. Connections are fresh, environment proxies are ignored and TLS certificates are verified. Redirects are not followed. Any HTTP response, including errors and redirects, establishes response latency; it does not assert that the application is healthy. A proxy accepting TCP or answering ICMP locally cannot complete this authenticated HTTPS exchange on behalf of an unreachable destination. Sites that reject HEAD can still return a measurable HTTP error response.

Internet candidates use the router's default route. A monitored site can choose a gateway exit; the probe then uses both halves of that exit: its DNS setting selects where the name is resolved (mode exit uses the next hop on port 53, custom the configured server, olr or none the router resolver), and the TCP socket carries the exit's current routing mark on Linux. This matches what a client of that exit experiences, including a fake-IP resolver whose answers only the paired gateway can use. DNS time remains outside the sample; timing starts once the connection is established. If a chosen exit is removed, disabled or unsupported, no default-route fallback is attempted. The DNS row independently times one lookup of example.com through the router.

The built-in Internet choices are Google, Baidu, Yandex and Cloudflare. With no saved target, one round probes each once and saves the fastest successful target to gateway.latency_target in olr.json. Subsequent rounds measure only that target, including after restart. Failure never changes the target. If all candidates fail, selection retries on the next one-minute round. The Internet target and DNS continue their one-minute refresh independently of monitored sites. Built-in and custom monitored sites run at minute 30 of each router-local calendar hour, using time.Local; changing the Internet target never triggers an extra site round. On startup before :30 the sampler waits; after :30 it measures only targets without an attempt in the current hour. It never fills earlier missing hours or overwrites a restored/manual current-hour measurement merely because the daemon restarted.

PUT /api/gateway/latency/target accepts {"target":"<listed URL>"}; an empty target requests a fresh selection. Changes wake the background monitor and discard any in-flight Internet result from the old selection. GET stays passive. The test page does not edit it; the route remains for API and CLI clients.

A click on one monitored site measures that site now. POST /api/gateway/latency/sites/{name}/measure answers 202 Accepted with the current snapshot; only the clicked row's measuring flag is set until its probe publishes. A second click while that probe runs is accepted and starts no second probe. POST /api/gateway/latency/measure does the same for every site in one round. API clients can pass ?category=<key> (or custom) to limit probes to that group. The /latency page does not use this batch route: it walks the sites in reading order through the per-site route so one row at a time can show its own probe. The merged table has no category refresh controls. Background rounds leave every row's flag false, so a row spins only where somebody asked. A row keeps its last completed value while the probe runs. Other sites, the Internet target and DNS are left alone. These routes change no configuration; they only ask for probes.

Common sites are part of the binary's catalog, not the operator's document. They are present on a fresh install, always probed, and cannot be removed. The catalog carries one URL per site — the faster of the app's main page and its static asset host, chosen from measurements on the reference router — and a category (communication, social, entertainment, news, shopping or tools). A CDN root may answer 403/404; the probe still counts the response as the edge's latency. A per-operator probe exit lives in gateway.latency_common as {"name":"Google","exit":"Gateway2"}, and omitting an entry leaves that site on the default route.

Up to 20 custom HTTPS URLs can be stored with PUT /api/gateway/latency/sites using objects such as {"name":"NAS","url":"https://nas.example/","exit":"Proxy"}. The same route carries catalog entries: an entry whose name matches a common site updates its exit and is not stored as a custom site. An empty array clears the custom list but not the catalog. exit is optional and must name a configured gateway exit. Names are unique and 1–40 characters; URLs cannot contain credentials, custom ports or fragments. Custom sites live in gateway.latency_sites in olr.json; measurements are stored separately in the runtime database. A custom site saved before the catalog existed, under a catalog name, moves to the catalog with its exit preserved.

The /latency page uses one merged table for catalog and custom sites, grouped into the catalog's categories (communication, social, entertainment, news, shopping, tools) with a final group for custom and uncategorized sites. One row per site and 24 fixed hourly positions for the router's current day (00–01 through 23–24). Each position holds the latest attempt begun in that calendar hour; manual tests replace the same hour's point rather than appending another. Missing hours remain empty, while failed attempts keep their error and a nil measurement. Each row ends with the arithmetic mean of that day's successful samples. There is no per-row test control: Test all asks for each site in turn through the per-site route and keeps the completed results visible; a site that fails or never answers does not stop the rest. Exits and custom sites are changed through the API or CLI; pin selection is the page's configuration exception.

Each row has a pin button before its site mark. An unpinned site's pin is hidden until its row is hovered or the button is focused; a pinned site keeps a primary pin visible, and a coarse-pointer device always shows it because it has no hover. Only that button toggles Overview visibility; the mark and name are not a control. While a pin change saves, its row shows progress and the other pin buttons wait. The homepage Latency card shows only pinned monitored sites; no sites are pinned by default. Pins are router configuration shared by all browsers and survive daemon restarts. They do not affect which sites are probed or their URLs, exits, latest results, hourly history, or in-flight probes.

PUT /api/gateway/latency/sites/{name}/pin accepts exactly one required boolean field, {"pinned":true} or {"pinned":false}, and returns 200 OK with the full LatencySnapshot (including Internet sites and monitored custom). The name is an exact, case-sensitive catalog or custom monitored-site name, URL encoded as one path segment. Missing/null/nonboolean pinned, malformed JSON, trailing JSON and unknown fields return 400 Bad Request; an unknown site returns 404 Not Found, including when unpinning. Missing monitor/configuration or a failed persistence operation returns 503 Service Unavailable.

Repeating the same selection is a no-op. Selection lives separately in gateway.latency_pins as an optional array of monitored-site names; an absent or empty list means none. Successful changes publish the gateway applied event. General gateway configuration changes are reflected in subsequent snapshots. Saving configuration removes unknown/deleted custom-site names and duplicate pins; deleting a custom site through either the site-list API or general configuration therefore clears its pin before the name can be reused. Renaming a custom site clears its old pin; changing its URL or exit under the same name retains the pin. These display selections never enter runtime history.

The response includes state (measuring, ok, unreachable, unavailable), nullable milliseconds, dns_milliseconds, checked_at, the selected target name and target_url, built-in Internet sites and the custom list. local_time is the current router-local RFC3339 time with its UTC offset, read fresh for every snapshot. The custom list holds catalog sites (builtin: true, with a category) followed by the operator's custom sites. A monitored site includes pinned: true when selected for the homepage; false is omitted. It also carries measuring while its on-demand probe runs, and chronological samples: one latest attempt per router calendar hour retained for 48 hours. Each sample has milliseconds, optional error, checked_at (the attempt's start in UTC), and hour_start (the router-local hour's start with its offset). Frontends use the calendar date/hour in local_time and hour_start, so the 24-slot view stays consistent even when the browser and router have different time zones. A repeated daylight-saving hour has distinct instants; a fixed 24-slot display uses the latest attempt for that clock hour. A skipped hour stays empty.

Completed attempts are synchronously upserted to the latency_samples table in /var/lib/open-linux-router/runtime.db, keyed by URL, exit and absolute hour start. Runtime schema 4 adds this table without changing configuration. History survives restarts, expires after 48 hours and has a 10,000-row database bound. Changing a name/icon preserves measurements; changing the URL or exit does not attach the prior target's measurements. The latest-started attempt wins when manual and automatic probes finish out of order; a probe spanning midnight or an hour boundary belongs to its start hour. Daemon cancellation clears progress without inventing a failure. Database read errors are logged and probing stays memory-only; write errors are logged, retain live results, and retry pending samples on the next completion and shutdown. Runtime history is never written to olr.json.

A failed fixed target retains its identity but clears its measurement. Each site carries its latest attempt, nullable measurement and short error. Custom sites keep their last completed outcome while the next probe runs; a completed failure replaces success. Unmeasured sites show a dash, and sub-millisecond results show <1 ms, never a rounded zero. Browser-session caching uses a new hourly-history key; old rolling samples are not merged back into snapshots, because durable history comes from the daemon.

The custom-site API preserves list order and accepts a custom icon. Icons may use automatic favicon discovery through GET /api/gateway/latency/sites/{name}/icon, a PNG/JPEG/WebP image (at most 96 KiB in stored form), or a theSVG icon ID. Uploaded images are stored as validated base64 in the saved site configuration; a theSVG ID names one of the marks bundled in olrd, which is served from the binary and never fetched from a third party (internal/brandlogo). Supplying an icon is independent of the latency probe.

docs.title: MCP surface
docs.summary: design.md §1 calls this project agent-manageable and §6.4 asks for "MCP tools generated from the same schema". This document says what got built, what did not, and which test holds each rule.
docs.html:
Status: the rules below are enforced by internal/daemon/conformance_test.go and internal/mcp/mcp_test.go. A route or tool that breaks one fails the build. Section references are to design.md unless prefixed cli: or dns:.

design.md §1 calls this project agent-manageable and §6.4 asks for "MCP tools generated from the same schema". This document says what got built, what did not, and which test holds each rule.

1. Where it is

POST /api/mcp one JSON-RPC request per call GET /api/mcp 405 — there is no server-to-client stream

Inside /api on purpose. Both listeners already authenticate that prefix — the bearer token on TCP, the socket's mode locally (§6.2) — so the MCP endpoint inherits it rather than growing a scheme of its own. An MCP endpoint mounted outside /api would be an unauthenticated admin surface on a router.

There is no olr mcp subcommand and no second binary. The server is an API client that happens to live in the same process, which is the next section.

Pointing a client at it:

claude mcp add --transport http olr http://<router>:8080/api/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $(ssh router cat /etc/open-linux-router/api-token)"

2. R1 — the MCP package reaches modules only through the API

internal/mcp imports no module package. Every tool call is an HTTP request handed to olrd's own API handler.

This is the rule the whole surface rests on. A tool call crosses the same validation, the same global apply lock (§3.6) and the same event publication that the WebUI and the CLI cross, because there is no other path from this package to a module. internal/webui states the same invariant for the SPA, for the same reason: §1 says all the surfaces are equal clients of the API, and that stops being true the first time one of them can reach further than the others.

The import graph enforces it. Nothing else would: a direct import would compile, the tools would work, and the difference would surface as a change that never reached the UI or a lock that covered nothing.

Held by TestMCPImportsNoModule.

3. R2 — nothing is a list of routes

Tools are derived at startup from /api/routes and /api/schema. A module that adds a route gets a tool without internal/mcp being edited.

Modules declare their surface as data (core.Route), core.Server.Mount builds the handler from that table, and /api/routes publishes it. A module therefore cannot serve a route it did not declare, which is what makes the published list trustworthy enough to generate from.

This is §3.2 rule 3 — one declaration, many surfaces — applied to routes rather than to config fields. The config half was already true; this is the half that lets a route reach an agent without being hand-written twice.

Held by TestToolsAreDerivedFromThePublishedRoutes.

4. R3 — a tool's arguments are the module's own schema, verbatim

A request body reaches inputSchema as the exact bytes core.Reflect produced. Query parameters become top-level properties; the body is nested under config.

Not "equivalent to" — the same bytes. Decoding the projection and re-encoding it through a second JSON Schema implementation would put a translation layer between the struct tag and the agent, which is the thing §8 chose one dialect to avoid, and it would silently drop what that implementation does not model. The $defs that internal/dhcp's pools rely on are a live example.

The body is nested rather than spread across the top level because a route may have both a body and parameters — every mutating route on gateway already carries dry_run and confirm — and a config field named confirm would otherwise be the same argument as the query parameter named confirm.

Plans take the relaxed projection: naming one field must not fail validation for omitting the others (§10).

Held by TestBodySchemaIsThePublishedProjectionVerbatim, TestPlanTakesTheRelaxedProjection.

5. R4 — one operation is named once

A tool's first word is a verb from the shared vocabulary (internal/cli/verbs.go), and the words match the CLI's spelling.

olr dhcp show leases → dhcp_show_leases olr dns show queries → dns_show_queries olr gateway status → gateway_status

Same argument as docs/cli.md's: verb drift is invisible in review, and MCP is the one surface nobody reads by hand, so it is where a "get" or a "fetch" would appear and never be noticed.

This rule earned its place immediately. The dry-run tools were written as dhcp_plan, and the test refused them: plan is not a verb the CLI has, because the CLI spells a dry run as --dry-run on show. They are dhcp_show_plan now — one operation, one name, whichever surface you meet it on.

Held by TestToolVerbsComeFromTheSharedVocabulary, TestToolNamesAreUnique.

6. R5 — every read is published, and no write is

A non-mutating route must declare a Tool. A mutating route must not.

Stated in that direction deliberately. "These routes are tools" needs editing whenever a module gains one, and forgetting is silent — the route works and the agent simply never learns it exists. "Every read must be published" fails loudly, and an exception has to be argued for in the test.

The second half is the increment boundary. §6.2 says a mutating route plans before it writes and refuses a disruptive plan without ?confirm=true, and only internal/gateway implements it; dhcp, dns and clients apply on the first request. Publishing a write today would hand an agent a tool that can drop the LAN with nothing between the model and the change but a tool name in an approval dialog — and the human approving it cannot see from dhcp_set_config that it disconnects them. The 409-plus-plan is what would show them.

So writes wait for the gate. TestNoMutatingRouteIsPublishedYet is deleted in the commit that lands it.

Held by TestEveryReadRouteIsPublishedAsATool, TestNoMutatingRouteIsPublishedYet.

7. R6 — a refusal reaches the model, addressed

A non-2xx response becomes a tool result with isError: true carrying the message and every addressed problem — never a JSON-RPC error.

A JSON-RPC error is handled by the client and never reaches the model, so a rejected config reported that way would leave the agent knowing only that something went wrong. Reported as a tool result it is text the model reads and can act on:

The request was refused (HTTP 422): invalid dhcp configuration pools[0]: start 192.168.1.10 is above end 10.0.0.5

Those are the same bytes the WebUI attaches to a form field and the CLI prints under a failed command — one envelope, rendered once, by core.ErrorBody.String. Writing that renderer is what exposed a defect the CLI had been shipping: dhcp and dns were putting the rendered problems in the envelope's message and in its problems[], so olr printed each one twice. The message summarises; the problems carry the detail.

A protocol-level failure — an unknown tool, an unknown method — stays a JSON-RPC error, because there is no tool to have failed and the model cannot fix it.

Held by TestRefusalIsAToolErrorNamingTheField, TestFailureTextDoesNotRepeatEachProblem, TestUnknownToolIsAProtocolError.

8. The protocol, and why it is written out

internal/mcp implements initialize, ping, tools/list, tools/call and the notifications, over the streamable HTTP transport, stateless. Roughly 300 lines. It advertises 2025-06-18 and negotiates down to 2025-03-26 or 2024-11-05.

The official Go SDK was measured first, not assumed away:

go-sdkwritten out
Go floor1.25 from v1.5.01.23, unchanged
Direct dependencies76, unchanged
Transitive additions8 at v1.7.0, 2 at v1.2.00
Protocol drifttheirsours

The floor is what decided it. design.md §8 commits to go 1.23 on the grounds that nothing needs a newer language version, and Debian 13 — the primary target — has to be able to build this. Taking the SDK means either freezing on v1.2.0, which speaks the same 2025-06-18 this does, or moving the floor for every consumer of the project to get a protocol revision.

And what it supplies is mostly what this server does not serve: sessions, resumability, SSE fan-out, sampling, prompts, resources. A tools-only server is one POST handler.

What we bought is a real liability — the spec revises roughly twice a year — and the mitigation is advertising a revision rather than the newest one. Clients negotiate down. If this server ever needs elicitation, structured content or server-initiated notifications, that calculation changes and the SDK should win.

Stateless, and it costs something. No Mcp-Session-Id, no server-to-client stream, so a tool list that changed mid-connection could not be announced. olrd's tool list is fixed at startup, so today there is nothing to announce.

9. What is not here

  • No writes. §6, above.
  • No resources or prompts. Only tools is declared in initialize, so a client will not ask.
  • No output schemas. §6.2's open gap: config structs are reflected, read and plan shapes are not. Tools return JSON as text, which agents read fine, but it is the same gap that keeps web/src/lib/api-types.ts hand-written. MCP is now the third consumer arguing for closing it.
  • No composite operations. "Set up a guest network" is a core route when it exists (§6.3), not something this package assembles — the same rule that keeps it out of the WebUI.

4. R3 — a tool's arguments are the module's own schema, verbatim
5. R4 — one operation is named once
6. R5 — every read is published, and no write is
7. R6 — a refusal reaches the model, addressed

docs.title: Network equipment
docs.summary: devices owns managed network equipment, its connection settings and brand adapters. It is distinct from clients, the MAC-keyed inventory of things on the LAN, and from link, which configures interfaces on the local router. This increment supplies the backend contract and two adapters; it does not rename the Gateway UI, draw a physical topology, provision a fleet or change local routing.
docs.html:
devices owns managed network equipment, its connection settings and brand adapters. It is distinct from clients, the MAC-keyed inventory of things on the LAN, and from link, which configures interfaces on the local router. This increment supplies the backend contract and two adapters; it does not rename the Gateway UI, draw a physical topology, provision a fleet or change local routing.

Identity and types

A configured device has an operator-assigned stable id (1–64 ASCII letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, starting with a letter/digit), optional name, adapter (mercury, openwrt or huawei), HTTP(S) management origin, username, password environment reference and optional roles. Roles are a set of router, switch, ap, ont: a single device may have several. A fiber ONT is usually ont and router at once, because it terminates the line and routes one WAN. An IP address, interface MAC or SSID is not a hardware identity. Manufacturer/model/firmware/MACs/uptime are observations, separate from the inventory.

Port, radio and wireless network IDs are scoped to the managed device. References must carry the device ID across devices. Mercury port IDs are decimal strings (1 through 9); OpenWrt uses netifd interface names. Names may change if the underlying platform renames an interface. Do not infer stable hardware identity from OpenWrt ifindex or interface name alone.

Data contract

GET /api/devices/contract publishes version: 1 and JSON Schemas derived from the Go structs for devices, snapshots, FDB queries/results and operations. /api/schema publishes inventory config; /api/routes publishes route metadata. Additive optional fields may extend v1; changes in field meanings need a version change.

A snapshot contains:

GroupFields and semantics
IdentityManufacturer, model, serial when known, firmware, hostname, interface MACs, roles, uptime seconds.
CollectionsA status for each independently read section: ok, unsupported, or error; timestamp and sanitized diagnostic. A failed section does not suppress successful sections.
CapabilitiesNamed abilities with supported, unsupported, or unknown, plus an optional reason. Ability to read never implies ability to write.
PortsID/name, canonical kind (ethernet, fiber, bridge, vlan, lag, wireless, other), MAC, parent, members, addresses, administrative enabled and actual link state, speed Mbps, duplex, RX/TX counters and optional Mbps readings, PVID, optional PoE.
VLANsDevice-local VID, name, tagged and untagged port IDs; vlan_enabled separately describes whether the switch's VLAN mode is active. Equal VIDs on separate devices do not prove connectivity.
FDBMAC, optional VLAN, reachable port ID, optional learning type. A lookup is distinct from exporting the whole table.
NeighborsLocal port, remote chassis/port/name, discovery source, optional expiry. Reserved in the common model; neither initial adapter supplies LLDP neighbors.
RadiosID, administrative enabled, band, runtime channel and channel width when known, the PHY standard the radio runs now (protocol) and the standards the driver advertises (protocols), noise floor, transmit power, country and recent channel utilization. configured_width_mhz separately reports the netifd configured width.
Wireless networksUnique device-local ID, radio/interface IDs, SSID, BSSID, mode, encryption mode (never key), netifd logical network names, and the roaming options the access point offers: 802.11r fast transition with its mobility domain, 802.11k neighbour reports and 802.11v BSS transition. Roaming is configuration read back, not a measurement: no client is followed from one BSS to another.
AssociationsClient MAC, wireless network and radio IDs, signal and average signal dBm, noise, connected and inactive time, directional link rates, MCS, PHY standard and width per direction, expected throughput, retries, failed transmissions, bytes and packets, transmit airtime, MFP and WMM state. Each direction can run a different standard, and an empty one means legacy or unreported. Link rate is not throughput. Missing counters stay unknown.
ONTPON mode, registration state, and — from the transceiver — receive and transmit power with the device's own acceptable window, temperature, voltage, bias current, module vendor/serial/date code, wavelengths and LOS. Health: CPU, memory and NAT session count. WAN: one row per carrier service with VLAN and priority, interface (PPPoE/DHCP/static), IPv4 address, gateway and DNS, IPv6 addresses and delegated prefix, uptime and RX/TX counters. Present only for a device that terminates a fiber line.
ScanOn request and outside the snapshot: one radio's neighbours — BSSID, optional SSID, primary channel, width, signal, transport family and security family. Duplicates by BSSID are collapsed and rows arrive in channel order. A scan is a dated sample taken while the radio was off its channel, never current neighbourhood state.

Missing optional metrics mean unknown/unavailable, not zero or false. ok with no rows means a successfully observed empty inventory. An absent row array with unsupported or error is not an empty network. Counts are unsigned 64-bit integers; consumers must preserve integer precision. RX/TX always use the reporting port/AP's own receive/transmit perspective. Counters may reset/wrap; no width or uninterrupted continuity is promised. Mercury RX/TX packet totals count good packets with errors separate, not cumulative bytes.

HTTP calls are sequential observations, not an atomic hardware snapshot. Timestamps bound an observation attempt; separate sections can represent different moments. Reads are on demand and bounded (service request budget 30 seconds), serialized by equipment lane. This increment does not persist snapshots, poll in the background or present old readings as current. A failed poll must not become an offline hardware assertion. In particular, an authentication failure does not prove the network link is down.

Capability vocabulary

Initial canonical keys are identity.read, ports.read, statistics.read, vlans.read, pvids.read, fdb.lookup, fdb.list, neighbors.read, radios.read, wireless.read, associations.read, optical.read, wan.read, ports.configure, vlans.configure, wireless.configure, poe.configure, device.reboot, client.disconnect.

unsupported means unavailable through this implemented adapter/API or current permission set, not a claim about all capabilities of the hardware. unknown means observation could not establish the answer. Missing capability keys must be treated as unsupported by a client. Device-wide operation support means at least one suitable target; preview revalidates the exact target and permissions.

Adapter boundary

The mandatory Go contract is Adapter.Read(ctx, Device) (Snapshot, error). Optional FDBLookup.LookupFDB handles a known MAC, Scanner.Scan(ctx, Device, radioID) takes one dated neighbour sample, keyed by the radio ID the snapshot reports, and Operator.Plan / Operator.Execute handle typed operations. A scan is separate from Read because it interrupts the radio; no snapshot ever contains one. Brand protocol and credentials stay in the adapter; normalization and cross-device topology inference belong above it. The service receives adapters explicitly, without a dynamic plugin loader.

An adapter supplies evidence, not a parent tree. Future topology inference should preserve local/remote endpoints, physical adjacency vs reachability vs wireless association, evidence source, age and uncertainty. Manual links must remain distinct from automatic evidence. Multipath, LAGs and wireless backhaul require a graph, not a single parent ID. This increment exposes the source facts; it does not fabricate inferred direct cables.

Mercury SE109 Pro

Adapter mercury targets SE109 Pro, captured on firmware 1.0.0 Build 20240914 Rel.40108:

  • Reads MainRpm.htm, PortStatisticsRpm.htm, Vlan8021QRpm.htm, Vlan8021QPvidRpm.htm independently.
  • Supports identity, physical ports, Mbps readings, good packet/error counters, VLAN membership and PVIDs. Array placeholders beyond max_port_num are excluded.
  • Parses a bounded subset of JavaScript literals (unquoted keys, single/double quoted strings, hex integers, arrays/objects, trailing commas). It never evaluates JavaScript. Expressions, calls, duplicate keys, excessive nesting and oversized payloads are rejected.
  • Reads firmware password-encoding constants only after matching the captured algorithm; an unknown algorithm is refused before submitting a password. Uses an isolated CookieJar, at most one password login per operation, a dynamically obtained g_tid, default TLS validation and no redirects.
  • Known-MAC lookup calls mac_address_search.cgi with the captured form fields. Full FDB export, LAG result numbering, LLDP, byte totals, PoE and remote writes are not implemented. MAC lookup requires successful runtime parsing; nonempty lookup results are covered by synthetic protocol fixtures, not a new live-hardware verification.

The sanitized fixtures derive from the earlier read-only research captures. No password, SessionID or live token is committed. Firmware changes require compatibility verification.

OpenWrt

Adapter openwrt speaks uhttpd ubus JSON-RPC at <origin>/ubus. The device needs uhttpd ubus/rpcd available and an account with appropriate ubus ACLs. There is no SSH/remote shell fallback. Username defaults to root when omitted; a dedicated account with only the required methods is also supported.

Read methods: system.board, system.info, network.device.status, network.interface.dump, network.wireless.status, per-AP hostapd.<ifname>.get_status and get_clients. Optional iwinfo.info and iwinfo.assoclist enrich the radio with the running PHY standard, width, noise, transmit power and country, and clients with signal, counters, rates, MCS, per-direction standard and expected throughput. netifd's status does not carry every wifi-iface option, so the roaming flags are also read from LuCI's read model when netifd answered; a build that reports them nowhere leaves roaming absent rather than off. iwinfo.scan answers only an explicit per-radio neighbour request, under a 25-second per-call bound instead of the usual 8. When a build does not grant netifd's wireless object or hostapd's status and client methods to the management session, the adapter falls back to LuCI's read model (luci-rpc.getWirelessDevices) and iwinfo.assoclist; utilization, MFP/WMM and airtime then remain unknown rather than failing the section. iwinfo.survey is not used: the tested firmware denies it, so there is no measured per-channel airtime to show. Scan results publish no hidden SSID guess and no key material — only the beacon's own SSID, which is empty for a hidden network. Wireless keys returned inside netifd configuration are discarded and never included in snapshots/errors. Runtime method/permission failures are reported by section. Netifd's generic Network device does not establish Ethernet media, so its port kind remains other.

Stock portable ubus does not expose the bridge FDB, switch VLAN/PVID table or LLDP neighbors used by this adapter; these remain unsupported. Different hostapd/wpad/rpcd builds can expose different methods. AP role can be observed from AP interfaces; full router/switch role detection is not inferred merely from OpenWrt being installed.

Only client.disconnect is implemented as a remote mutation. It validates a unicast MAC and an observed AP interface, reads hostapd status, checks del_client method signature and checks session ACL permission. It sends addr, deauth: true, reason: 5, ban_time: 0. This disconnects rather than permanently blocks a client; it may reconnect immediately. SSID/channel/VLAN/port configuration and reboot are not implemented.

OpenWrt protocol fixtures are synthetic, matching the supported stock API shapes; this change has no live-device compatibility claim. An actual firmware/account combination should be checked with a snapshot before relying on its reported capabilities.

Huawei ONT

Adapter huawei reads the web management pages of a Huawei fiber ONT: the OptiXstar line and the HG-series before it. The pages are the carrier-customized ones (BJUNICOM, GDCU, JSCU …); the build only changes branding and which menu entries are hidden, not the status trees this adapter reads. The adapter is therefore named for the vendor, not for the operator that shipped the box.

Login is the challenge the ONT's own login.asp performs: POST /asp/GetRandCount.asp returns a single-use token, and POST /login.cgi answers UserName, base64 PassWord, Language and x.X_HW_Token, replying with a session cookie whose name differs between the HTTP and HTTPS UI (Cookie / CookieHttp). The adapter holds that cookie explicitly rather than in a jar, sends no cookie to the token request, and follows no redirect. A rejected login is reported once and never retried in a loop: each retry spends one of the ONT's three attempts and starts a one-minute lockout. Username defaults to user, the normal-user account; the admin account (CUAdmin on most carrier builds) is not needed for status pages.

Each status page publishes its table as JavaScript constructor calls, for example new stDeviceInfo(...) or new WanPPP(...). The adapter reads the argument lists as data through a bounded scanner — quoted strings with \xNN escapes, bare numbers, at most 256 rows of 128 arguments in a 4 MiB page — and never evaluates the page. Field positions are the constructor's own published order; a page with too few arguments is reported as unreadable instead of being guessed at.

Pages read, each a separate collection:

  • /html/ssmp/deviceinfo/deviceinfo.asp — model, serial, hardware/software version, MACs, uptime, PON mode and state, customisation code, CPU/memory/NAT.
  • /html/amp/opticinfo/opticinfo.asp — transceiver readings plus the opticTxRxRef window, parsed from the page's own notation (0.6-5.6dBm:-28.5--10.0dBm).
  • /html/amp/ethinfo/ethinfo.asp — four LAN ports from geInfos joined with LANStats counters on the LANPort.N index, and the uplink mode from stConfigPort. Counters are 32-bit pairs recombined; a pair that would overflow is reported absent, not wrapped.
  • /html/bbsp/common/wan_list_cache_wan.asp — the WAN list, joined by instance path with get_wan_list_ipwanstat.asp / get_wan_list_pppwanstat.asp counters and with wan_list_cache_wanipv6.asp addresses and prefixes (joined on the PVC's MAC, the only field both views carry).

The PON link appears as a fiber port ahead of the Ethernet ports, because its state comes from the transceiver rather than the Ethernet table. PPPoE passwords arrive as the ONT's own placeholder text and are dropped; usernames are kept because they identify the service. Wireless, VLAN, MAC-table and neighbour reads are not claimed: this firmware has no such API, and a snapshot with no radios must not look like a device whose radios were off.

The page layout and constructor order were captured from an OptiXstar V271-20 on V5R023C10S328 (Beijing Unicom build) reachable over HTTP. Fixtures are trimmed and sanitised: serial numbers, MACs, addresses, IPv6 prefixes, module serial and BRAS name are replaced, and the PPPoE password is already the device's own redaction. Firmware that reorders a constructor is detected as an unreadable section, not silently misread.

Web page

/devices is the inventory in the WebUI: one row per managed box, with its adapter, management origin and roles, and one page per device at /devices/{id}. Adding, editing and forgetting happen there, through the same dialog the Wireless page uses for its access point; the empty state offers a switch or an access point and stores the management password in the configuration, so onboarding never requires setting a variable in olrd's environment.

The page below /devices/{id} is read-only, and which page it is follows the adapter — the inventory's device type. Each type answers the questions that device can answer, in its own tabs and its own words:

PageTabsShows
Switch (mercury)Overview, Ports, VLAN, MAC lookupIdentity and the state of every collection this read attempted; link state, speed, duplex, counters and errors in the device's own port order; device-local VLAN membership with tagged and untagged ports and whether VLAN mode is active; a bounded fdb.lookup for one address, VLAN optional.
OpenWrt (openwrt)Overview, PortsIdentity, uptime and the collection states; the port table; a radio and client count that links to /wireless.
Fiber ONT (huawei)Line, WAN, PortsPON mode, registration, carrier build, CPU/memory/NAT, and the transceiver's readings against the window the ONT publishes; one row per carrier service with its service VLAN and 802.1p priority, address, IPv6 prefix and counters; the PON line and LAN ports.

Wi-Fi stays on /wireless: an access point's radios, clients, channels and scans are a view of that device, not a second copy of it, and the OpenWrt page shows only a count and a link. An ONT's VLAN is a carrier service tag on a WAN row, never switch port membership: the two mean different things and do not share a table. roles still records what a box is in the operator's words, but the adapter picks the page, because a role set cannot tell a switch page what a switch page says — and a shared page can only be the union of every type's concerns, with unsupported capabilities used to hide the parts a box was never going to have.

Each view reports the collections its own read attempted, with the adapter's reason for any it could not obtain, so a section that failed is never drawn as an empty table. The device's capability list stays on every page as a disclosure, as evidence rather than as a tab filter: a box that cannot read VLANs has no VLAN tab, not a greyed-out one.

The list is configuration only. Opening a device is what contacts it — the daemon reads on demand and nothing polls the hardware from the page, so a row does not claim liveness it has not observed. A section the adapter cannot read renders as unavailable with the adapter's reason, never as an empty table.

The URL is /devices, not /network: in this product a network is the subnet object Gateway serves (and /gateway/networks already redirects to DHCP), while /api/devices is the module's own route prefix. The page and the API are deliberately not named the same thing, because they are not the same noun.

Inventory and secrets

Inventory lives in the devices subtree of the existing configuration store, with strict decoding, shared apply lock, ETags and preservation of other modules. Configuration backup includes the inventory and validates it on restore, without connecting to equipment.

A device's management credential is either stored in the inventory as password, or named by password_env, which points at a variable in the daemon process environment rather than the shell running an API client. A stored password wins when both are present. The page's add/edit dialog writes the stored form, which is what makes an access point usable without changing the daemon's environment; password_env remains for deployments that keep credentials outside the configuration file.

Every read surface replaces a stored password with ******** (network.RedactedSecret), and sending that mask back means "unchanged", so a form nobody retyped cannot overwrite the real credential with asterisks. The value never appears in responses, events or error bodies. Like the DNS credentials already in the same document, a stored password travels with a configuration backup: treat a backup file as credential-bearing, and re-enter the password after restoring onto a different host if that is the policy.

HTTP origins can be LAN addresses. HTTPS validates the host's trust chain; the API has no insecure-TLS bypass. Redirects are refused to avoid sending login material elsewhere. HTTP is supported for equipment whose management UI only offers HTTP; choose a trusted management network.

Example inventory:

{
  "network": {
    "devices": [
      {"id":"core-switch","name":"Core switch","adapter":"mercury","address":"https://mercury.example.net","username":"admin","password_env":"OLR_MERCURY_PASSWORD","roles":["switch"]},
      {"id":"living-room","name":"Living room AP","adapter":"openwrt","address":"https://ap.example.net","username":"root","password_env":"OLR_AP_PASSWORD","roles":["ap"]}
    ]
  }
}

HTTP and CLI

Routes below are relative to /api/devices:

Method/pathMeaning
GET /configStored inventory, no remote reads.
PUT/PATCH /configReplace/merge inventory only. Arrays follow normal merge-patch replacement.
PUT/DELETE /{id}Add/replace/forget one inventory entry. Does not change hardware.
GET /contractVersioned model schemas.
GET /{id}/snapshotFresh observations with collections/capabilities.
GET /{id}/capabilitiesFresh device capability assessment (performs reads).
GET /{id}/fdb?mac=…&vlan=…Known-MAC lookup; VLAN optional.
POST /{id}/operations/planRead-only preview; JSON Operation, or query kind, target, mac for generated MCP clients.
POST /{id}/operations/executeJSON {operation, confirmation} from preview.

Invalid input returns 400, unknown device 404, unsupported ability 422, stale/used confirmation 409, upstream failure 502, timeout 504. A successful snapshot may contain failed sections; inspect collections, not just HTTP status. Error bodies follow the existing core error envelope and omit remote HTML, tokens, passwords and credential-bearing URLs.

olr devices add core-switch --adapter mercury --address https://mercury.example.net --username admin --password-env OLR_MERCURY_PASSWORD
olr devices add living-room --adapter openwrt --address https://ap.example.net --password-env OLR_AP_PASSWORD
olr devices show config
olr devices show contract
olr devices show snapshot living-room
olr devices show capabilities living-room
olr devices show fdb core-switch --mac 02:11:22:33:44:55 --vlan 1
olr devices show operation living-room --target phy0-ap0 --mac 02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee
# After reviewing impact, use the same operation and returned confirmation:
olr devices set client living-room phy0-ap0 02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee --confirmation '<returned confirmation>'

New CLI responses are structured JSON, including when using the default output mode. --dry-run on add/remove prints inventory intent without saving; on set client it returns a preview without disconnecting.

Execution confirmation is random, process-local, valid for five minutes and bound to the full configured device plus exact operation. It is consumed before calling the adapter, including failed or ambiguous calls. A changed inventory entry invalidates an old plan. Do not automatically re-plan/replay after a timeout: re-read device state and obtain a new user decision. Accepted responses are not reported as verified disconnections. Confirmation does not promise transactionality or rollback on the remote hardware.

MCP projects read routes and operation preview from the same route table. Inventory writes and remote execution are intentionally not published as MCP tools, matching the repository-wide current write-publication policy.

Verification

Run go test ./internal/devices ./internal/mcp ./internal/daemon ./cmd/olr and make check. Tests use httptest for authentication, protocol shape, permission checks, partial failures, numeric precision, malformed input, response limits, redirects, context cancellation and non-replay. No test modifies real network equipment.

docs.title: Network quality
docs.originalTitle: Network quality: measurement and scoring design
docs.summary: Provide a broad, explainable network assessment across real services and networks, rather than a single speed test against one arbitrarily chosen server. An operator should be able to expand a category into service results, then inspect the measurements and path that explain a result.
docs.html:
Status: stage 1 reference assessment implemented; broader coverage is a design proposal. The five top-level categories, simple aggregation rules and overall point budgets are agreed. Individual tests, endpoint choices, per-metric scoring curves, internal category weights and release boundaries still need review. This document is a capability roadmap, not a claim that these tests already exist. The Overview radar now displays measured results; the implementation scope and initial curves are listed in §13.

1. Product goal and scope

Provide a broad, explainable network assessment across real services and networks, rather than a single speed test against one arbitrarily chosen server. An operator should be able to expand a category into service results, then inspect the measurements and path that explain a result.

The five categories are:

CategoryQuestion answered
SpeedHow quickly can this connection transfer data to and from different services?
LatencyHow long do network and service interactions take?
StabilityHow consistently does the connection perform, including under load?
FunctionalityWhich services, protocols and connection capabilities work?
Wi-FiHow well do observed wireless links perform?

OLR serves users in every region. Do not divide targets, results, profiles or scores into domestic/international groups or assume a user's home country. Organize targets by service, provider/network and capability. Geography, where known, can describe an actual endpoint or measurement location; it must not define which services a user is expected to use. Test profiles can select services and use cases, independently of region.

Coverage is intentionally incremental. An unimplemented test is not a failed test. A comprehensive design does not require every test to run in every session. Default measurements originate at the router over its default route; selected exits and client-originated measurements are separate scopes. Router results must not be presented as measurements of every client's experience.

2. Targets and measurement methods

Separate the target catalog from measurement methods and score calculations. One target can supply evidence for several categories. A single connection can, for example, produce connection timing and an access result; a download can produce throughput and transfer-variation data. Reuse evidence without repeating traffic or counting the same limitation several times in a score.

Each catalog entry needs a stable ID and version, service/provider labels, supported test methods, endpoint/resource definition, expected response, supported address families and protocols, and time/byte/concurrency limits. Record actual connected IPs and effective endpoints for each run: DNS and CDN selection can change the node serving a resource. Provider attribution needs evidence; a service may use multiple CDNs.

The names below are candidate coverage, not verified endpoint integrations. Before shipping an adapter, establish an appropriate, permitted test resource, its expected behavior, operational limits and maintenance strategy. Some services need authentication, signed media URLs, client execution or a cooperating server. Unsupported integrations remain explicitly unavailable. Do not replace a media test with a homepage fetch and keep the media claim.

Endpoint adapters should distinguish a changed resource, rate limit or service challenge from evidence of a connection failure. Tests must have bounded redirects and resource use. Operator-supplied targets need an explicit target policy rather than inheriting arbitrary redirect or private-address access.

3. Speed

Preserve target-specific results and upload/download directions. Differentiate short transfers, sustained throughput and single/multiple connections.

SubtestCandidate coverageMeasurements
Public CDN downloadCloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, CloudFrontSustained Mbps, transferred bytes, duration, ramp-up time
Additional CDN/network coverageAlibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, Wangsu, Volcengine and other independently operated networksSame measurements, organized by provider rather than region
Video media deliveryYouTube, Douyin, Bilibili, NetflixMedia-segment fetch time, delivery Mbps and sustained delivery capacity
Software/file distributionGitHub Releases, OS/package mirrors and update sourcesDownload Mbps and long-transfer behavior

Cloud storageSupported object stores and file servicesDownload and, with a suitable endpoint, upload Mbps

Use repeatable payloads and record cache/compression behavior, stream count and transfer size. Establish that a resource is large enough for the intended test. A byte-capped or short transfer can yield a valid observed rate without proving the connection's maximum capacity. Non-overlapping throughput tests avoid unintentional contention; intentional concurrent tests are labeled load tests.

Media transfer measurements do not establish actual playback resolution, startup, rebuffering or rendering performance without a player participating. Likewise, one CDN resource does not benchmark every node in that provider.

4. Latency

Keep timing layers separate. The existing Overview HTTPS measurement times an application round trip from an established connection to the first response byte of a HEAD request. It excludes DNS, TCP/TLS setup and document download, but includes server processing; it is not network RTT. See Overview latency.

SubtestMeasurements and interpretation
Client-to-router/local endpointRTT distribution; requires a client-side probe
Upstream pathRTT to responding upstream nodes; nonresponse alone is not a fault
Network RTTICMP round trips to multiple independent supported targets
TCP connectionTCP handshake duration per service/CDN target
TLS connectionTLS handshake duration, recording full/resumed sessions
DNSQuery duration and outcome through the configured resolver path; distinguish controlled cached/uncached cases where feasible
First byteRequest-to-first-response-byte time with explicitly defined timing boundaries
Small request completionComplete response time for a bounded, known small resource
QUIC connectionQUIC/HTTP/3 establishment timing where supported
Service-specific responseComparable measurements for selected video, search, developer, game and cloud service targets

Preserve sample count, median and P95 where enough observations exist. Compute statistics within each target/path/protocol before combining results. A target at 20 ms and another at 100 ms do not imply 80 ms of jitter. TCP, TLS, RTT and first-byte values are different metrics, not interchangeable samples. Server processing contributes to application response time. Record fresh/reused connections and precise timing definitions so comparisons remain meaningful.

5. Stability

Stability includes behavior under load; load responsiveness is a subtest, not a sixth category. Long-term availability is useful historical context rather than a separate radar axis.

SubtestMeasurements
RTT variationWithin-target RTT variation and tail latency, with a versioned statistical definition
Probe lossSent/replied/timed-out counts for a specified protocol and target
Interruptions and recoveryConsecutive-failure events, duration, recovery time and observation coverage

Store the idle baseline and loaded intervals together. Call a baseline idle only when observations support that description; otherwise report ambient traffic or an uncontrolled baseline. Tests that do not actually fill the bottleneck must not claim to measure maximum-load behavior.

ICMP nonresponse can reflect filtering or rate limiting. TCP retransmissions are transport evidence, not a direct measurement of physical-link packet loss. Keep local collection errors separate from network timeouts. A failed single service does not prove a whole-connection outage. Historical availability must report observation gaps; daemon downtime is not measured internet downtime.

Group access results by service, not raw URL count. Wi-Fi results require a stated AP/client/link scope. The router may have no radio or may use an external AP without telemetry. Unknown Wi-Fi quality must remain unavailable rather than being inferred from internet speed.

8. Data model

Use three layers: immutable measurement evidence, windowed metric summaries, then versioned scores. These are conceptual contracts; exact Go/JSON types, storage schema and API routes are implementation decisions for a later review.

8.1 Measurement evidence

Every observation references a finite run or background collection window and records:

Field groupRequired information
IdentityObservation/run IDs, target/catalog version, method/version
ScopeOrigin (router/client), client/AP/link where applicable, requested exit/interface and effective path evidence
ConnectionRequested family/protocol, actual family/protocol, resolved/connected addresses and effective endpoint; DNS path separately
ConditionsIdle/uncontrolled/download/upload/bidirectional load, concurrency, connection reuse and ambient traffic evidence
TimeStart/end timestamps; elapsed durations measured with a monotonic clock
OutcomeSuccess, failure, inconclusive, skipped, unsupported, cancelled or collector error; failure stage and stable reason code
MeasurementsTyped metric-specific values with explicit units, sample counts and bounded time series where needed
ResourcesBytes transferred, duration and applied limits
RelationshipsBaseline/load links and shared evidence IDs across categories

Metric payloads should be a typed union keyed by measurement kind, rather than an unstructured string map. Failed or interrupted runs may preserve valid partial observations, clearly marked as partial. Exclude credentials and signed URL secrets from persisted/displayed endpoint metadata.

8.2 Metric summaries

Summarize comparable observations by target, scope, address family, transport, method and load condition. Keep the window, attempted/valid/failed/error sample counts, freshness, distribution statistics and referenced evidence IDs.

Examples include directional Mbps; per-target RTT median/P95; per-target probe counts and variation; idle/loaded RTT deltas; individual functionality checks; and per-client Wi-Fi metrics. Throughput and load metrics from the same speed test share a run ID. Do not silently mix exits, clients, IPv4/IPv6, idle/load conditions or observations separated by a path/configuration change.

8.3 Score snapshots

A score snapshot records its generation time, catalog version, use-case profile ID/version, scoring version and the scope of each result. Each of the five categories contains:

  • State: measuring, ready, partial, stale or unavailable, plus a reason code.
  • Nullable 0–100 score, oriented higher-is-better.
  • Metric/subtest results and evidence references explaining the score.
  • Actual measurement window and expiration, including per-component times where source measurements differ in age.
  • Coverage: expected, implemented, attempted and usable scored components, their effective weights, and omitted components with reasons.

The snapshot also contains a nullable overall 0–100 score, its state and coverage, and each category's point budget and earned contribution. Preserve unrounded scores for calculation; round only for display. Expose the formula and contributions so the overall result can be explained as a sum of points.

Collection outcome, freshness and score are distinct. No test means no score; confirmed failure is usable evidence and may yield a low score. All RTT probes timing out can establish probe failure but cannot supply a measured RTT of zero or infinity. Unsupported, not selected, not implemented, collector error and tested failure must remain distinguishable.

Snapshot generation time is not measurement time. A fresh background sample must not make yesterday's speed test appear newly measured. Retention and restart behavior must be explicit: a memory-only restart creates observation gaps, and expired history remains historical rather than current evidence.

9. Scoring and presentation rules

Scores are approximate references, not precise predictions of every user's experience. Keep aggregation understandable: normalize measurements to 0–100, then use the following three rules. The reference assessment's initial curves, weights and evidence requirements are defined in §13 and can evolve by version.

9.1 Three aggregation rules

RelationshipRuleExample
Alternative ways to satisfy the same useMaximum scoreEither IPv4 or IPv6 can complete the same service transaction
Different aspects contributing to experienceWeighted addition using fixed point budgetsSpeed, latency and stability contribute separate points
Repeated or representative comparable observationsArithmetic mean, with explicit weights where neededRepeated runs or independent services in the same group

Define the question before choosing the rule. For basic service access, max(IPv4 access score, IPv6 access score) represents either family working. For dual-stack completeness, both families contribute separately. One family working perfectly and the other failing must not reduce the basic access result to 50 merely because two alternatives were tested.

Different CDN/service results contribute to breadth of experience: average them within reviewed groups instead of taking only the fastest service. Balance service/provider weights so extra URLs or repeated samples do not increase a provider's importance. Publish which observations and weights form each mean.

Do not use addition to turn prerequisite stages into partial service success. DNS, connection and TLS may all succeed while the required application response fails; that transaction still failed. Keep stage results as diagnostic evidence. Similarly, alternative paths cannot bypass the prerequisites of the use being tested: record which path actually completed that use.

Each scored component needs a stable ID, a normalization rule, an aggregation relationship, fixed weights/budget where applicable, required evidence and its coverage policy. Not every diagnostic measurement needs to earn points.

9.2 Overall score: a 100-point budget

Keep each radar category on a 0–100 scale. These base weights express the relative importance of categories with usable current results. Normalize their weights to fill 100 points, including when some tests are not implemented yet.

CategoryBase weight
Speed25 points
Latency25 points
Stability25 points
Wi-Fi15 points
Functionality10 points
Total100 points
overall = speed * 0.25
        + latency * 0.25
        + stability * 0.25
        + wifi * 0.15
        + functionality * 0.10

The formula above applies when all five categories are scored. In general:

category = sum(scored component score * component weight)
         / sum(weights of scored components)
overall = sum(scored category score * category base weight)
        / sum(base weights of scored categories)
category effective points = 100 * category base weight
                          / sum(base weights of scored categories)
category earned points = category score * category effective points / 100

Only usable, fresh results enter either denominator. A confirmed zero is a scored result and stays in the denominator. If no category can be scored, the total is null. Every supported assessment can reach 100, regardless of how many future tests remain unimplemented.

For example, scores of 80, 90, 70, 80 and 60 respectively contribute 20 + 22.5 + 17.5 + 12 + 6 = 78 overall points. Show this breakdown in details. Use the same budget-and-addition approach within categories once their internal weights are reviewed. With Wi-Fi unmeasured, scores of 80, 90, 70 and 60 use base weights 25, 25, 25 and 10, giving 77.6 overall out of 100. No geometric means, squared penalties or hidden shortfall multipliers are needed for the overall score.

9.3 Coverage and presentation

Coverage is separate from quality. An unimplemented test is not evidence of a poor network. Exclude unimplemented, unselected, insufficient, invalid and stale results, then explicitly normalize the remaining weights within categories and across categories. The result view leads with category and test scores and keeps the arithmetic out of the page: it never asks a reader to add up weight contributions, and the rule that produces the total is documented here rather than printed on every visit. Each piece of evidence sits under the row it scores, opened by that row, so the page shows one level of claim at a time. An unmeasured Wi-Fi category remains a dash while the measured categories share 100 points. A ready total means the current assessment is scored, not that the entire planned test catalog has been implemented or measured. The UI groups the same reference score into presentation labels — Excellent 90–100, Good 75–89, Fair 60–74 and Poor below 60 — without changing normalization. Missing, cancelled, timed-out and expired results show a dash and no label rather than a number.

For an alternative-path maximum, choose the higher normalized measured score and retain its path evidence. Never treat an unknown alternative as a confirmed failure. Cancelled or timed-out assessments retain partial evidence but do not publish a finished total; running and expired assessments also withhold it.

  • Preserve raw results even when no defensible score formula exists yet.
  • Review absolute versus expected-bandwidth speed scoring. Do not silently use Overview display limits or QoS shaping configuration as the user's target.
  • Group and weight by service/network/capability before aggregation, so adding many URLs for one provider cannot dominate a category.
  • Profiles express chosen services/use cases, with versioned weights. They do not define regional expectations. Scores from different profiles, coverage or formula versions are not automatically comparable.
  • Missing tests never become zero. Show which categories/components supplied the result and which were excluded. Enforce each metric's minimum evidence before scoring, without reserving points for future implementations. Adding scored tests or changing their weights updates the scoring version.
  • Avoid scoring the same outage, NAT restriction or access failure repeatedly just because several derived checks describe it.

The radar retains five axes but cannot turn absent axes into zero or draw an apparently complete measured polygon from missing values. Provide an accessible text/detail view with scores, raw values, freshness, scope and coverage. Do not mix simulated and live scores into a single apparently measured result. This implementation replaces the simulated preview with measured results and a normalized total for the available scope.

9.4 Report layout

The assessment report is one column: an overall-score band, then the five categories. A category opens to its scored tests, and a test opens to the measurements behind it. Nothing is summarised twice and nothing is explained in a block of its own.

  • The overall band carries the score, its grade label, how many categories were scored and the measured coverage. Coverage alone needs a sentence — it does not reduce the score — so it is the one figure with a hover hint.
  • Speed opens to the reference transfer: download and upload in Mbps, the server it used, and the one-server caveat. These numbers are the evidence behind the category, not a second score beside it.
  • Latency, Stability and Functionality list one row per service. Opening a service shows its own attempts, weighted to the question that category asks: DNS/TCP/HTTPS timings for Latency, the ordered success sequence for Stability, and the resource outcome and error for Functionality. Because one set of six attempts feeds all three, the same attempts appear in each, each time showing only the columns that category is scored from.
  • NAT observations are Functionality evidence, not a category and not a score. They appear as a row with no number, say "Diagnostic only, not scored", and explain in their own detail why an observed mapping proves no inbound access.

UI changes update the content guide and style guide.

10. Execution and existing building blocks

Separate lightweight background sampling, on-demand assessment, and specialist tests requiring a client or external peer. A snapshot read must not launch tests. Bandwidth/load tests run on demand initially, with progress, cancellation, duration/byte budgets and controlled concurrency. Only deliberate load tests should compete with another measurement. Report limits and partial completion.

Inbound, P2P and mapping checks need an explicit test lifecycle. Ordinary assessment must not silently change firewall, forwarding, UPnP/PCP or other router configuration. Any temporary listener/mapping needs a bounded lifetime and owned-resource cleanup; its implementation is a separate reviewed step.

See device link testing for local-test scope. Reuse test implementations behind shared measurement interfaces where appropriate rather than invoking existing HTTP handlers from a new scoring system.
