13. Reference implementation: reference-v1 / quality-v3

This is an initial reference assessment, not the complete service catalog. Snapshots identify the fixed reference profile at version 1 separately from the scoring and catalog versions. All measurements originate at the router over its default route, without environment proxies. The UI is reached through Overview's Quality card, whose assessment page at /quality uses the shared header, content area and footer, with Overview selected in navigation. It replaces the fixed sample scores and renames Reachability to Functionality.

API and lifecycle

  • GET /api/tools/quality passively returns the latest snapshot and calculated category/overall results. It is also published as the tools_show_quality read tool. The initial state is idle, with null scores.
  • POST /api/tools/quality?scope=all&speed=true starts a finite asynchronous full assessment and returns 202. The assessment page always sends speed=true; API callers may omit it for a lighter run. scope=responses reruns every service probe, scope=target&target=cloudflare reruns one service, scope=speed reruns the reference transfer and scope=nat reruns the NAT observations. A scoped run requires a completed snapshot and merges its fresh evidence into the other results. Another assessment, reference speed test or NatTypeTester test holds the shared runner reservations and produces 409. Regular user traffic is not controlled.
  • DELETE /api/tools/quality requests cancellation. The runner releases its reservations after stopping and retains completed evidence. Daemon shutdown also cancels it. Closing the assessment view does not cancel a test.
  • A full assessment replaces the previous in-memory result. A scoped run replaces only the targets, speed or NAT evidence it names and recalculates every affected score. While a scoped run is active, running_scope and running_target identify it and state stays completed, so readers keep the last scores; completed_at advances to the last successful update. A cancelled scoped run changes neither the published evidence nor the checkpoint. Tests run only on demand. Scores do not expire and stay available until a full assessment or a scoped rerun replaces their evidence. Finished assessments (including cancelled or timed-out full runs with partial evidence) are atomically saved to /var/lib/open-linux-router/quality.json and restored after daemon or router restart. An interrupted run leaves the previous checkpoint intact until it finishes; an abrupt shutdown therefore restores the last finished run. Category components carry target and kind so a reader can group the timing, stability and access measurements of one service into that service's single test item.

The run first samples the following fixed resources with IPv4 and IPv6 independently: Cloudflare https://speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=0 (200), Google https://www.google.com/generate_204 (204), and GitHub https://api.github.com/zen (200). Each target/family makes six sequential fresh HTTPS HEAD requests; the six target/family workers run concurrently. Each request has a five-second deadline, a 32 KiB response-header limit and no redirect following or document-body transfer. There is no uncached-DNS claim. Only the first resolved address for each family is attempted in each sample.

Evidence includes start/end time, actual address, HTTP status, failure stage, DNS lookup time, TCP connect time excluding DNS, and time from established TLS connection acquisition to the first HTTP response byte. TLS certificates are verified. Unexpected HTTP statuses, including challenges and rate limits, are inconclusive access evidence rather than a scored network failure. An expected status verifies only that HEAD resource transaction; it does not verify response body content or all functionality of the named service.

The Cloudflare reference transfer runs after response sampling in a full assessment, or alone when its test is rerun, with a 90-second deadline. OLR invokes the upstream Rust cloudflare-speed-cli with JSON output and history saving disabled; OLR does not reimplement its measurement algorithm. The packaged version is v1.0.10, with six concurrent workers and ten-second download and upload phases. It has no fixed byte cap and can consume substantial data. The assessment page always runs it; the API leaves speed optional and off by default for callers that need a lighter run. This measures the router's default route to Cloudflare, not Wi-Fi or all internet services. Speed scoring uses the existing curves, weighting download 70% and upload 30%; missing, invalid or timed-out transfers are excluded. Scoring version quality-v3 identifies this change of reference provider. The standalone speed tests are one tool each — Speedtest by Ookla, Cloudflare Speed Test and Fast.com — because the three measure different paths and an operator arrives already knowing which one they want; a page whose command is missing says so instead of offering the test. Ookla keeps its nearby server picker and probes latency only when the test runs. Cloudflare uses the same packaged CLI as the reference transfer, and Fast.com uses the packaged Zig fast-cli. All three accept a way out: Ookla marks its own sockets with SO_MARK, while the two command-line tools are started under a reserved group id and an nftables rule marks every socket that group opens with the exit's fwmark (meta skgid … meta mark set … in a type route output chain). That is the mechanism the inspection proxy already uses for mitmweb; the group is never created in /etc/group, the table is olr_speed and not olr_route, and a zero mark means the router's default route and installs no rule. A chosen way out also refuses that group's IPv6 sockets (meta nfproto ipv6 reject with icmpv6 admin-prohibited). Exit tables send IPv6 to unreachable, but a local socket settles its source address on the default route before this chain runs, so an AAAA connection would sit in SYN-SENT until TCP gave up instead of failing; refusing the family at once lets a tool that resolves both fall back to IPv4 — fast-cli opens every address it resolves — rather than outliving the run's 90-second deadline. What is left of that class of failure is the exit's own path: a connect that never answers. Each command-line attempt is therefore capped (40 seconds for Fast.com, 60 for Cloudflare) and a run that ends without a measurement is given a second process inside the same 90-second budget. The tools resolve their hosts and open their connections themselves, so the next attempt usually gets through; Ookla, which walks its own server list, is not retried. The two command-line services cannot choose a server, because the service does. Fast.com reports latency and download/upload but no jitter, and its numbers describe the Netflix Open Connect path rather than general internet quality.

A running test publishes its stages, not only its end. While POST /api/tools/speedtest is open, GET /api/tools/speedtest/progress reports the stage in flight, the server being tested, the values already settled and the rate the current transfer is reaching; the elapsed time comes from the run's own start on the router's clock. Ookla can report latency, download and upload separately because the library runs them in that order, and its transfer callbacks supply the live rate. The tool page draws that run as two dials on a logarithmic 0–10 Gbps scale, the way LibreSpeed draws its own: the direction being measured carries its live rate, the other holds its last reading, and both settle on the result with latency and jitter above them. The two command-line services measure both directions inside one process whose only output is the final JSON, so they report one transfer stage and no rate: their dials stay empty until the result arrives rather than inventing intermediate numbers. The page polls, like the rest of the UI, because EventSource cannot send the API's Authorization header. A stage that has not measured anything stays absent rather than becoming a zero, and the live rate is dropped as soon as its transfer ends.

The .deb includes the unmodified CLI, its GPLv3 license and corresponding source under /usr/share/doc/olr/cloudflare-speed-cli. make cloudflare-speed downloads pinned amd64/arm64 musl builds and verifies committed SHA-256 hashes. Build hosts need curl, tar, xz and sha256sum. Single-binary tarball users must install cloudflare-speed-cli separately on the router's PATH, using the upstream release or cargo install cloudflare-speed-cli --version 1.0.10 --locked. An absent CLI is reported as an unmeasured speed component, without silently falling back to another provider. Proxy environment variables are removed from the child process so they cannot change the measured path.

The .deb also includes the unmodified MIT fast-cli v0.3.10 and its license under /usr/share/doc/olr/fast-cli. make fast-cli downloads pinned amd64/arm64 static builds and verifies committed SHA-256 hashes; build hosts need curl, tar and sha256sum. Single-binary tarball users must install fast-cli separately on the router's PATH, using the upstream release. The tool has the fast.com app token compiled in, so a token rotation needs a newer release; the test reports the CLI's error and does not fall back to another service. The token is not the only way the API refuses a run: from a source address Netflix does not serve — mainland China among them — it answers 403 Not Available before any transfer starts. fast-cli puts that reason on stderr while its JSON only says Failed to get URLs, so the tool passes the last stderr line through to the page's technical details; reading it separates a blocked path from an expired token. A blocked path needs a way out in a country the service serves, not a newer binary.

The .deb also includes the unmodified MIT NatTypeTester 10.0.10 console binary as /usr/bin/natty. make natty downloads the pinned linux-x64/linux-arm64 archives and verifies committed SHA-256 hashes; build hosts need curl, 7z and sha256sum. The binary is native AOT and needs no .NET runtime, but it needs ICU for globalization; the tool runs it with DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_INVARIANT=1 so a box without libicu still gets the English labels its output is parsed by. The upstream linux builds need glibc 2.38 or newer, which Debian 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 provide. Single-binary tarball users must install the upstream console release as natty on the router's PATH. Its two probes run in parallel and share a 15-second budget; a partial answer names the probe that failed. NAT results are diagnostic only and do not prove public IPv4 assignment, inbound or P2P access. A full assessment has a 150-second deadline; scoped reruns use shorter deadlines (65 seconds for all service probes, 40 seconds for one service, 100 seconds for the reference transfer and 20 seconds for NAT). No configuration changes, temporary inbound listeners or port mappings are made.

Component base weights

CategoryImplemented componentsFuture/unmeasured components
Speed (25 points)Reference transfer: 40% of category; within this, download 70%, upload 30%Service-specific transfers: 60%
Latency (25 points)TCP connect 60%, DNS 15%, HTTPS response 25%, each averaged equally across the three targetsUnsupported/missing timings remain unscored
Stability (25 points)Connection establishment success 40%; TCP timing variation 30%, averaged equally across the three targetsBehavior under load: 30%
Wi-Fi (15 points)NoneClient/AP measurements: 100%
Functionality (10 points)Test-resource access: 50%, averaged equally across the three servicesProtocol capabilities 25%; inbound/P2P 25%

For access, either family returning the expected status earns that service's 100; both families failing all attempts yields 0. Inconclusive or incomplete evidence with no success remains unscored. For timing and stability, select the family with the higher normalized measured score per target/category; keep that family's fields together rather than mixing paths. This is a best measured family reference, not a prediction of a particular client's family selection or fallback. Missing alternatives are not known failures.

Timing scores require at least four valid measurements and use their median. Connection continuity requires all six attempts with non-collector outcomes and is 100 * established TCP connections / attempts; it is not packet loss or long-term availability. Timing variation uses the mean absolute difference of consecutive successful TCP connect durations, requires at least three adjacent pairs in a six-attempt run, and does not bridge failed attempts. These are short reference samples, not representative historical stability or loaded behavior.

Initial normalization curves

Use linear interpolation between these anchors and clamp beyond the endpoints. Negative/nonfinite measurements are invalid. These initial experience hints are versioned and can be calibrated later without changing the aggregation rules. They are not statistical confidence estimates.

MetricMeasurement → score anchors
Download Mbps0→0, 3→20, 10→40, 25→60, 75→80, 150→90, 500→100
Upload Mbps0→0, 1→20, 3→40, 10→60, 30→80, 75→90, 200→100
TCP connect ms0→100, 10→100, 30→90, 60→75, 100→60, 200→35, 500→0
DNS lookup ms0→100, 10→100, 30→90, 60→75, 100→60, 200→35, 500→0
HTTPS response ms0→100, 30→100, 100→90, 200→75, 500→50, 1000→20, 2000→0
TCP variation ms0→100, 2→95, 5→85, 10→70, 20→50, 50→20, 100→0

Per category, normalize scored component weights to sum to 1. Reference transfer therefore supplies 100% of the current speed score; stability uses connection success and timing variation in the ratio 4:3 when both are usable; functionality uses the equal mean of scored service-access results.

Normalize the base weights of scored categories to a 100-point total. With bandwidth enabled and all implemented metrics usable, Speed, Latency, Stability and Functionality have effective point budgets of 29.41, 29.41, 29.41 and 11.76. Without bandwidth testing they become 41.67, 41.67 and 16.67 for Latency, Stability and Functionality. Either assessment can score 100. Wi-Fi remains unmeasured and excluded until supported measurements exist.

The API exposes component weight (base) and effective_weight (normalized within the category). Category budget retains its base weight; available_points is its effective share of the normalized total and earned_points is its score times that share divided by 100. Overall available_points is 100 when any fresh category is scored; earned_points is the sum of category contributions. coverage_percent retains the weighted fraction of the planned catalog with usable evidence as separate metadata; it neither reduces the quality score nor gates it. Category partial denotes limited measured scope, while overall ready denotes a scored assessment. Running, cancelled, timed-out and stale snapshots withhold the overall score.

Scoring version quality-v2 introduces this normalization; quality-v1 withheld totals pending the full planned catalog. The reference profile and catalog remain version 1 because their targets and base weights are unchanged. Future tests and weights can evolve by version without reserving points now.

docs.title: Page review baseline
docs.summary: The objective is fast identification of useful information, a visible range of OLR capabilities, and a calm, consistent interface. This record accompanies the content guide and visual guide.
docs.html:
The objective is fast identification of useful information, a visible range of OLR capabilities, and a calm, consistent interface. This record accompanies the content guide and visual guide.

PagesReview decision
OverviewShow Status, Traffic, Latency and Map; uptime leads Status. Omit System, information icons and the map legend/top-ten hint; retain charts and separate direction limits.
Quality reportOne column: the overall-score band, then the five categories. No standalone transfer card, scoring-explanation block or evidence dump: the reference transfer sits under Speed, each service's attempts open under its own row (timings for Latency, sequence for Stability, outcome for Functionality), and NAT observations are an unscored diagnostic under Functionality. Measured coverage is the only figure with a hover hint.
DeviceSeparate observed facts from editable settings within the existing card; keep all fields; keep retained per-site activity, saved requests and current DNS queries inside the inspection panel.
WireGuard deviceThe tunnel's answer, not the device list's: the label edited in place in the heading with the name beside it, the picture from the same picker a device uses, then address, public key, what it sends home and a way to replace the configuration file, last handshake and where from, with activity, current rate and totals from the address-keyed counters, the services published at its tunnel address in the same row a device page uses, and DNS queries by tunnel address. Omit vendor, group, reservation and per-device priority/limits — keyed by a MAC a tunnel does not have — and answer inspection with one word rather than a switch that cannot work.
GroupPreserve member lists and batch controls; remove repeated MAC/direct-membership prose; keep overwrite and non-inheritance consequences.
Device/group QoSState that configuration is saved but not enforced; keep forms and shared group-cap semantics.
InspectionOne persistent switch and card. Keep retained activity and saved request history available with inspection off; use Saved/Live choices for requests while active. Setup holds CA guidance and global 30-day/5-GiB router retention defaults. Show inline body previews and full native downloads, confirm per-device archive clearing, and state that unfinished flows are not yet durable.
GatewayA directory in the same launcher as Access and Advanced: six groups in the order an operator arrives at them — Internet (DHCP, PPPoE, static address), Interfaces & routing (interfaces, routes, external rules), DHCP (dnsmasq, Kea), DNS (unbound, dnsmasq, mosdns, AdGuard Home), Firewall (nftables, firewalld, ufw, port forwarding, external filtering) and Intrusion prevention (fail2ban, CrowdSec) — each a letter tile in the group's hue. Firewalld, ufw, fail2ban and CrowdSec link to their projects' sites and say the setup is external; nothing claims an OLR page it does not have. A choice OLR cannot configure yet keeps its tile, muted and inert, and says nothing opens; a link tile opens the one page that configures the choice. No status strip, no switch and no draft on the directory; the interface cards and the IPv4/IPv6 stacks are gone, and links that targeted gateway#interfaces target gateway/interfaces.
Interfaces/routing and interface detailKeep controls and all observed fields; carry link speed, every address, live rates, totals and the served DHCP range on the detail page, since the landing card no longer opens a dialog; shorten management and routing explanations without moving controls.
ExitsPreserve list/edit forms; distinguish blocking, unknown and failed checks; remove repeated failure prose.
UsagePreserve measurement controls and counters; show a uniquely matched device name with its address; download precedes upload; disclose accounting limitations.
External routing rulesDistinguish loading, failure, unknown and empty; preserve readable raw evidence and provide retry.
DHCP details, ranges, reservations, advancedPut status/details first; preserve lists, range forms and address fields; concise headings and managed-configuration constraints.
DNS details, blocking, names, upstream, listening, enforcement, advancedPreserve filters, values and forms; group activity accounting metadata; shorten repeated explanations; retain binding, TLS verification and protocol limitations.
FirewallOne vertical Sankey with three visual rows: external semantic categories above one virtual OLR / Firewall node, trusted/LAN and router-local categories below. Both sides arrive at OLR; outer nodes state source and Allowed/Blocked decision. Use one actual packet scale and only nonzero categories. Matching conditions include source, destination, packets and bytes. Wrap labels and adapt chart width; overflowing charts scroll from the leading edge with a visible hint. Preserve switch and warnings; native, disabled, unverified and unavailable counters do not claim automatic traffic measurements. Editing lives at /firewall/rules.
AccessRemove duplicate hero introduction; keep the established directional groups, and link each tile straight to its configuration page or project documentation instead of a dialog.
SOCKS5 outboundKeep status, authentication and address fields; concise support scope and routing next step.
WireGuard and SOCKS5 serverWireGuard answers on one card: its state, switch, public address and server key together, with the device list below it. SOCKS5 keeps its status and password card. Remove duplicate WireGuard labels and onboarding prose; retain exposure and password information.
HTTPS ingressPreserve certificate details and all service domains/targets; show configuration counts accurately; keep service-authentication warning.
Port forwardsKeep shared routing switch and counters; distinguish unknown rules from inactive rules; configuration counts do not promise public reachability.
External filteringDistinguish loading/error/unknown/empty; retain policy and counters without claiming end-to-end connectivity.
Tools directoryUse five consistent Lucide outline icons on themed surfaces, full names and chevrons; remove baked-in raster backgrounds.
All five tool operationsPreserve inputs/results and router-originated measurement scope; remove duplicate page subtitle; shorten selector hints; retain bandwidth and privacy consequences.
AdvancedKeep existing capability entries; remove generic shell description.
DDNSPreserve provider/source/publication information and forms; explicit loading/error/unknown status; short empty state.
IPTVKeep signal-path/source-prefix forms and preview/apply flow; concise prerequisites; disclose long scope limitations; pending status is not off.
Administrator accessKeep password/security controls; remove redundant introduction.
CreditsOne ungrouped table with no visible header row, no section rows and no website column: the first column is the project mark and name as one link, followed by version and usage. Keep every feature-carrying project and the libraries that implement a listed feature (pro-bing, for example), with full dependency and license lists linked from the manifests; stacked records below 768px.
Sign-in, initial setup, first-run, not-foundPreserve existing components and safety consequences; concise setup steps and missing-page message.
DialogsRetain existing common fields, advanced disclosures and apply previews; remove redundant exit-name help; clearing saved inspection requests uses the shared confirmation Dialog.

Review does not require changing every file. Keep useful existing content and layouts where they meet the standard. Future iterations should validate empty, populated, loading and error states as well as desktop/mobile and both themes. Browser fixture checks validate presentation, not live router networking.

Visual consistency review — 2026-10-12

Reviewed all 43 current pages and entry states at 1440px, 375px and 768px, plus desktop dark mode (172 captures). Coverage includes device/group details, all Gateway/DNS/DHCP pages, Firewall, all Access pages, all five diagnostics, Advanced/DDNS/IPTV, administrator access, Credits, not-found, both sign-in methods, setup and first-run. Opened the add dialogs for exits, DHCP ranges and reservations, DNS blocking and local names, and port forwards on desktop and phone. No browser exceptions or page-wide horizontal overflow were observed. The synthetic ingress service icon is absent; its intended fallback is shown.

Corrections: use one centered 1280px shell for every route, align Overview metric heading line boxes, keep the health dot beside its label on phones, replace background-baked tool illustrations with consistent themed outline icons, and let switch panels share the page boundaries while retaining readable form widths. Administrator password controls keep a 720px maximum inside their full-width card. Existing device imagery and useful monitoring/data space are preserved.

Validated with Node 24 web lint/build/tests and Go 1.27 Linux vet/tests. Lint has existing warnings; production build retains the existing bundle-size warning. The environment lacks make, so the Go commands behind make check were run directly.

Gateway landing review — 2026-10-21

The page read as unfinished for structural reasons rather than colour: two levels of border around the interface cards, a right-hand column 120px taller than what it summarised (leaving an empty band inside the panel), a second set of section headings indented 68px behind the first, 660px service cards holding 200px of content, and three wordings of "Details".

Corrections: interface cards lost the 9px role text and the two 3px squares drawn on the shared glyph — the role is now a badge beside the name, and the card carries name, state, address and rates only. The interface grid wraps instead of scrolling locally, so a fourth NIC is not hidden at the edge. Way out and Services are panels of their own, so every block on the page is a Card with the same title contract, and the DHCP/DNS rows are links with their state on the right.

It then went further than a shared strip. A status strip was tried and removed: its one switch was a one-click way to take every network behind the router off the internet and close its forwarded ports, and without the switch the strip repeated the routing details page. Routing state, drift, the module switch and the IPv4/IPv6 forwarding switches all live at interfaces#forwarding, beside the sentences that say what turning them off closes; Overview reports a gateway fault. The landing page is the objects only, and the Interfaces heading is its single settings entry.

Validated against fixture data at 1440×1000, 1024×1000, 768×1200 and 390×1200 in both themes, plus the empty, loading and error states of each panel and the interface page. No page-wide overflow or horizontal scroll at 375px. Hash targets #interfaces, #dhcp and #dns still scroll. Mocked browser checks validate presentation, not live networking.

Interface cards review — 2026-10-21

The landing card opened a dialog holding what the card could not: the network it carries, the negotiated link speed, MAC, every address and both totals. A dialog is the wrong shape for that — it is a page's worth of readings behind a click, with its own "Interface settings" link at the bottom — so the card now links straight to the interface page and the dialog is gone.

The interface page took over the readings and gained the two that were only ever on the tile: what it is moving now and what it has moved in total, both read from the same NIC counters as the card. It also states the DHCP range its network serves and how much of it is in use, so "this interface's LAN is running out of addresses" is visible where the interface is inspected rather than one link away. Everything the dialog held is still reachable, and the keyboard path is shorter: one tab stop to the page instead of button → dialog → tab into it.

Gateway stacks review — 2026-10-21

The page answered "what is this box plugged into" and then left the operator to work out the rest. IPv6 in particular was one line in Way out: the delegated prefix, the LAN's /64, whether anyone advertised it, whether the kernel forwarded it, and whether an exit dropped it were each in a different module, and finding them required knowing which module owned which half.

Way out and Services are replaced by two stacks, IPv4 and IPv6, each cut across the modules in packet order: Upstream, LAN, DHCP, Forwarding, Exit, DNS, with the clients card reading SLAAC or DHCPv6 on the IPv6 stack. Each card states that stage's answer for that family and links to the one page that changes it, so the question "is IPv6 working, and where do I fix it" is answered without a module map. Missing stages are named in the card — no /64, nobody advertising, forwarding off — instead of being absent, because an absent row reads as "nothing to do" rather than "not configured". The clients card is titled for what an operator came to change: DHCP on IPv4 — the module's name and the word they arrive with — and the protocol running on IPv6: SLAAC, DHCPv6, or both when networks differ. Those are terms an operator already knows, and that card opens the address ranges that carry each network's advertisement mode. The Forwarding card reports what its switch decides rather than where the sysctl was written: devices reach the internet or they do not, with NAT and the port-forward count beside it on IPv4.

Each stack ends with the routing table, drawn as a seventh card of the same kind although it is not a stage and not a module: every card above writes into it and the kernel consults it after all of them. It sits in the family's own stack because a route table is per family — a block below both stacks named IPv4 and IPv6 a second time and asked the reader to hold two places at once for one family's routing. It counts routes, says whether that family has a default route and whether any of its tables belongs to somebody else; its page lists every route grouped by table — the box's main table, each exit's own table with the rule priority that selects it, and any table a foreign rule points at — and is read-only, because a static route is its own object and a page reporting the table must not become a second place to write it.

The stacks are a read model. Every card is a link: no draft, no plan, no apply of its own, so the same module appearing once per family is one object seen twice and cannot disagree with itself. That is also why the page can afford two full stacks without becoming a second settings page, and why design.md §4.3's "no page that sets IPv6 across modules" still holds — it is amended there to name this view explicitly.

Hash targets stay: #interfaces is the interface card, and #dhcp/#dns/#routes still land on the IPv4 DHCP, DNS and Routes cards, though the settings trees now open the section pages themselves. The interface card is unchanged, and every previous Way-out fact — both routes, the resolvers, the unmanaged-rule count — has a home in the stacks except the unmanaged rules, which remain on interfaces#forwarding.

Validated as a read-only page: lint, type-check, unit tests and a production build pass. Live router state was not available, so the cards were checked against types and fixtures, not against a running box.

WireGuard card review — 2026-10-21

The page opened with two cards that each held half of one answer. A status strip counted "1 of 2 connected" above a list that already names every device and ends each row with exactly that state, and below it a settings card carried the switch whose consequence the strip repeated in a second voice ("Devices connected over WireGuard can reach every address on your network"). Neither card was wrong, and neither was what somebody came to the page for.

They are one card now: the mark and the title, the tunnel's state as a word beside it, the Settings button and the switch on the same line, then the three facts the device list cannot give — where devices dial, the network their addresses come from, and the key they check. The word follows the box and the switch follows intent, so a reboot that leaves the settings stored and the interface gone reads "Not running" with the catch-up alert directly above it, and "we could not tell" stays its own answer rather than becoming a fault. The off state keeps one sentence, because a list of saved devices looks identical whether or not the tunnel is up.

The count is gone rather than moved. A row already ends in Connected, an elapsed time or Never connected, so "1 of 2" summarised the rows directly underneath it. What remains above the list is what a page's first glance is for: blockers, a foreign interface, drift, and a public address that has not been set.

Validated against fixture data at 1440×900 in both themes and at 390, 375 and 320 wide, in the running, off and unknown states: no page-wide horizontal overflow, and the switch stays reachable at every width the card title wraps at. Live router state was not available, so this checks presentation rather than networking.

WireGuard device configuration — 2026-10-21

The page could describe a device completely and could not give back the one thing that gets lost. A configuration file is handed over once and its private key is stored nowhere (remote-access §4.1), which is deliberate and stays: there is no file to re-serve. What was missing was the honest next step, which used to be "remove the device and add it again" — a path that renumbers it, drops its label and drops its picture, and was written down only in the dialog that shows the file, at the moment nobody needed it.

The facts table now ends that question with a Configuration row: a New file button whose tooltip says why there was nothing to download, a confirm dialog that states the loss (that device cannot dial in until the new file is imported, which the daemon classifies as disruptive and refuses without it), and then the same handover dialog an added device gets, saying once and only once. The name, the address, what it sends home and its picture do not move.

The command is the same operation under the vocabulary that already exists: olr remote set peer <name> --new-key prints the file rather than drawing it, and refuses to be combined with a rename, because a handover and a label change answering one exit code would be a lie about which one failed.

Validated with fixture responses for the whole sequence — row, refusal, confirm, handover — at 1440×1000 and 390×844, plus lint, type-check, unit tests and a production build. The daemon side is covered by TestReissuingADeviceReturnsANewConfiguration; live router state was not available, so the presentation check runs against fixtures.

WireGuard device actions — 2026-10-21

The Configuration row put a button inside a table of facts, and the fact it labelled was "there is a file, once". As a row it named a category rather than the thing an operator is missing, and its button, New file, referred to a file that does not exist until it is clicked. It also ended the card in a band under a rule, because a footer was where page-level actions had always been put.

The two actions a dialed-in device has — hand it a new setup file, edit it — are one pair now, in the lower right corner of the card, in the space the three counters leave beside the taller facts column. There is no rule: the pair belongs to the facts above it, and a line would announce another section of the page in a card that has none. The button names what the click hands over, so the row that had to explain it is gone; why the file cannot be downloaded again stays in its tooltip and in the confirm dialog, which is where the loss is decided.

Validated against the scratch daemon at 1440×1000 and 390×844, in both themes, with no horizontal overflow, and clicked through to the handover dialog from the moved button. The daemon side is unchanged.

docs.title: Port forwarding
docs.summary: One sentence is the whole feature:
docs.html:
Status: built. The object is a port forward, and it belongs to internal/gateway. Section references are to design.md unless prefixed gateway:, which means docs/gateway.md — the module's own document, of which this is a feature document the way docs/ddns.md is one of dial's.

One sentence is the whole feature:

Something on the internet connects to this router on a port, and the connection is delivered to one client on your network instead.

0. Why this is not a firewall module any more

It used to be one, and this document used to open by admitting the problem: "built, and named for more than it does". internal/firewall had no zones, no rule lists and no filtering policy — it was a NAT module wearing a firewall's name, and it kept the name on one bet: that filtering was close enough behind that renaming twice would be the more expensive mistake.

That bet was called off. olr is not building a firewall for now — nftables is there for anyone who wants to write rules, and olr does not offer a feature over it. With no filtering coming, a module named firewall that does no filtering is just a name blocking the one it describes, so the object moved to where it belongs and the name was freed for whenever real filtering arrives.

Where it belongs is gateway, and the argument is one line: a forward is translation at the boundary between this network and the internet, and that boundary is exactly what gateway already owns. Its three concerns are one question asked in both directions —

TableQuestion
Exits and assignmentolr_routewhere does traffic leaving a network go (gateway:§1)
Egress NATolr_nathow does leaving traffic get an address that can be replied to (gateway:§3.9)
Port forwardsolr_natwhat arrives from outside, and where does it go (this document)

The hairpin pair (§4) is the standing evidence that the two directions are one feature rather than two: it is a DNAT and a masquerade that only work together, and under the old split they were the only reason olr_nat had a postrouting chain at all.

What did not change: the object, the ruleset, the validation, the hairpin argument, the warnings. Everything below this section is what it always was, with olr firewall now spelled olr gateway.

1. The object: a forward

1.1 Definition

A forward is a standing instruction to redirect connections arriving from outside, addressed to this router on one port, to an address and port inside.

Four properties and a name, and each answers a question the operator already has:

FieldOperator's questionExample
namewhat do I call thisweb
inwhere does it arrivewan0
protocoltcp, udp or bothtcp
porton which port8080, or 30000-30010
toand goes where192.168.1.10:80
hairpindoes it work from inside tooon by default (§4)

in is an interface rather than "the internet", and that is not a placeholder for a better word. A box can have two uplinks, and a forward that silently applied to both would be a policy nobody wrote. Naming the interface makes the scope of the rule exactly as wide as the operator said it was — and it is the same staging argument gateway:§2.5 makes: the field becomes a network name when link grows networks, and the stored document does not change shape.

1.2 The destination is an address, not a client

to stores 192.168.1.10:80. It does not store a reference to a client in the clients inventory, and that is a decision rather than an omission.

A forward is a kernel rule that has to exist the moment a packet arrives, at boot, before any lease has been handed out and while the client is switched off. A client reference would have to be resolved to an address at apply time, so the rule would either be absent until the client appeared — which is a port that works some mornings — or be programmed against a remembered address, which is a client reference that has quietly become an address anyway, with one more place for the two to disagree.

What the operator loses is the case where the client's address changes and the forward silently points at whatever took it over. The answer to that is a fixed lease, which dhcp already has, and the surfaces say so: the WebUI's dialog offers a client picker that fills the address in and warns when that client has no fixed address, and olr gateway add forward accepts the address the operator can see in olr clients show. The stored value is an address either way. The picker is a convenience for typing it, not a second model.

1.3 Port ranges may not be shifted

A single port may be remapped freely — 8080 outside to 80 inside is the motivating case and the most common one. A range may only be forwarded to the same range.

This is a kernel property surfaced rather than a policy we chose. Netfilter's NAT core keeps the original port when it already falls inside the requested range (l4proto_in_range in get_unique_tuple), which is what makes 30000-30010 → 192.168.1.10:30000-30010 an exact identity mapping. Ask it to shift a range instead — 30000-30010 outside to 40000-40010 inside — and the original port is not in range, so netfilter falls through to picking a free port arbitrarily. Connections still arrive; they arrive on unpredictable ports.

That is the worst available failure: it works, and it delivers to the wrong place, and nothing in the configuration looks wrong. So validation refuses it with the reason, rather than programming a rule whose behaviour we would then have to explain. An operator who genuinely wants a shifted range writes one forward per port, which is honest about what the kernel is being asked to do.

2. The operator model

There is no ladder here and no inheritance. A forward is a flat, independent thing: it either matches a packet or it does not, and two forwards cannot disagree about one packet because validation refuses the overlap (§5.1) rather than resolving it.

That is a smaller model than the exits half's, deliberately. "Where does my phone go?" needs a ladder because every client has an answer whether or not anybody set one. "What reaches my NAS from outside?" has the answer nothing until somebody writes it down, and a list of what somebody wrote down is a complete account of it. Adding structure to that would be modelling for its own sake.

2.1 Everything else stays shut, and we do not say otherwise

Superseded in part (docs/firewall.md). olr now has a firewall — one switch, off by default. With it on, the forward chain lets through exactly what a forward translated, so a forward is still the whole permission and there is nothing to open separately. With it off, what follows is still true.

olr has no filtering policy. It does not maintain a default-deny stance on the forward hook, and this feature does not create one. What keeps the rest of the network unreachable from outside is that the addresses inside are private and nothing routes to them — plus whatever forward-hook policy the box already has from somewhere else (§6).

This matters because it bounds what a forward means. Creating one does not "open a hole in the firewall", because there is no firewall of ours for it to be a hole in. It installs a NAT translation. If something else on the box is filtering forwarded traffic, that filter still applies and the forward may not reach — which is exactly §6, and it is reported rather than worked around.

3. Mechanism

3.1 The ruleset

table inet olr_nat {
  counter fwd1

  chain prerouting {                # type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat
    iifname "wan0" meta nfproto ipv4 fib daddr type local \
        tcp dport 8080 counter name "fwd1" dnat ip to 192.168.1.10:80
    iifname "lan0" meta nfproto ipv4 fib daddr type local \
        tcp dport 8080 dnat ip to 192.168.1.10:80
  }

  chain postrouting {               # type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat
    ip saddr 192.168.1.0/24 ip daddr 192.168.1.10 tcp dport 80 masquerade
  }
}

Four details in there are load-bearing, and each is a mistake somebody makes by hand.

3.2 fib daddr type local, not the WAN address

The obvious rule matches the router's public address. That address comes from DHCP or PPPoE and changes, so the obvious rule is one whose correctness expires without warning — and re-rendering it on every address change would make the firewall table churn every lease renewal.

fib daddr type local asks the kernel the question we actually mean: is this packet addressed to this box? It is true for whatever address the uplink currently holds, for a second address added later, and for the loopback — and it is false for traffic merely passing through, which is how it also keeps a forward from capturing transit traffic that happens to use the same port.

3.3 meta nfproto ipv4 on every rule

The table is inet, which sees both families. §7 explains why there is no IPv6 forwarding, but the table is inet anyway so that the day filtering arrives it does not need a second table.

That makes the family guard mandatory rather than tidy. Without it, an IPv4 payload offset applied to an IPv6 packet reads whatever is at that offset in the v6 header. internal/gateway/kernel_linux.go's sourceExprs carries the same guard and says the same thing; this is the second module to need it and it will not be the last.

3.4 Named counters, one per forward

Anonymous inline counters are zeroed when the chain is re-rendered, and this module re-renders its whole table on every apply (§3.6). So adding a second forward would silently reset the first one's numbers — gateway:§3.3's lesson, which cost a bug there and is being paid forward here.

Has this forward ever been hit? is the first question anybody asks when a port does not work, and it separates "the packet never arrived" from "the packet arrived and something further in dropped it". Those have completely different next steps, so the counter is worth an object.

The counter is named from the forward's slot — a small integer allocated on save and kept for the forward's lifetime — rather than from its name. Same reasoning as gateway:§3.2's slots: renaming a forward should not reset the number somebody is watching, and inserting a forward that sorts earlier should not renumber the others. It is also the only spelling that is certainly a legal nftables identifier, which an operator-chosen name is not.

3.5 The hairpin pair

Two rules, and they are one feature. §4 is the whole argument.

3.6 The table is replaced wholesale, in one transaction

olr_nat is deleted and rebuilt on every apply, in a single netlink batch, which is what internal/gateway/kernel_linux.go does with olr_route and for the same reasons: the batch is atomic so no half-built ruleset is ever visible, and a hand-edit inside our table is corrected on the next apply.

nft flush ruleset remains banned outright (§3.4). We delete one table, by name, and nothing else on the box is touched.

4. Hairpin NAT, and why it is on by default

The complaint is universal and never phrased as a bug report: "I set up the port forward and it works from my phone on mobile data, but not from my laptop at home."

A client on the LAN looks up the operator's dynamic-DNS name, gets the router's public address, and connects. The DNAT rule as written matches iifname "wan0", so it does not fire, and the connection goes to the router itself and is refused.

Adding the LAN-side DNAT is half the fix and produces a subtler failure. The client at 192.168.1.20 now has its packet rewritten to 192.168.1.10, which is on its own segment — so the server replies directly to 192.168.1.20 from 192.168.1.10, bypassing the router entirely. The client receives a reply from an address it never sent to and drops it. The connection hangs rather than failing, which is worse.

The masquerade is the other half: rewriting the client's source address to the router's makes the server reply through the router, where conntrack can undo both translations.

It is on by default because off-by-default is a setting nobody discovers. The failure it prevents does not present as a missing feature — it presents as the port forward being broken, tested from the one machine the operator has to hand.

4.1 What it costs, stated

The server sees the router's address as the source of every hairpinned connection, not the real client's. A web server's access log fills with one address; per-client rules on the server stop discriminating; fail2ban on the server can lock out the router and with it the whole house.

That is a real cost and it is why --no-hairpin exists. It is the right choice for an operator whose internal clients reach the service by its internal address anyway — which is the better answer in general, and is what split-horizon DNS is for.

And olr owns a resolver, so it is worth being exact about why it cannot just do that. dns renders local-zone ... static entries into unbound (docs/dns.md §4.6), so the mechanism is there. What is missing is narrower and names the work: local names are stored relative to the local domain — sony-tv, not a fully-qualified name — so the entry split-horizon actually needs, home.example.net → 192.168.1.10, has nowhere to live. Until some object can hold a public name with a private answer, olr genuinely cannot make this choice on the operator's behalf, and so it makes the one that fails visibly rather than the one that fails at 2am in someone else's log file. §10.4.

The warning is on the surface, not only in this document: validation emits it for every forward with hairpin on.

5. Failure modes

Each of these presents as "the port forward does not work", which is why they are checks and reported facts rather than troubleshooting notes.

5.1 The ones validation refuses

Why
Two forwards overlapping on (in, protocol, port)genuinely ambiguous; first-match would be a precedence model nobody can see (§2.3 of gateway, one level down)
to is an address on this boxa forward to ourselves is a loop, and the operator meant a local service
to is unspecified, loopback or multicastnot a destination a client can hold
in has not been adopted§7 — we do not program rules on an interface nobody handed us
A shifted port range§1.3; the kernel would deliver to arbitrary ports
An IPv6 address in to§7

5.2 The ones the plan reports, because they are somebody else's state

Another table filtering the forward hook. ufw, firewalld, Docker and a distribution's own /etc/nftables.conf all install chains on the forward hook, and several default to policy drop. In nftables a drop is final: our accept in our table cannot override a drop in theirs, because every table sees every packet and the most restrictive verdict wins.

So this is not something we can fix, and pretending otherwise would be worse than saying nothing. The plan detects it and says so:

nftables chain filter/FORWARD in table inet firewalld has policy drop, so something else on this box is filtering forwarded traffic and this forward may not reach 192.168.1.10.

The same move gateway:§6 makes with foreign ip rule entries, with one deliberate difference: gateway refuses and this one does not. Two owners of the routing table is a correctness problem that silently misroutes; a foreign forward-chain policy is a thing that might be exactly what the operator configured on purpose, and might already have an accept rule for this traffic that we cannot evaluate. Refusing would block a legitimate setup on a guess. So: report, apply, and let the counter (§3.4) settle the question.

A local service already listening on the port. Forwarding wan0:22 while sshd listens on :22 is the one that costs the operator their session: DNAT runs in prerouting, before the local delivery decision, so the rule takes effect and the next SSH connection from outside goes to the other machine. The operator is holding the connection it breaks.

core.TCPPortInUse and core.UDPPortInUse already exist for dhcp's preflight and answer exactly this, so the plan warns with the port named. It is a warning and not a refusal, because "forward SSH to the NAS and administer this box from the LAN" is a legitimate thing to want — but it is never a thing to do by accident.

5.3 The one that is ours and is a bug we had to fix

See §6. It is not a firewall failure mode; it is a gateway one that only port forwarding makes visible.

5.4 The one where nothing is wrong and it still cannot work

Every check above asks whether the configuration is coherent. This one asks the question the operator actually has: can a connection from the internet reach this router at all?

If the interface a forward faces outward on does not hold a routable address, the answer is no, and nothing in olr_nat can change it. The forward validates, applies, renders correct rules, and never carries a packet — which is the worst shape a failure can take, because there is nothing to find by looking at it.

Three readings of in's address, all warnings, in warnUnreachableUplink:

The interface holdsWhat it means
an address in 100.64.0.0/10the ISP has put this box behind their NAT; nothing outside can open a connection to it, ever
a private (RFC 1918) addressthis box is behind another router; the forward works once that client forwards the same port here
no IPv4 addressthere is nothing for a connection to arrive on yet

Warnings and not refusals, deliberately. Double NAT is ugly, not broken: a box behind an ISP-supplied modem-router carries forwarded traffic perfectly well as soon as the upstream client is told to send it here, and that is an extremely common home topology. Refusing would block a configuration that works. The address is also a reading of now — an uplink can be mid-DHCP, or behind a modem being swapped — and a refusal would freeze a transient state.

The CGNAT row is the one worth the code on its own. It is the diagnosis docs/ddns.md §3.2 calls the one thing DDNS can offer that nothing else in the product can, read here from the other side: core.IsCGNAT is shared by both modules precisely so the two cannot come to disagree about which addresses are hopeless. dial still owns noticing — the reflector source is the only one that sees what the internet sees, and a forward's warning points at it.

What this does not do is check whether the port is open from outside. That needs a third party to try it, and asking one is a decision on the scale of the reflector's, not a rider on a validation rule. Until then the counter (§3.4) answers the other half: whether anything has arrived.

6. The return path, and the routing-half bug this exposed

On any box that has an exit configured, port forwarding silently did not work when this landed. Both halves are gateway's now — the fix is in the routing half and the symptom is in this one — and it is recorded in both documents because neither half is wrong on its own.

Follow a forwarded connection on a box where lan0 is assigned to the exit "Proxy". olr_route's classify chain runs in prerouting at mangle priority, and gateway:§3.5 restricts it to forwarded traffic with fib daddr type != local:

PacketWhat classify seesResult
Inbound SYN, before DNATdestination is still the router's own address, so fib daddr type != local is falsemark 0 — correct
The server's SYN/ACK backsource 192.168.1.10 matches lan0's source rule; destination is the public internetmarked for Proxy — wrong

The reply looks exactly like an ordinary LAN machine opening an outbound connection, because conntrack does not restore the original source address until postrouting. So the policy route sends it into the proxy, and the connection dies half-open.

The fix is one guard added to gateway's sourceExprs:

ct status & 0x20 (IPS_DST_NAT) == 0
A connection whose destination we rewrote is not one we choose an exit for.

The semantics are general, which is what makes this a fix rather than a back door for one module: the reply leg of any DNATed connection belongs to whoever originated the translation, and its path is decided by the conntrack entry, not by our source rules.

The declared cost. Traffic DNATed by somebody else's table — a Docker published port, a hand-written rule — also loses its exit assignment. That is a behaviour change for a setup that mixed the two, and it is the correct direction to be wrong in: an unassigned connection takes the box's normal path and works, while the alternative breaks it. gateway:§3.5 carries the same note.

7. IPv6 is deliberately absent

There is no to that may be an IPv6 address, no v6 form of a forward, and no switch that mentions v6. This is the most likely thing in the document to be read as an oversight, so the reasoning is here rather than only in §9.

IPv6 has no NAT and needs none: a client inside already has a globally routable address, so "forwarding" a v6 port is not a translation at all. It is a filtering decision — permitting inbound connections to an address that is already reachable in principle.

olr has no filtering policy (§2.1). We do not maintain a default-deny stance on the forward hook, so there is nothing for a v6 "forward" to open. Worse, an accept in our table cannot override a drop in somebody else's (§5.2), so on the boxes where inbound v6 is blocked — which is the only case where the feature would mean anything — ours would not work.

A switch that appears on four surfaces and reliably does nothing is worse than a missing feature. The operator configures it, tests it, finds the port shut, and debugs their network instead of reading a scope table.

So it waits for a filtering feature, where it would be one rule in a policy we own and can reason about — and §0 records that no such feature is coming for now. Until then to takes an IPv4 address and validation says why.

8. Scope

v1DNAT from one interface to one addressthe object
port remapping, and identity port ranges§1.3
hairpin NAT, on by default, with a warning§4
per-forward named counters§3.4
foreign forward-policy detection, reported§5.2
local-port conflict warning§5.2
unreachable-uplink warning (CGNAT, double NAT, no address)§5.4
v2a source allow-list (--from)belongs to filtering, not to NAT — see §9
IPv6 inbound permitsneeds the filtering half to exist (§7)
per-forward enable/disable without deleting
an external "is this port open?" probe§5.4 — needs the third-party decision made first
Laterzones and a filter policya firewall module, if one is ever built — §0
an nftables reader for the whole box (design.md §4.2)which also closes gateway:§10's observation gap
NeverUPnP / NAT-PMP / PCP§9

9. Considered and rejected

  • UPnP, NAT-PMP and PCP. The protocols by which an application on the LAN opens a port without asking anybody. They are genuinely useful — games and consoles want them — and they are rejected because the object they create is not the object this feature has. A forward here is something the operator wrote down, visible in a list, surviving a reboot, removable by the person who made it. A UPnP mapping is a hole punched by whatever software asked, with a lease, attributable to no person, and the security history is dire: malware inside the network opening its own inbound path is the textbook case. If it ever lands it needs its own object, its own list, its own expiry, and a per-client consent model — which is a feature, not a flag on this one.

§8 says "never" here rather than "never in olr", and the qualifier is load-bearing. What the operator wants is not UPnP; it is inbound working without being configured, and that need has two mechanisms. The other one is endpoint-independent (full-cone) NAT — the thing a console means by "NAT Type", and a property of how the box translates rather than an object anybody creates. Linux has no upstream implementation of it: masquerade gives endpoint-independent mapping with address-and-port-dependent filtering, which is "moderate" on every console's test, and the out-of-tree modules that change this have never been merged and break on kernel upgrades. So the complaint will arrive and this feature will have nothing to offer it. That is worth knowing in advance rather than discovering in an issue, and it is a different question from whether to run a daemon that punches holes on request.

  • A source allow-list (--from 203.0.113.0/24) in v1. The most-requested neighbouring feature and the most tempting to add, because one ip saddr match in the DNAT rule appears to buy it. It is rejected on a boundary rather than on merit: restricting who may connect is filtering, and putting the first filtering rule in the NAT chain would mean the second one has nowhere to go. It would also be a filter that fails open in a way nobody expects — a source not in the list is not DNATed, which means it reaches the router's own port rather than being refused, so adding an allow-list would quietly expose a local service to the addresses it was meant to exclude. That is not a rule to ship ahead of the chain that would handle it properly.
  • Modelling the destination as a client reference. §1.2.
  • A dmz or "forward everything to this host" object. One rule, universally regretted, and it teaches a worse habit than naming the three ports somebody actually needs.

The sharper reason is what a DMZ host is: a default route for inbound traffic. That only means something on a box with a filtering policy, where "default" is deny and the DMZ host is the declared exception. §2.1 says olr has no such policy, so here it would mean something else entirely — every port on this router, including the ones this router is itself listening on, now belongs to that host. DNAT runs in prerouting, before the local delivery decision (§5.2), so :22, ingress's :80 and :443, and the port the operator administers the box over would all leave with it.

It is worth being explicit that this is not expressible as a range forward, because 1-65535 → host would pass §1.3's identity rule and look like the same thing. It is not: it is the paragraph above, arrived at by accident, with §5.2's local-port warning firing once for every socket on the box. If a DMZ object is ever wanted it belongs to the filtering half, where "default" has a meaning to be an exception to.

  • Matching the WAN address explicitly instead of fib daddr type local. §3.2. It is what every hand-written example does, and it is why those examples break on the next lease renewal.
  • Refusing to apply when another table filters the forward hook, as gateway:§6 refuses foreign ip rule entries. §5.2 has the argument: the two situations look alike and are not. Routing has one owner or it misroutes; filtering composes, and the foreign policy may already permit exactly this traffic.
  • Putting these rules in olr_route. They have different lifetimes and different hooks, and folding them together would mean disabling routing policy took the port forwards with it. design.md §4.2's rule is one table per concern; olr_nat is gateway's (§0).

10. Open

  1. Whether in should accept "any uplink" once dial lands. Today it names one interface. A box with a failover WAN wants both, and the honest spelling of that is a network, not a wildcard — so it waits on link's networks rather than getting a special value now.
  1. Whether the local-port conflict check should be a refusal for the port the request arrived on. Forwarding the port you are currently connected over is the lockout case gateway:§5.1 classifies as disruptive; here it is only a warning, because the connection is not moved, it is the next one that goes elsewhere. Arguably that is still worth the confirm gate.
  1. How a forward should read when the target client is offline. The rule is correct and the connection is refused, which is right, but the screen could say so — it needs clients presence, and the join belongs on the status endpoint rather than in the rule.
  1. Whether split-horizon DNS should be an object, so hairpin can default off. §4.1 is the argument: the masquerade hides the real client, and the better answer is for internal clients to resolve the name to the internal address. dns renders local-zone static entries for the local domain (docs/dns.md §4.6), and a name inside that zone is answered there, so it cannot hold a public name with a private answer. What has since become possible is the cheaper half: a record in the operator's own public zone pointing at a LAN address, which dns.private_domains exempts from anti-rebinding (docs/dns.md §4.6a). That resolves the hairpin problem without a second object — the name is genuinely public, its answer is genuinely private, and nothing is overridden locally. What it does not do is keep a private answer out of public DNS, so an operator who considers that disclosure a problem still needs the split-horizon object, and this stays open for them.
  1. Replies leave by the wrong uplink on a box with two. §6's ct status & IPS_DST_NAT == 0 guard is right for one uplink and, on two, strips the reply of the only mark that could have steered it: a connection arrives on wan1, the reply takes the main table to wan0, conntrack rewrites its source to wan1's address on the way out, and the far side's ISP drops it as spoofed. Nothing is marked for this today. The fix is not gateway's source rules — those are about which exit we choose — but saving the arriving interface into ct mark at prerouting, before DNAT, and restoring it for the reply. It is the same failover-WAN decision as §10.1 and should be taken with it, because a second uplink that silently breaks every forward on the first one is worse than not supporting two.
  1. §10.1's precondition has arrived and this has not noticed. It defers "any uplink" to link's networks rather than a special value; link now has them (internal/link/config.go, Network with Members), while the forwards' LinkView still asks only about interfaces by name. design.md §4.1 is explicit that dependents read a network and "do not read interface names", so this is drift against the stated architecture rather than a preference. Noted here so §10.1 is re-opened rather than quietly stale.
