docs.title: Remote access
docs.summary: OLR manages WireGuard device access and a separate SOCKS5 server. The shared endpoint is the public hostname or address clients use. Each object has its own configuration, status, plan and apply routes. WireGuard programs kernel state; SOCKS5 renders a credential-bearing 3proxy configuration and supervises its unit.
docs.html:
OLR manages WireGuard device access and a separate SOCKS5 server. The shared endpoint is the public hostname or address clients use. Each object has its own configuration, status, plan and apply routes. WireGuard programs kernel state; SOCKS5 renders a credential-bearing 3proxy configuration and supervises its unit.

2. The object: a peer

A peer is a device that may dial in. One is a phone, one is a laptop, one is a work machine the operator wants to keep separate.

The operator gives two things:

FieldExample
namephonethe device's name, here and later in devices
routeshomewhat the device sends through the tunnel

Three more are optional and change only how the device reads: display_name, and the category and icon that decide its picture (§2.2).

Everything else is derived and never asked:

  • the key pair — generated on the box, §4
  • the address on the dial-in network — allocated, §3
  • AllowedIPs on the server side — the peer's own address and nothing else
  • the whole client configuration — rendered and handed back once, §6

So adding a peer is one name, and that is the claim this module makes. olr remote add peer phone prints a configuration file that works.

2.1 What a peer is not

It is not an account, and there is no password. WireGuard authenticates by key pair: a peer is a public key, and the name is olr's label for it. Two consequences worth stating because they surprise people who expect a VPN to have logins:

  • Revoking access is removing the peer. There is nothing to disable; the key stops being accepted the moment the peer is gone, and any session it had dies with it.
  • A peer is a device, not a person. An operator with a phone and a laptop has two peers. Sharing one client configuration between two devices appears to work and then breaks intermittently, because both ends of a WireGuard session assume one endpoint per key — so the validator cannot catch it and the documentation has to say it instead.

2.2 Renaming is a label change, not a re-issue

A device has a name and, if the operator wants one, a label. The name is the key: it is the last segment of the item routes (/api/remote/wireguard/peers/li-mbp), the positional argument every command takes, the unique key of the device list, and the name olr remote add peer hands to olr dns as the local name to answer. So it has to stay a DNS label — letters, digits and hyphens — and it is refused otherwise.

That is a poor fit for the thing a person actually calls their laptop. "Li's Macbook Pro" is what belongs on a screen, a URL path segment is not, and olr dns add host "Li's Macbook Pro" is not a name any resolver would take. So display_name is free text — trimmed, bounded, free of control characters, and otherwise the operator's business — and it is what every surface shows when it is set. It is not unique, because the name already is.

The two are edited in different places for that reason: the label where it is read (the device's own page heading, or the display-name field in the tunnel's device dialog), the name where the device's settings are. Renaming either one changes nothing on the box.

The name being a label rather than something the tunnel carries has a second consequence, and it is the pleasant one: renaming a peer changes nothing on the box. Render does not put the name into the desired state — only keys and addresses reach wg setconf — so olr remote set peer phone --name handset (or the name field in the device dialog) produces an empty plan: no wg setconf, no new key, no new address, and the configuration already imported on the device keeps working.

That is why removing and adding the peer again is not the answer to a typo in a name. A new peer gets the next free address and a fresh key pair (§3, §4), so the file on the device stops matching — a re-issue for what the operator intended as a cosmetic edit.

A picture is the same kind of thing. A peer carries category and icon, and both are labels for exactly the reason the name is one: Render writes neither, so choosing one also produces an empty plan — no wg setconf, no re-issue, nothing for the device to notice. They live on the peer entry rather than anywhere else, so a rename carries them and removing the peer takes them away with it.

The vocabulary is devices' rather than a second one spelled here — one list of categories, one set of pictures, one validator (design.md §4.1). That is a borrow of words, not of identity: nothing in that module is keyed by anything but a MAC, and a peer still has none (§3.3). It is what keeps the picture picker on this page, the picker on a device's page and the API's schema from being three answers to "which pictures exist".

Two things deliberately do not follow a rename, and both are another owner's:

  • A local name in dns. olr dns add host stored that name separately, and §3's rule — stored intent is never derived from another module's addresses — applies to a rename as much as to an add. The rename's response says so.
  • The comment at the top of the imported file. It still carries the old name. It is a comment; nothing reads it.

What is refused is refused before anything is written: a name another device already holds (409), a device that does not exist (404), and a name the validator would not accept for a device at all (422, the same rule olr remote add peer uses).

3. The dial-in segment is a network

The phone that dials in is a device on a network at home. That is a design decision rather than a description, and the alternative was live: the dial-in clients could have been "remote clients", a list belonging to this module and visible nowhere else.

Modelling them as a network is what lets the rest of olr apply to them without being written twice. This section used to list three integrations that fell out of it for free. Then somebody went and read the three modules, and only one of them is free — the corrected version is below, because a justification that overstates its own payoff is worse than a smaller true one.

What it actually costs
gateway's Internet vianothing — it already worksassignments are keyed by kernel interface (internal/gateway/config.go), so olr gateway set via wg0 <exit> sends a peer's traffic out a chosen exit today. gateway:§2.5 will re-key these to network names eventually; until it does, the absence of a network is not felt
dns answering phone.home.example.comone command, the same one every other device costsolr dns add host phone --address 10.6.0.2
a peer appearing in devicesblocked, and not on this module§3.3
a peer appearing on the overview's network mapits own box above the router, keyed by name§3.4

The second row is the one that looked like a gap and is not. A local name in dns is stored intent, never derived from another module's addresses: internal/dns/dhcp.go argues the case at length for DHCP reservations, and every word of it applies here. A name that came from a peer would be correct exactly once; rendered bytes are what drift is measured against (design.md §5.4), so a peer edit would leave dns drifted until somebody applied it — and re-applying dns from inside a remote change would break the promise underneath every mutating route in olr, that one request is planned and the plan decides whether it lands.

So a dial-in device is named exactly the way a device on the LAN is named, and what this module owes is not a mechanism but a pointer: olr remote add peer prints the olr dns add host line with the address already filled in. That is design.md §5.6's rule — automatic behaviour is declared, never inferred — applied to the smallest possible case.

3.3 A peer is not a device, and devices is why

devices is keyed by MAC. Not incidentally — design.md §4.4 says so in as many words, Merge in internal/devices/presence.go drops any sighting whose MAC will not parse, and the vendor lookup, the icon detection and the fixed address all hang off it.

A WireGuard peer has no MAC. It is a public key at the end of a tunnel; there is no layer 2. So putting one in the device list needs one of three things, and two of them are worse than the gap:

  • Synthesise a MAC per peer. A fabricated hardware address in the operator's own device list, with a vendor lookup that would confidently report something. This is the shape of lie the whole Origin field in internal/devices/list.go exists to prevent.
  • Re-key devices on something wider than a MAC. Defensible, possibly right eventually, and a change to a foundation module that four others reference. Not something a new module gets to force on its way in.
  • Leave it. A peer is listed by olr remote show peers, with its address, its last handshake and where it was last seen from — which is more than the device list would show, and in the one vocabulary that is true of it.

The third is what is built, and §11 #2 keeps the question open rather than closed.

The gap was worth closing on screen without closing it in the model. /devices/:mac and /devices/wireguard/<name> look alike because they answer one question — what is this client doing — and the second is the tunnel's answer, drawn in the same place: the name and picture a device at home also has, address, key, what it sends home, when it last handshaked and from where. The header itself is one component (web/src/features/devices/device-header.tsx), shared so the two pages cannot drift apart again.

One state, and only this page has it. A peer's Connected badge is a claim the box can support: every configuration this router renders carries PersistentKeepalive = 25, so a connected peer handshakes at least every two minutes and internal/remote/view.go's three-minute window turns "no handshake" into "not connected". A device at home has no equivalent — its DHCP lease outlives its presence by hours, and /proc/net/arp reports a STALE neighbour entry as complete — so its page claims no presence at all: the lists and the map say when it was last heard, never whether it is online. That is why this page keeps the two rows a device page does not draw: Last heard is the handshake, and only the tunnel can date it; Way in is the tunnel it arrived on, and only the tunnel can name it. What the two pages do share is the facts table and the key each is addressed by — the MAC there, the configured name here — beside the three readings that are keyed by address rather than by hardware, and so need no pretending: the activity history and the traffic counters (gateway keys its accounting on the local device address at either end of the box — forwarded through it, or the far end of a socket here, which is what an ingress name is — and a tunnel address is one), and the DNS query log (dnsrelay records the source address, and the resolver already answers on the tunnel's own — internal/dns/dialin.go).

What is deliberately absent is everything keyed by MAC: vendor, group, address reservation, per-device priority and speed limits (qos classifies with src_mac/dst_mac), and inspection (internal/inspection matches ether saddr before the traffic reaches the network). Those are not switches somebody turned off, and the page says so once rather than showing a control that cannot work.

3.1 Registered, not managed — who writes the address

This is the first time in olr that two modules touch one interface, and it needed resolving rather than assuming.

link owns networks, and applying one writes the router's address to the kernel (internal/link/apply.go, DesiredFor). But wg0 does not exist until this module creates it, and a WireGuard address is not like an Ethernet address in the way that matters:

Assigning the interface's address and assigning a peer's address are one act. Both are fixed at the moment a client configuration is generated, and both are written into a file the operator copies to a phone. A design where link owns one and this module owns the other splits a single decision across two owners for no gain.

So: this module owns the interface and its address. link is not asked to create it, is not asked to address it, and — this is the part that must not be skipped — wg0 is never added to link.Adopted. Adoption is the operator consenting to hand over their NIC (design.md §7); wg0 is olr's own, and there is nothing for anyone to consent to.

And the network is not registered with link at all, which is a reversal of what this section first said. The plan was to register it once a consumer existed. Going to find that consumer is what produced the table above: gateway does not need one, dns must not have one, and devices cannot use one. What is left is a registration with no reader — and one active cost, because dhcp keys off link's networks, so a registered dial-in network would show up on the DHCP page offering to serve addresses on a network whose addresses are not served at all (§3.2).

So remote owns the interface, its address and the segment, and link is not told. The day something needs to name this network, the thing to weigh is whether link grows a notion of a network it does not address — not whether to paper over it here.

3.2 The asymmetry that has to be said out loud

A dial-in network looks like every other network and behaves unlike one in a single respect, and an operator will meet it:

These addresses are not served. They are baked into each client configuration when it is generated.

There is no DHCP here and there never will be — the address is inside the tunnel, and the tunnel does not exist until the client already knows its own address. So an operator who goes to the DHCP page looking for the dial-in network will not find it, and an operator who changes the subnet has invalidated every client configuration they have already handed out.

That second consequence is why changing the subnet is classified disruptive (§7.4) even though nothing is disconnected at the instant it is applied. The damage is to files that already left the box.

3.4 On the map, as a box of their own

§3.3 leaves a peer nowhere in devices, and a network map with nothing on it for a phone that is connected right now is a map that is wrong about the router's own state. So the overview draws each peer itself, and this section is the two decisions that took.

Above the router, in the band. Everything under the router hangs off something — a group by its column, a device by its row — and a card of its own down there would need every group's line to run through it or squeeze past it. Above the router there is exactly one box per line, each joining the router directly, which is what a peer is: a device on the far side of this box. So the band holds where traffic arrives, and a peer is its only kind of box: where traffic leaves is not a thing on this network, and drawing each observed next hop there was a row of cards above the router saying less than Link's routing summary does. Gateway policy exits stay off the map for the same reason: an exit this box chooses among is not a thing outside it.

Four states, not two. connected (a handshake inside internal/remote/view.go's three-minute window), away (last seen at a time), never (no handshake ever — almost always a configuration that was not imported, or a port that does not reach the box), and unknown (the kernel could not be read, which is an absence of an answer and never a "no"). They are the same four PeerBadge draws on the tunnel's own page, for the same reason: "never connected" is the one state the operator can still fix, and folding it into "offline" hides the only failure this module reliably produces.

A peer is not a fault. The one colour the map spends is red, on a way out that has stopped answering; a sleeping laptop is not that, so its card is drawn in the same neutral as everything else and says when it last called.

Drawn as a device, with the way in on its picture. The card is a device node: the peer's own picture from the same picker a device uses, its label over its tunnel address, and the state in the narrow figure column a device row keeps for its rate or its last-heard time. A card that announced the tunnel in place of any of those — a WireGuard mark instead of the picture, a dashed outline nothing else on the map uses — told an operator which module to edit rather than which machine this is.

That rule was written as "no mark at all", and what it produced was the one thing a card above the router could not help being: indistinguishable at a glance from a device under it, which is exactly what a map exists to spare somebody. The way in is now a badge on the corner of the picture: the WireGuard mark at full brand colour, on the white disc a protocol's artwork gets on the Access page, ringed in the card's colour so it reads as a badge rather than as a second picture. A mark on the picture is not a mark instead of it — which is the thing this section refuses — and it costs the card no width, no line of type and no second reading order. The method also stays in the tooltip ("over wg0"). The peer's own page wears the same badge on the same picture (WayBadge, web/src/features/remote/way-badge.tsx), so the two views agree about what this device is and how it got here.

The state stays because it is the one thing a tunnel can answer and a device cannot (§3.3): a device list reports when it was last heard, while a keepalive makes "connected right now" a fact here. connected draws as a filled dot instead of the word, because the word read as a description of the card rather than as its state; the word stays as the card's title and its accessible name. The other three stay words: an absence of evidence must never be a status light.

The card says the label, the click target says the name. display_name when there is one and the name otherwise, because a card in a band is read by a person — while what it opens is the device's page, keyed by the name (§2.2). The two are separate fields on the map's own shape for that reason: one string that meant both at once was a card that opened nothing the day a label arrived.

RemoteStatus.peers is the only input. A box with the tunnel switched off gets no box, no empty container and no "WireGuard is off" note — the map is about what is on the network, and remote's page is where a module that is off is described.

4. Keys

A WireGuard key pair is 32 bytes of X25519. olr generates both halves itself, with crypto/ecdh from the standard library — not by running wg genkey, and not with a new dependency.

That is worth one sentence of justification because shelling out would have been the obvious thing: key generation is the one operation in this module that has to work on a machine with no wg and no Linux, because that is where the tests run. Doing it in the standard library makes the whole of key handling pure, testable anywhere, and independent of whether the backend is installed.

The private key is clamped exactly as wg genkey clamps it, so a key generated here and a key generated there are indistinguishable.

4.1 Where the keys live, and what never leaves

Two key pairs exist per peer relationship and they are treated differently:

KeyStoredLeaves the box
the box's private keyin the configuration document, redacted everywherenever
the box's public keyderived on demandin every client configuration
a peer's public keyin the configuration documentno
a peer's private keynowhereonce, in the client configuration

The last row is the one that carries a cost, and it is taken deliberately. olr generates the peer's key pair so that adding a peer is one command, hands the complete client configuration back in the response to that command, and keeps only the public half. There is no route that returns that file a second time, because there is nothing left to build it from.

A lost client configuration is a re-issue, not a re-download. POST /api/remote/wireguard/peers/{name}/reissue (the New setup file button on the device's page) generates a new key pair and hands over the file that matches it. The old file stops working the moment the kernel takes the new public key.

Everything else about the device stays where it was, which is the argument for having the route at all: removing the peer and adding it again used to be the only way back, and it renumbers (§3, NextAddress), drops the label and drops the picture — three things an operator who lost a phone's configuration never asked to change. The response is a handover like the add's, so it carries the same warning and the same one-chance rule; it is held behind the disruptive gate as well, because until the new file is imported that device cannot dial in.

Storing the peer's private key would make the config re-showable and is what most WireGuard front-ends do. It is refused here for the reason ingress:§4.1 gives about the DNS provider token, one step further along: a credential that is never stored cannot be disclosed by a backup, a screenshot, or a GET somebody forgot to redact. The convenience lost is one click when a file goes missing, and a key that changes when that happens is the safer of the two answers anyway.

An operator who would rather generate the key on the device itself can: olr remote add peer laptop --public-key <key> stores the public half and declines to print a client configuration at all, because it cannot write one without a private key it does not have. The tunnel settings are printed instead, for the operator to paste into a configuration they complete themselves.

5. The backend: wg, and never wg-quick

olr ships no WireGuard. The data path is in the kernel; what has to be installed is wireguard-tools, which is in every distribution's repository and is declared the way every other backend is (core.Dependency, Inert: true — the package installs two binaries and starts nothing).

5.1 wg-quick would trip olr's own refusal

wg-quick is the obvious way to bring a WireGuard interface up and it is the wrong one here, for a reason found by reading olr's own code rather than by taste.

wg-quick up with AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0 installs its own policy routing: an ip rule at priority 32765 selecting table 51820, which carries a default route. gateway's observeRules (internal/gateway/kernel_linux.go) flags any foreign ip rule selecting a table that carries a default route, because that is the definition of a second owner of "where does traffic go" — and gateway:§6 then refuses the whole apply.

So using wg-quick inside olr would mean olr breaking olr: the tunnel comes up and olr gateway stops working, with a refusal message about somebody else's routing daemon that is in fact us.

The collision is not a reason to avoid WireGuard. It is a reason to avoid wg-quick, whose entire job is the part olr already does:

wg-quick doesolr does
create the interfacenetlink, internal/remote/kernel_linux.go
set the addressnetlink, same file
bring the link upnetlink, same file
load the peer configurationwg setconf
install ip rules and routesnothing — that is gateway's

The last row is the whole point. A tunnel olr created installs no competing rule, so Internet via keeps working, and the one useful thing wg-quick would have brought is the one thing that must not happen.

5.2 What olr executes, and the rule it bends

wg setconf <interface> <file> is the only subprocess this module runs. That needs stating against design.md §3.6, which says olrd executes no subprocesses, and which already carries two exceptions (caddy validate, and the package manager as a transient unit).

This is a third, and it is the mild kind: wg reads one file we just wrote and writes kernel state through its own netlink socket. It touches no filesystem path, needs nothing the unit does not already have — every olr unit runs as root with no sandbox (design.md §3.5) — and is bounded.

The alternative, wgctrl, would configure the peers over netlink from inside olrd and delete the exec. It was not taken for batch 1 on dependency budget: go.mod has six direct dependencies and that restraint has already decided several arguments in this codebase. Everything wg is used for sits behind Kernel (kernel.go), which is the seam design.md §10 requires anyway, so swapping it later is a change to one file.

There is no configuration file. The rendered configuration is handed to wg setconf on standard input — wg setconf wg0 /dev/stdin — so the box's private key never reaches a filesystem at all. This is the same mechanism wg-quick uses (it passes a process substitution), and it is worth the small unfamiliarity: the document already holds the one copy of the key that design.md §3.4 says the operator's data lives in, and a second copy at rest, even for the milliseconds between writing a temporary file and deleting it, would be a second thing to protect with no reader.

So this module writes no file, which is a departure from design.md §7's "generated files live under rendered/". The generated artefact here is kernel state, not something a daemon re-reads — exactly the situation gateway and gateway is already in.

6. What a client configuration says

The file handed back when a peer is created is the product of this module as much as the tunnel is. Every line of it is derived:

[Interface]
PrivateKey = <generated, shown once>
Address    = 10.6.0.2/32
DNS        = 10.6.0.1

[Peer]
PublicKey           = <the box's>
Endpoint            = home.example.net:51820
AllowedIPs          = 10.6.0.0/24, 192.168.1.0/24
PersistentKeepalive = 25

6.1 Endpoint is the one thing olr cannot derive, and it belongs to the box

It is the public name or address a client dials, and nothing here knows it: the uplink address may be behind a carrier NAT, and the name that tracks it lives at a DNS provider. So it is required as soon as anything is switched on, and the validator refuses rather than rendering a configuration that cannot connect.

It sits at the module level rather than inside either object, because both need exactly this value and a field typed twice is a field that can disagree with itself — design.md §4.1's rule occurring inside one module rather than across two. An operator who moves house changes it once.

The consequence is that it carries no port: each object listens on its own, so a port here could only ever be right for one of them. An object whose public port differs from the one it listens on says so with its own public_port, and the validator refuses a port on the shared field rather than guessing which object it was meant for.

An operator who is already using olr dial has the answer — it is the name they keep current there — and the refusal says so. Reading it from dial automatically was considered and declined: dial holds a list of records and nothing says which one is this box's front door, so olr would be guessing at a value whose wrongness presents as "the VPN just doesn't connect".

6.2 AllowedIPs means two different things and we name only one

On the server side, a peer's AllowedIPs is a filter: which source addresses that key may use. olr derives it — the peer's own address, a /32, and nothing else — and does not offer it as a field. Anything wider is a cryptokey-routing decision with no operator-facing question behind it.

On the client side, the same word means the opposite thing: what the device sends into the tunnel. That is a real choice with a real trade, so it is a field, and it is spelled in the operator's words rather than WireGuard's:

routesThe device sends home
home (default)the home networks and the dial-in networkthe NAS, the printer, the router's own UI; everything else goes out the coffee shop's Wi-Fi as normal
everythingall of itthe device appears to be at home for every purpose, including its public IP address

home is the default for a reason the client-side/router-side symmetry usually hides: the client is a phone out in the world, and full-tunnel drags its video calls across the operator's home upload. The "configure it once on the router" instinct that is right for devices at home is wrong here, because olr is not in the path of anything the phone does until the phone decides it should be.

Which is also why changing it later is not something olr can do. The value lives in the file on the device and nowhere else — the tunnel does not know it and cannot be told — so olr remote set on an existing peer stores the new intent, produces no kernel change whatsoever, and answers with the one line the operator has to edit on the device. Saying nothing there would be the worst of the three options: the operator would believe it had been done.

The prefixes behind home are read from link's networks per request, never copied (design.md §4.1). A box with no networks configured yet gets a warning saying the configuration will reach the router and nothing behind it.

Peers leave by the router's own address. A peer holds an address on no network this box serves, so a device on one of them sees a source it cannot route to — 10.6.0.7 is neither on its network nor on its default route — and its reply leaves by whatever gateway it has and never comes back. Every network link serves therefore gets a masquerade for the dial-in subnet, so the device sees the connection coming from this router on that network and replies to it:

oifname "br-lan" ip saddr 10.6.0.0/24 masquerade

olr diff prints the same rule as nft dialin out br-lan from 10.6.0.0/24. The cost is the one every masquerade has: a device's log, or a rule written against its address, shows the router rather than the peer.

The rule is skipped when the tunnel's subnet overlaps a network this box serves — remote refuses to create such a tunnel, and if link later moves a network onto its prefix, rewriting that network's own source range would break every device on it. A tunnel whose addresses collide is unusable either way, and writing nothing is the safe half of that failure.

The tunnel's subnet is in the egress masquerade's source set for the same reason, which is what makes routes everything reach the internet at all: a peer that sends all of its traffic leaves with the uplink's address, the same one a laptop on the LAN leaves with.

6.3 DNS points at the router

So that a dial-in device resolves local names the way a device at home does: nas.home.example.com has to answer, or "reach the whole network" is only true for people who memorised addresses. The address is the box's own on the dial-in network, which is inside AllowedIPs in both modes, so it works for split tunnels too.

dns answers on that address by construction rather than by an operator remembering to pin it: it subscribes to the tunnel's address (design.md §4.1's remote → dns arrow) and binds it leniently, so a tunnel that comes up after the relay does is still answered on. A tunnel that is on while dns is off is the one combination olr cannot make work; olr dns status reports the served set so "not configured" and "not served" stay distinguishable.

6.4 PersistentKeepalive = 25

Rendered always. Without it a peer behind NAT is reachable only while it is sending, so the operator's phone is contactable from home for a minute after it last spoke and then silently is not. Twenty-five seconds is upstream's recommendation and is below every NAT timeout worth worrying about.

7. Mechanism

Intent in the configuration document under remote (design.md §3.2 rule 1). No rendered file that survives an apply, no backend to supervise — what this module configures is the kernel, which makes it gateway-shaped and not ingress-shaped.

7.1 There is no unit

This is the surprising half and it is worth being explicit, because every other module with a backend has one. WireGuard's data path is in the kernel. There is no daemon to start, nothing for systemd to supervise, and wg-quick@wg0.service is the unit this module exists not to use (§5.1).

design.md §3.5's test decides it: does it have to keep running while olrd is stopped? The tunnel does, and it does — kernel state outlives olrd without anyone's help. So there is nothing to put in a unit.

What kernel state does not outlive is a reboot. So this module is applied at olrd startup, exactly as gateway is, and for exactly the same reason: the configuration would otherwise survive perfectly and be in force nowhere.

7.2 Apply order

Bottom-up, and each intermediate state has to be one where a peer either connects correctly or does not connect at all — never one where a handshake succeeds and the traffic goes nowhere:

create the interface  →  address it  →  wg setconf  →  bring it up

Up is last on purpose. An interface that is up with no peers configured is a socket accepting handshakes it will reject; the window is milliseconds and it produces a client that reports a failure at the exact moment olr is making things work, which is the sort of thing that gets reported as a bug in the wrong place.

Tearing down is the reverse and ends by deleting the interface, because a WireGuard interface with no configuration is indistinguishable, to anybody reading ip link, from one that is broken.

7.3 The escape hatch

remote.wireguard.raw_wireguard_conf, per design.md §3.2 rule 5: appended verbatim to what wg setconf is given. WireGuard's own configuration format has few knobs olr does not model — a pre-shared key, an FwMark — and this is the whole of the answer to all of them.

It is additive and cannot restate what olr renders, checked the same way ingress checks its Caddyfile hatch: textually, erring toward allowing, with the authoritative check being wg setconf refusing the file before anything else happens.

7.4 Impact, in the operator's terms

ImpactWhat it means here
nonenothing the kernel reads changes
reloada peer is added, or its client-side routes change. No live tunnel is disturbed — wg setconf keeps the session state of every peer whose key is unchanged
restartthe listen port or the box's address moves. Live tunnels drop and re-establish by themselves, because a WireGuard client retries forever
disruptivesomething stops working and does not come back on its own

disruptive is reached by four things and each of them is a fact rather than a guess:

  • removing a peer that has connected — compared against the keys the kernel is actually holding, not against the stored list, so removing a peer nobody ever used is not dressed up as an outage;
  • changing the subnet or the box's key — every client configuration already handed out becomes wrong, and no retry fixes a file on somebody's phone;
  • disabling the module — the way in goes away;
  • changing the listen port while the endpoint is a bare address — the same problem as the subnet: the file says the old port.

8. SOCKS5

/api/remote/socks5 exposes config, status, plan, apply and credential-link routes. The link is deliberately absent from MCP tools because it contains the password. Config and plan responses redact secrets.

The proxy listens on every interface and has no other shape. It stands alone: nothing in it is derived from the tunnel, and a box serves it with WireGuard switched off — a proxy is a way out of this network, and the tunnel that gets devices in plays no part in that. SOCKS5 carries no transport encryption, so the backend attaches its exposure warning whenever the proxy is on, and the UI renders it. Replacing credentials can invalidate existing links and uses the normal disruptive-change confirmation gate.

There used to be a listen scope that could confine the listener to the WireGuard address. It was removed rather than kept: it coupled two independent objects, it was never reachable from the UI or the CLI, and the encryption it implied is one SOCKS5 does not have. A stored listen: internet is accepted and dropped on the next save; a stored listen: tunnel is refused by the validator rather than converted, because turning a proxy that only a dialled-in device could reach into one the internet can reach is not a change olr may make on somebody's behalf.

8.1 The binary is found, not assumed

olr ships no 3proxy. The unit ships naming /usr/lib/open-linux-router/3proxy — the place the install hint tells an operator who builds it by hand to put it — and FindSocks looks there first, then $PATH, then the sbin directories.

3proxy's own package installs to /usr/bin instead, and the ordinary order of events is install olr, enable it, turn SOCKS5 on, then install 3proxy. So the path the unit names and the binary the box has are allowed to differ, and the apply is what closes the gap: it writes /etc/systemd/system/olr-socks5.service.d/10-path.conf naming the binary it found and reloads systemd (internal/remote/socks_unit.go).

A drop-in rather than an edited unit, because olr enable rewrites the units on every upgrade; and written by the apply rather than by olr enable, because installing 3proxy is the step that comes last. Without it the unit fails at ExecStart with 203/EXEC — a rendered config that is exactly right, a proxy that never starts, and nothing on screen connecting the two.

9. Removed protocol migration

Shadowsocks is no longer supported. Its API, CLI, renderer, installer guidance, service unit and launcher entry have been removed. Old stored sections are ignored on read and dropped when remote configuration is next saved. They cannot enable a listener or open a firewall port. Package upgrades stop and mask only olr-shadowsocks.service; independently installed services are outside OLR ownership. Old rendered credential files are not deleted automatically. Standalone-binary upgrades must stop and disable the old OLR service before replacing the binary.

headings.text: 3. The dial-in segment is a network

docs.title: Remote access interface
docs.summary: Access shows three square-tile grids: Networking, Add a way out and Add a way in. There is no System default row or purpose filter. A technology can appear in both directional grids; each tile is a link to the configuration owner for that direction, so there is no intermediate dialog. Hover/focus explains functions and observed state, and the tile's accessible name carries that state for touch and screen readers. A technology OLR does not configure links to the project's own documentation in a new tab.
docs.html:
Access shows three square-tile grids: Networking, Add a way out and Add a way in. There is no System default row or purpose filter. A technology can appear in both directional grids; each tile is a link to the configuration owner for that direction, so there is no intermediate dialog. Hover/focus explains functions and observed state, and the tile's accessible name carries that state for touch and screen readers. A technology OLR does not configure links to the project's own documentation in a new tab.

Tiles use bundled project artwork from web/public/access-logos, taken from theSVG wherever the library carries the project, so the launcher matches the marks used elsewhere in the interface. Headscale is the one mark outside the library, from its own repository. The rest are protocols rather than projects: SOCKS5, Gateway, frp and SSH wear a capital initial on a tinted tile, which keeps two entries sharing an initial (SSH and SOCKS5) apart by hue instead of by borrowed branding. See the logo directory README for provenance.

Port forwarding is not in this directory. It is a forwarding rule rather than a remote-access technology, it shares one nftables ruleset with the firewall, and it lives under Advanced → System. The grid, heading and tile live in components/layout/launcher.tsx, which Advanced uses as well.

Connection model

web/src/features/access/catalog.ts defines direction, kind, name, purpose and canonical configuration URL. A way is a connection capability, not a promise that all connections can be selected in every context. Protocol does not decide direction: SOCKS5 appears in both directions with different configuration owners.

DirectionKindConfiguration ownerCanonical URL
OutGateway or existing VPN interfacegateway exits/access/gateway
OutExternal SOCKS5socksout/access/socks5
OutTunnel Broker / HEdial.tunnelbroker/access/tunnelbroker
InWireGuardremote.wireguard and remote endpoint/access/wireguard
InSOCKS5 serverremote SOCKS5/access/socks-server

System default is a built-in way out, displayed separately with observed IPv4 and IPv6 routes. It cannot be added or deleted. No default-for-networks setting is introduced. Networks, groups and devices retain their existing inheritance and route selection; Access owns discovery and connection configuration. Blocking is a routing policy rather than an addable connection.

Each connection keeps one configuration owner and its current lifecycle. A proxy or HE tunnel's generated interface is not another connection to create. HE keeps its routed prefixes, activation and LAN assignment; its source routing still precedes gateway policy, and native IPv6 retains its route. No generic selector, automatic prefix migration, new failover or dependency chaining is introduced. Tunnel/proxy establishment depends on an underlying path; future configurable dependencies must reject cycles and keep transport traffic out of its own tunnel.

Ways in express either joining the network, borrowing its internet access or publishing a service. Those intents share a directory, not permissions or a universal configuration form. Credentials and exposure remain in their own workflows. The directory references each technology once, with a separate tile per direction where it has multiple configuration owners. Publishing a service by domain name is not in this directory: it is Advanced → Services → Caddy (/advanced/caddy), reached from the Advanced directory or from a device's service action. The old /access/ingress address redirects there.

Former Gateway URLs and Advanced addresses redirect while preserving query parameters and fragments. There is no combined remote access page: the old /access/remote address redirects to /access/wireguard, and WireGuard and SOCKS5 each keep their own view. Directory tiles link to individual views of the same configuration, with independent status summaries.

The landing page reads existing configuration and status endpoints. It never applies network changes. A failed observation is shown as unavailable rather than off, and saved intent with a stopped service is shown as needing attention. The outbound SOCKS5 summary describes the local TUN service, not the reachability of the external proxy. Protocol settings and configuration apply paths remain on their respective pages.

Validation

Caddy-directory revision: publishing moved out of Access entirely, to Advanced → Services → Caddy (/advanced/caddy), and /access/ingress, /advanced/ingress and /ingress redirect there with their query string and fragment intact. The page keeps its device-row entry points and its live "addresses / certificate" answer on the tile, which wears Caddy's own mark from theSVG (web/public/service-logos/caddy.svg) on the launcher's white tile. Node 24 lint (27 existing warnings, 0 errors), the production build, all 56 UI tests and the interface-rate checks pass. A headless browser against a scratch daemon verifies the Services grid carries a Caddy tile whose link and accessible name are /advanced/caddy and Caddy · Off, that all three former addresses land on /advanced/caddy (including ?device=), that Access no longer offers the page, and that the document does not overflow at a true 375-pixel viewport (scrollWidth 375). Screenshots at 1440 and 375 in light and dark themes: /tmp/olr-caddy-review. Linux-targeted go vet passes, and go test ./... passes except TestCloudflareResultAndScore, which fails identically on unmodified main. No live router settings were changed.

Advanced-directory revision: port forwarding, external filtering and administrator access left this section for Advanced; the directory is the technology list only. Node 24 lint (existing warnings only), production build and all UI tests pass, including the summaries that now answer for port forwarding and the two services. No browser pass against a live router was run for this revision, and no live router settings were changed.

Direct-navigation revision: removing Nebula, HTTP and HTTPS leaves five Networking tiles, four ways out and five ways in. Node 24 lint, production build, all 42 UI tests and the interface-rate checks pass. A headless browser against a scratch daemon verifies every tile is an anchor, that configuration tiles route in place (Gateway, SOCKS5 and NAT open /access/gateway, /access/socks5 and /access/forwards), that no dialog element exists, that unintegrated tiles keep target="_blank" with rel="noopener noreferrer", and that nothing overflows at 375 pixels. Screenshots at 1440 and 375 pixels in light and dark themes: /tmp/access-{light,dark}-{1440,375}.png. No live router settings changed.

Protocol removal: Go 1.27 Linux vet and all tests pass. Node 24 lint (existing warnings only), all 29 UI tests, interface-rate checks and production build pass. Browser checks verify removed technologies are absent, retained technologies and SOCKS5 configuration links remain, bundled logos load and no page overflows at 375, 768 and 1440 pixels in light and dark themes. Screenshots are in /tmp/olr-protocol-removal-review. No live router configuration was changed.

Direction/logo revision: Node 24 lint, production build, all UI tests and Linux Go 1.27 vet/tests pass. Browser checks at 375, 768 and 1440 pixels in both themes verify the two headings, removed default/filter controls, square tiles, loaded local logos, hover/focus explanations, keyboard dialogs and configuration links. Screenshots: /tmp/olr-access-logos-review. No live router settings changed.

Previous directory revision:

Technology-directory checks cover all 24 tiles at 375, 768 and 1440 pixels in light and dark themes, square proportions, horizontal overflow, hover, keyboard activation, detail dialogs, purpose filtering, both SOCKS5 actions and external documentation links. Screenshots are retained in /tmp/olr-access-directory-review. Node 24 lint, production build and all 25 UI tests plus interface-rate checks pass; lint retains existing unrelated warnings. Linux Go vet and tests pass with Go 1.27. These checks use synthetic responses and do not change live router settings.

Earlier connection/status refactor validation:

UI lint, production build and all UI tests pass with Node 24, including ten Access status regression tests. Linux Go vet and tests pass with Go 1.27 (the commands behind make check were run directly because make was unavailable). Browser checks for the tile refactor use synthetic API responses at 375, 768 and 1440 pixel widths in light/dark themes, keyboard focus, overflow checks, individual configuration pages, the two Gateway redirects with query and hash preservation, and read-failure state. Screenshots are captured for review. No live router settings were changed.

Illustration

web/src/assets/access-connections.webp is a decorative, transparent 256 × 256 WebP (8,690 bytes), displayed at 64–96 CSS pixels with empty alternative text. It was generated using the built-in MyLifeDB generate_image tool with gpt-image-2, medium quality and a square size request, then resized with Pillow and encoded at quality 88. Its alpha channel is preserved. It is a page illustration, not a replacement for the application's logo.

Final generation prompt:

Use case: stylized-concept
Asset type: compact decorative illustration for Open Linux Router's Access settings page, displayed at 96px beside a short introduction, not a hero banner or replacement brand logo.
Primary request: a refined physical sculpture suggesting private connections into and out of a home network: two interlocking open rounded loops, one satin porcelain silver and one restrained system blue, with two tiny connection nodes.
Scene/backdrop: genuinely transparent background.
Style/medium: premium minimalist 3D product illustration, precise smooth curves, matte ceramic, soft studio lighting, subtle contact shadows, crisp silhouette.
Composition/framing: centered small balanced sculpture occupying 80 percent of square frame, readable at small scale. Quiet and functional, suitable on both white and charcoal UI backgrounds.
Color palette: porcelain gray and muted medium blue matching a neutral system-style control panel.
Constraints: transparent alpha; no text, no letters, no watermark, no gradients in backdrop, no frame, no glow, no additional objects or wires.

docs.title: Request inspection
docs.summary: Inspection is a client setting that stays on until you turn it off. Page reloads, OLR daemon restarts, package upgrades and router reboots preserve that choice. Completed and failed captured HTTP(S) requests are saved with their full native mitmproxy content, so stopping inspection does not erase what was already saved. Only one client can be inspected at a time; saved history for every client remains available while its switch is off or another client is being inspected.
docs.html:
Inspection is a client setting that stays on until you turn it off. Page reloads, OLR daemon restarts, package upgrades and router reboots preserve that choice. Completed and failed captured HTTP(S) requests are saved with their full native mitmproxy content, so stopping inspection does not erase what was already saved. Only one client can be inspected at a time; saved history for every client remains available while its switch is off or another client is being inspected.

Setup

Install mitmproxy (mitmweb) on the Linux router before starting. On Debian, use sudo apt install mitmproxy. It is optional rather than a package dependency.

  1. Open the client page, check its IPv4 addresses, and turn Inspection on. OLR creates its CA on the first start. The switch starts interception directly.
  2. Open the gear beside the switch. Scan the QR code on the client or follow Open setup guide to the public five-step guide at /inspection-setup.html. The certificate download is at step two. The guide and public certificate need no administrator token; they never expose the private key.
  3. Install and trust the CA on the client for HTTPS. On iPhone, enable full trust in Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings after installing the profile. Compare its SHA-256 fingerprint with the guide's current CA.
  4. Browse from that client and open saved requests or the Live request viewer. HTTP needs no CA. HTTPS content is available only when the app accepts the CA.
  5. Turn Inspection off when you want interception to stop. Saved requests and activity remain available. Remove the CA from the client when it is no longer needed; stopping inspection does not revoke the client's trust.

OLR keeps the CA, client switch and inspection data beneath /var/lib/open-linux-router/inspection with restricted permissions. Removing or backing up that directory also affects the CA trusted by clients. The API serves only the public PEM, never its private key. If the configured proxy cannot start, the client page keeps the switch on, shows the reason and offers Retry.

Saved requests and the Live viewer

The Inspection card shows Activity, current DNS queries while active, and Requests. Requests opens saved history by default. During active inspection, Saved and Live select between that history and the embedded mitmweb viewer. Saved history is independent of the live viewer's rolling memory list.

Search saved requests and use Load older requests to page through them. Each row shows the timestamp, method, URL, HTTP status (or failure) and archived size. Select a row to read request/response headers and text bodies inline. Each body preview is limited to 64 KiB and labels truncation; binary bodies are identified instead of rendered as text. Failed requests can have no response. Download .mitm downloads the full native flow, including content beyond the preview. Open it in mitmproxy or mitmweb, for example mitmweb -r inspection-ID.mitm. Downloads use the administrator bearer credential in an HTTP header, never a URL.

The archive saves a flow after the captured HTTP request completes or fails. A request still in progress is not yet a durable archive: stopping or crashing the proxy can lose that unfinished content. A router reboot also ends those requests. An OLR daemon restart does not stop an already running inspection proxy on the packaged Linux service; its completed flows continue to be archived while the control daemon is restarting. Archiving failures appear explicitly in the card. A live response alone is not proof that its archive was successfully written.

Clear saved requests opens a confirmation dialog and deletes only the current client's saved request/response archive. It leaves other clients' archives and site activity intact, and an enabled inspection continues capturing new requests. Turning Inspection off leaves all saved history intact.

The gear dialog contains global retention settings. Defaults are 30 days and 5 GiB of saved request storage total across all clients on this router. The request list shows client usage and router-wide usage against that shared cap. The oldest saved requests are removed when the age or storage limit is reached. Retention is adjustable from 1 to 365 days and from 1 MiB to 1 TiB. Reducing a limit can remove older saved requests immediately. This is bounded local history; export flows you need to keep beyond those limits. Filesystem metadata and transient files can require additional disk space beyond saved archive usage.

The live viewer keeps the latest 1000 flows in memory so leaving inspection on cannot grow its working set without bound. This limit does not limit the archive to 1000 flows. Mitmweb binds only to router loopback (127.0.0.1:18082); OLR embeds it at /inspection-web/ for the active client. The browser obtains a short-lived HttpOnly viewer cookie through the authenticated API, and OLR adds the proxy's bearer token server-side for HTTP and WebSocket traffic. No second login or LAN listener is required. Turning Inspection off revokes live access.

Retained site activity and DNS

The Activity chart offers 4 hours, 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days. It reads retained samples by client MAC, including when the client has no current address, inspection is off, or another client is active. Its total is for the selected range. Samples are collected only while this client's inspection is on; saved samples survive stop/start and OLR restarts. There are no samples during control-daemon downtime, and retaining earlier samples does not fill those gaps. Site samples have a separate fixed bound of 30 days and 64 MiB across clients; they do not consume the configurable 5 GiB saved-request allowance.

Sites use registrable domains under the public suffix list, so a suffix such as com.cn is not itself presented as a site. The chart uses the DNS relay's address names, then names observed by the proxy for the same client/destination pair. Connections outside interception's scope can remain unnamed. Activity is sampled connection traffic, not the request archive's file size or a complete browsing history. Clearing saved requests does not clear these activity samples.

DNS queries are a separate recent network-wide sample matched to the client's current IPs; the relay's query log must be enabled. A DNS lookup is not proof of a visit. The DNS sample is not the saved request archive.

Scope and service behavior

OLR intercepts only selected source IPv4 traffic on TCP ports 80/443 to public destinations. IPv6, UDP/443 (QUIC), LAN destinations, other ports and non-HTTP protocols are outside scope. OLR does not block QUIC to force fallback. A client can have up to eight explicitly selected IPv4 addresses. Check their ownership: OLR does not prove the MAC owns them or automatically follow reassignment. Certificate pinning and separate app trust stores can prevent decryption or make an app fail to connect. The page does not claim a complete list of connections.

When the client has an explicit gateway exit, OLR marks only mitmweb's upstream packets to follow that exit so fake-IP DNS answers can remain usable. Without an explicit exit, 198.18.0.0/15 destinations bypass interception. Stop and restart inspection after changing the client's exit to pick up that change.

On packaged Linux systems the inspection proxy runs as its own systemd service, independent of the OLR daemon, so a control-daemon deployment does not interrupt capture. Reboot starts the configured inspection again. An explicit stop ends the proxy and restores normal forwarding. OLR waits for proxy readiness before installing interception and reconciles its own nftables rules after failure. The listener guard accepts only selected sources whose conntrack original TCP destination was port 80/443; direct LAN connections to the proxy port are dropped. Do not use ct status dnat alone to identify these redirects.

Redirect-rule packet counts and accepted proxy socket counts are diagnostics, not evidence of a completed or saved response. A zero redirect count after a known IPv4 HTTP request indicates a rule mismatch; growing redirects with zero proxy accepts points to delivery between netfilter and the proxy.

Startup errors include recent proxy stderr with its viewer token redacted. Retry shows progress and preserves the failure reason. Process cleanup requests normal termination before forced termination so standalone PyInstaller extraction files can be removed by their owner. OLR does not sweep unrelated temporary files.

Validate on a real Linux router before relying on the interception path: HTTP, trusted HTTPS, pinned apps, IPv4 changes, QUIC, proxy failure, OLR restart, reboot, archive persistence/retention and nftables cleanup. macOS Go/UI checks cannot exercise that path.

The opt-in TestManagedSystemdContinuity smoke test validates the generated unit on a real root/systemd host with mitmweb installed. Build the inspection test binary for that host, then run sudo env OLR_INSPECTION_SYSTEMD_SMOKE=1 ./inspection.test -test.v -test.run '^TestManagedSystemdContinuity$'. It uses its own temporary service, CA, and loopback ports 28081/28082, with a no-op stop hook instead of nftables. It verifies an unchanged proxy PID and continued capture after control-plane detachment, then checks retained records after proxy restart. The test removes its own service and temporary data.

History API

All endpoints below require the same administrator authentication as other API operations. MAC identifies the archive owner independently of current addresses.

Method and pathPurpose
GET /api/inspection/history?mac=&before=&limit=&search=Newest-first saved entries, opaque pagination cursor, client/router byte usage and current retention limits
GET /api/inspection/history/detail?mac=&id=Saved entry metadata with request/response headers and bounded text previews
GET /api/inspection/history/flow?mac=&id=Full native .mitm download
DELETE /api/inspection/history?mac=Clear this client's saved request archive only, after explicit UI confirmation
GET /api/inspection/retentionGlobal {days,max_bytes} retention settings
PUT /api/inspection/retentionUpdate global {days,max_bytes} limits
`GET /api/inspection/activity?mac=&range=4h\24h\7d\30d`Retained activity buckets and current recording state

History entries carry id, Unix-seconds at, method, url, status and bytes. status: 0 identifies failed captured requests. List responses include entries, next_before, per-client retained_bytes, router-wide total_bytes, retention_days and global max_bytes. Detail messages are nullable and include headers: [{name,value}], body, body_bytes, body_truncated and body_binary; a failed flow may also include error. Inspection status includes history_error when archiving fails.
