docs.title: Visual style guide
docs.summary: This is the shared reference for future UI changes. The direction is a precise, calm network console with lightly tangible surfaces. Clarity of network state comes first; polish comes from alignment, typography, restrained depth and consistent interaction. Keep the existing Geist typeface, router identity and device imagery.
docs.html:
This is the shared reference for future UI changes. The direction is a precise, calm network console with lightly tangible surfaces. Clarity of network state comes first; polish comes from alignment, typography, restrained depth and consistent interaction. Keep the existing Geist typeface, router identity and device imagery.

For information hierarchy, wording and progressive disclosure, follow the content and presentation standards.

For the cross-page component inventory, typography roles, surface interactions and migration targets, follow the semantic component contracts. That document defines shared size variants and records the implementation audit; route-specific behavior below remains applicable.

Findings and decisions

The audit found inconsistent content widths and headings, oversized tool illustrations, repeated borders, scattered save buttons, values hidden on phones, a cramped six-section navigation and inconsistent color meanings. The shared shell, heading, list and control primitives now define the baseline. Use them before creating page-specific styling.

Content cleanup must preserve existing data space and component consistency. Remove redundant wording before changing density. Keep established metric cards, charts and common fields; avoid introducing extra presentation variants for secondary information. See the page review record.

Color and surfaces

Configuration backup reuses PageHeading, Card, Input and Button. Use a shared Alert for the validated restore review. Keep file selection and restore actions reachable on phones; wrap module names, errors and long addresses.

Connectivity recovery uses the shared Alert and Button components above the application shell. Match shell width/gutters, wrap actions on phones, and retain visible errors and remaining confirmation time on every page and after reload.

World traffic is the one map where hue belongs to data rather than to status. Every location gets one translucent amber arc of the same weight: 2px where the map fits the world into a laptop or a large window, about 1px in the card preview and on a phone, where the same world is only a few hundred pixels wide. Amber sits outside the country palette, so traffic reads as an overlay on geography; the arc fades in at the router, and a blurred halo underneath accumulates where arcs bunch up so busy junctions read as light rather than as spaghetti. An arc holds its weight for as long as its location reports traffic in the sampled window and fades only when the location leaves it: a line that dimmed while the flow continued would claim a connection had ended, and the sampler cannot know that — it differences conntrack counters and reports a rate over a rolling window, with no connection start or end. Width does not carry volume for the same reason it was flattened: four thicknesses compared badly across dozens of arcs, and the ranked rates live in the details dialog, so the map stays a presence and direction picture. A few arcs at a time — never more than five, and fewer when the map is sparse — carry a soft warm highlight out and back along the line, four seconds each way, drawn as a short blurred stroke with a feathered tail and faded ends. A new location takes the next free turn and the rest queue by fewest turns and longest wait, so every arc gets its light within a minute and the map never becomes a field of moving sparks. Each arc keeps its own phase, so the lights that are lit sit at different points. Motion, not colour, carries the direction, and the pale warm light keeps amber as the map's only hue. There are no endpoint dots — nearby destinations would turn them into a cluster of specks at the hub, and the converging arcs already mark both ends. The glow is a map effect only; it does not introduce glow elsewhere.

Use semantic Tailwind tokens from web/src/index.css, never page-local gray or blue approximations. Light and dark themes are designed as separate contrast pairs.

RoleLightDark
Canvas / background#f6f7f9#111318
Card / popover#ffffff#1a1d24
Main text#171b22#f1f3f7
Secondary text#5b6472#abb4c3
Subtle surface#f0f2f5#232731
Divider#e2e6ec#343b48
Input border#a4adbb#67758b
Primary text / focus#1d4ed8#8ab4ff
Solid primary action#2563eb#2563eb
Text on solid primary#ffffff#ffffff
Receive / download#1d4ed8#8ab4ff
Transmit / upload#0f766e#6bd4c6
Success text#167447#70d8a5
Warning text#935a10#f1c071
Destructive text#b42335#ff9daa

Use primary-fill with primary-foreground for filled actions. Use primary for links and selected navigation. The selected section in desktop navigation is a 40px primary/10 tinted pill rather than a rule under the label; the tint is a shape, so the selection survives without reading the hue. Use success-foreground and warning-foreground for readable status text. Color accompanies a label or icon; it never replaces one. A normally blocked DNS request is neutral activity, not an incident. Reserve destructive emphasis for errors and destructive actions.

Cards use a one-pixel border and shadow-xs. Shadows clarify elevation rather than decorate every nested row. A list inside CardContent does not need a second border. Use muted fills for small metrics, not another elevated card. Use panel-surface for custom panels and interactive-surface for actual link/button surfaces. Hover changes color, never shadow depth. Radius tokens are 8px (rounded-lg), 12px (rounded-xl) and 16px (rounded-2xl). Dialogs use 16px and shadow-md. Card spacing and title size are independent variants.

Layout and hierarchy

Desktop and mobile navigation use Overview, Gateway, Wireless, Access and Advanced, in that order. Wireless shows a managed access point's radios, findings and associated clients; it is read-only in this increment. Firewall, port forwarding, administrator access and the five diagnostic pages are reached through Advanced and highlight Advanced in navigation, including on their detail pages. Firewall and the tool pages keep their addresses; port forwarding and administrator access moved from Access, so their old addresses redirect rather than disappear.

Firewall's arrival diagram uses a centered firewall boundary spanning 40% of the chart width inside its 24px gutters. Pack incoming bands contiguously along each edge, with logarithmic widths normalized separately for each side and a 4px minimum. Keep each curved path region about 88px tall and packet values with their units on one line. Reserve separate label space so small traffic categories remain readable.

Access has three app-launcher grids headed “Networking”, “Add a way out” and “Add a way in”, in that order. Networking contains WireGuard, Tailscale, NetBird, ZeroTier and Headscale, shown once rather than repeated in the directional groups. Keep their existing configuration actions available. Do not show System default or purpose filters. Each tile shows a locally bundled project logo above a short name, without an enclosing card, border, shadow or corner arrow. Preserve brand colors on a white 64px rounded icon backing in both themes. SOCKS5 and Advanced's Port forwarding use the reviewed original app icons in web/public/feature-icons: simple flat color blocks on a softly colored rounded tile, without 3D or material effects. These fill the 64px backing without a second white inset; remove the generated masters' outside white field before bundling. Use frp's official website icon as project artwork. Other protocols without approved artwork retain a capital initial on a tinted tile; the hue keeps shared initials apart. Use three columns on phones, five from 640px, seven from 1024px and eight from 1280px, with 12px horizontal and 24px vertical gaps. Keep names below icons with an 8px gap and visible keyboard focus around the whole tile. Group headings use 24px/32px semibold text. Each tile is a link with one destination: the configuration page for the direction it belongs to, or the project's documentation in a new tab when OLR does not configure it. Do not open a dialog on click. Hover/focus explains function and state, and the accessible name repeats that state for touch and screen readers. External setup stays explicit.

Advanced is the same launcher, with three grids headed “System”, “Services” and “Diagnostics”, in that order. System holds the machine and what may reach it (firewall, administrator access, port forwarding); Services holds the background jobs it runs for the network (DDNS, IPTV multicast); Diagnostics holds the five tools. Each tile wears a capital initial on a tinted tile, and the tiles of one group share a single hue, so the tint groups them without a legend. The one exception is a diagnostic that names an upstream tool: it wears that tool's own app icon. NextTrace's artwork carries its own rounded background, so it fills the 64px tile instead of sitting inside a white or tinted one. Keep such artwork bundled under web/public/tool-logos with its provenance recorded there, and never borrow the mark of a protocol or of a service a test merely contacts — a speed test keeps its initial, because the measurement is OLR's, not Ookla's.

A tile is a mark and one line of name. No name wraps and nothing prints under it: a row of two-line labels makes the next group's heading look misplaced, and a directory that reports nine statuses has stopped being a directory. Keep the tile's name short enough for one line — the page behind it may carry the longer name, as Admin access opens Administrator access. The state still travels with the tile: hover/focus explains the function and the current answer, and the accessible name repeats it for touch and screen readers. Keep the directory's tiles and the shared launcher in components/layout/launcher.tsx; a tool tile links to its diagnostic page, and there is no Tools directory page in between.

Credits opens with its title and then one ungrouped table: no visible header row, no section rows, and no website column. The first column is the destination — mark and name together as one link — followed by the version and the feature the project carries. List every project that carries a feature, and a Go or web library only where it is that feature's supplier; the complete dependency and license lists stay linked from go.mod and web/package.json. Project marks are bundled under web/public/credit-logos (or reused from the feature directories) and sit on a white tile in both themes; a row without approved artwork keeps a neutral initial. Below 768px the rows become stacked records with the same three fields, rather than a horizontally scrolling table.

Tunnel Broker uses one scrollable page with five numbered sections and a sticky step navigation immediately below the 64px shell header. Keep section anchors clear of both bars and scroll the navigation locally on narrow screens. The page title is accessible but visually hidden; avoid a repeated introductory heading above the step navigation.

Gateway's landing page is a directory, in the launcher Access and Advanced already use: six groups in the order an operator arrives at them — Internet, Interfaces & routing, DHCP, DNS, Firewall and Intrusion prevention — each holding one tile per way of building that part. Use three columns on phones, five from 640px, seven from 1024px and eight from 1280px, with the group's 24px/32px heading above it and each tile a letter in the group's hue, so the tint groups the tiles without a legend. Names stay on one line and nothing prints under them.

A choice OLR cannot configure yet keeps its tile at 55% opacity, with no pointer and no destination: a group states what it will contain instead of growing a tile at a time. It is not an external setup, so it never borrows that state's language, and its tooltip says plainly that nothing opens. A tile that is a link opens the one page that configures the choice. A choice OLR does not configure at all — firewalld, ufw, fail2ban, CrowdSec — links to the project's own site in a new tab instead, and its tooltip says the setup is external. The directory has no status strip, no switch, no draft, and no tile that opens a dialog.

The interface cards and the two stacks, IPv4 and IPv6, that used to be this page are not on it any more: a stack card's answer and the switch that changes it were always one page away, and links that used to target gateway#interfaces now target gateway/interfaces.

The shell has a 1280px maximum width, a 64px header and horizontal gutters of 16px on phones, 24px from 640px, and 32px from 1280px. Content starts with 24px vertical space on phones and 32px on larger screens.

All page containers use the available shell width, centered in the viewport. Header, page headings, cards and footer share the same outer boundaries. Do not apply route-dependent page widths. Individual fields and explanatory paragraphs may constrain their own reading width without narrowing the entire page. Section landing pages omit the visible heading already named in navigation; retain an sr-only h1 for assistive technology, with no heading gap. Detail and operation pages use PageHeading and SubPage: a visible title, an explanation only when needed, and an optional primary action. Sub-pages do not repeat the section navigation, because the shell's section tabs already name the section they are under. Gateway's nested DNS and DHCP settings are the one exception: those pages keep a Gateway › DNS breadcrumb, since the top bar can only name Gateway, while the page that carries its section's own name (details) shows none. Preserve existing redirects and deep links when moving settings.

The spacing vocabulary is 4, 8, 12, 16, 24 and 32px. Use 32px between major sections, 16–24px inside cards and 8px between label and control. Basic corner radii are 8px for controls/small inset surfaces, 12px for panels and 16px for larger enclosing surfaces. Avoid arbitrary one-off radii. Overview metric cards use 12px padding on phones and 16px on larger screens, an 8px heading gap, 36px metric rows and 4px between rows. Interactive rows retain 44px targets on phones; site latency items use unfilled 32px rows with 6px vertical gaps. Only download/upload rates use inset meter surfaces in Overview cards. Status, public addresses, latency, totals and uptime use plain rows; monitored sites retain their icons without capsule backgrounds. Cumulative traffic rows use Download and Upload labels with plain byte values. On desktop, Overview cards share title and primary metric boundaries. Totals and site probes follow their primary metrics without divider lines. Status flows naturally. Below desktop, cards use their own content height. Site probes use two columns on phones and three from 640px. Overview shows only sites pinned from /latency; no site is pinned by default. Internet and DNS keep their existing rows. With no pins, omit the site grid and its padding. Base the card's expanded height on the number of pinned sites rather than the full catalog. Internet target selection and monitored-site configuration remain API/CLI operations; /latency presents measurements, test actions and Overview pin toggles. The /latency page is a test view, not an editor. Show all sites in one list panel, divided into plain 16px semibold category headings: no band, rule or count, a 40px heading row, and 16px between one group and the next. The heading stays at the left when the panel scrolls horizontally, and the rows beneath it are indented by the pin slot.

Each row has a 24px pin slot before a bare icon and name, 24 aligned 20px square samples with 4px visible gaps, and a right-aligned average. Keep the name column fixed at 176px on phones and 192px from 640px, with an 8px/12px gap to the sample grid, rather than letting the name column absorb available width. The sample band is 24 slots of 24px (576px), left-aligned; it does not stretch to fill the row. The samples retain fixed router-local hours from 00:00–01:00 to 23:00–24:00; do not slide or reorder them as measurements arrive. Missing, future and skipped hours stay neutral gray, and a failed attempt uses the same neutral fill because it is not a value on the day's scale. Use success below 100 ms, warning from 100 to 499 ms and destructive at 500 ms and above. Retests replace the current hour. Tooltips and accessible names identify each exact date, range and outcome. While a site's on-demand probe runs, its current-hour square becomes a primary spinner and crossfades and scales into the result over 200ms. The average is the arithmetic mean of that day's successful samples, right-aligned in its own column, with the same colour bands and an em dash when none succeeded. Keep columns aligned across sites, and scroll the panel horizontally on narrow screens while keeping site identities pinned at the left.

Prefer the locally bundled theSVG mark for built-in sites, then favicon discovery and bare initials, without added backgrounds, borders or clipping. Adapt black marks for contrast in dark mode without a backing.

The pin is a 24px button before the mark, not the whole identity. An unpinned pin is transparent until its row is hovered or the button is focused, and stays visible on coarse pointers; a pinned pin remains visible in primary. Hover changes only the pin's background and icon colour; the mark and name do not react. During a save, show progress on that row and serialize pin changes. Commit the visible state only after a successful save, and expose failures without dropping measurements. Pin choices persist in router configuration and do not start a measurement. There is no add, remove or site-edit control.

Test all sits beside the page heading and updates only the current hour. It asks for sites one at a time in reading order and names the progress position on the button. It does not highlight or scroll the active row; a failed or timed-out site does not stop the rest, and completed results stay visible. There are no category or row test controls. The public-network summary uses a locally bundled flag-icons country flag. Clicking any Status row opens its details in a shared dialog, without chevrons. Public addresses use monospace and wrap within the dialog. Status rows fill the card width. Give flags and health icons the same 16px leading slot so text starts align. System health uses the same dialog interaction as uptime, with module names on the left and status values aligned right. Keep module details as plain rows.

Typography and imagery

Use Geist Variable with system sans-serif fallback. Page titles are 24px/32px, weight 600. Panel titles are generally 16px, weight 600. Body and controls are 14px; descriptions and technical metadata are 13–14px with relaxed line height. Use 12px only for compact auxiliary metadata. Mobile text inputs are 16px to avoid browser zoom. Use tabular numerals for live rates and counters, and monospace for addresses, commands and configuration.

Device imagery identifies device categories. Device icon selection is one search box over two catalogues — the pictures bundled in the binary, matched on labels, makers, categories and tags, and theSVG's marks, matched on the daemon (internal/brandlogo: exactly, then by prefix and substring, then on a near miss, so a dropped or transposed letter still finds the mark) — so it works on a router with no internet and draws no third-party image. The box sits above a list that scrolls on its own, so it is still there when the list is long. Below it, two blocks: brand pictures grouped one labelled section per maker — Apple, Samsung, Huawei — with makers holding one picture sharing a trailing Other brands section, then one Common grid mixing every unbranded picture and its variants. A query replaces both blocks with results, bundled pictures first and theSVG's marks under their own heading. Operating-system marks are no longer offered there; stored marks still draw. See web/src/assets/device-icons/ICONS.md. Render chosen logos in the same muted tile as operating-system marks throughout device views. A device that dialed in wears the Way in badge in the lower-right corner of that picture — the same badge in the map's band card and on its own page — because the picture is the same in both places and the badge is the only thing that says the tunnel brought it.

Tool directory entries use Lucide outline icons with a 1.75px stroke in a themed 56px surface (48px on phones), an 18px name and one directional chevron. Avoid raster illustrations with baked-in backgrounds. Overview metric headings have the same 24px line box; auxiliary icons extend their hit area without increasing the heading height. Descriptions and instructions belong on the individual tool page. No decorative glows or additional gradients are needed. Use Lucide consistently for functional icons, normally 16–20px. The two-color brand mark retains its own colors in both themes.

Controls, lists and dialogs

Ingress pending repairs reuse Alert above the settings and a warning status dot. List remaining errors with service names and wrapping text; keep the existing single-service edit dialog and save action.

Use the shared Button, Input, Select, Textarea, Switch, Card and Dialog components. Regular controls are 36px high on desktop, sm is 32px, and mobile button/input/select targets are at least 44px high. Switch visuals are 44 × 24px with an expanded mobile hit area; busy keeps an applying switch at full contrast and disabled is reserved for a change the router will refuse. Focus uses the primary ring and must remain visible. Hover and active changes use color; avoid positional movement.

State, switch placement, button rank and row glyphs follow the control language contract. Five tones are shared — ok, warn, fault, off, unknown — and a word's tone is fixed in lib/state.ts, never chosen per page. A state is drawn in one of three shapes: StatusPill for the subject of a card, StatusInline (dot and word) for an item in a list, and the status strip for a module's verdict. Measurements stay plain values; only a grade is a pill. A row or card header shows at most one control: a chevron means "this row leads somewhere", a pencil means "this row can be changed", an ellipsis opens a menu, and a rotating chevron expands in place. Editing and removing live on the page the row leads to, not beside its link; a switch displaces the chevron rather than sitting next to it.

Inline editable fields keep the input, explanation and save action within the same 720px field area. Show saving, error and completion where the action occurs. Device titles are edited by clicking the name, with the displayed value prefilled. Blur or Enter saves; Escape discards. No pencil or save/cancel controls accompany the title. The name input is 320px wide, capped by available space. Device traffic activity sits behind the title, aligned right and fading to transparent toward the overlapping name and icon. Omit the visible presence chip: lists and the map say when a device was last heard, and the device page does not repeat it. Each day is one column, newest on the right, with six four-hour dots from midnight downward. Future periods stay blank, and dot tooltips appear immediately. A divider separates the title from two columns of 36px desktop / 44px mobile minimum-height label/value rows: stable identity and settings on the left, routing, priority and traffic on the right. Group uses a clickable tag with a muted surface that opens its edit dialog. Device traffic reuses Overview meters with visible direction labels. At desktop widths both halves share five grid rows: Vendor/Uplink, MAC/Priority, IP/Download, Group/Upload and Services/Total. The hardware address is a mono fact row, not a chip beside the title; the dialed-in page puts its configured name in the same place. Services shows matching configured services as 28px icon tiles linking directly to their published webpages. A matching 28px outlined add button opens Ingress with the device prefilled. An empty list shows only the add button. Total uses the Overview Traffic meter's neutral text arrows (↓/↑), with the same size and weight, and byte values, with no caption after them: it sums the title matrix rather than a counter, and that matrix is where the window is read. Match row padding and let wrapped content grow both sides together; feedback follows the aligned rows. Device speed bars use half their available value width from 640px, aligned right; on phones they retain the full width so rates and limit actions remain readable. The device title contains a right-aligned traffic matrix occupying two thirds of the title width: one column per day and six four-hour periods per column. Cells stay 14px square with 3px corners. Derive the row gap from the 96px matrix height, six cells and 1px vertical padding; use that same gap horizontally. Fit as many complete date columns as the available width allows; wider layouts show more dates rather than stretching cells. Keep today at the right edge, the current-period hint and 1px inner padding. Fade only the leftmost 20% toward overlapping identity content; keep the rest fully visible, including zero/unknown dots. Use the shared opaque activity palette: zero/unknown uses the empty gray, low nonzero traffic uses a stronger neutral gray (#cfd4db light / #48515e dark), and the remaining four levels use green intensities, using 25%, 50% and 75% of the greater of the retained 90-day four-hour peak and 1 GiB as boundaries. Green starts at 10 MiB; boundary values keep the lighter tier. Use no decorative borders or inset rings; cell fills and spacing define the grid. Retain visible keyboard focus. No axes, legend, heading or helper text; tooltips provide dates, units and sample state. Uplink and Priority lead the right column with compact segmented selectors. Clicking each labeled speed bar opens its limit dialog; omit separate limit fields and the QoS divider/status row. Device policies apply automatically, without a switch. Keep QoS controls on devices; Gateway does not expose aggregate link-rate settings. Blank device limits mean unlimited; pending placement must remain distinct from active state. Preserve existing confirmation and apply-preview behavior for network changes. Group details reuse the device summary card: a 64px icon and title above a divider, then two columns with a 64px desktop gutter and 32px stacked spacing. Use the shared device label/value rows for parent, member counts and subgroup tags on the left, with matching Uplink and Priority segmented controls on the right. Keep batch apply actions and scope beside those controls, followed by the device list in its own panel. Use the device page's 16px panel spacing. Device detail rows use two zones: left-aligned labels and right-aligned values or controls, with 36px desktop / 44px mobile minimum row height. Keep disclosure chevrons beside their values rather than in a separate action column. Clicking the IP opens a dialog with an address and fixed toggle, without a pencil. A Fixed badge follows reserved addresses. Device traffic rates have Download and Upload labels beside narrower, arrow-free inset meters; the recorded total sits below Upload. Uplink sits above Priority in the right column. Both use segmented controls with 28px desktop buttons, 2px container padding and 44px mobile targets. Uplink applies through the existing network-change confirmation flow. Separate the desktop identity/settings and traffic halves with a 64px gutter; stack them with 32px spacing below desktop. Never style a pending or failed read as a disabled service. Device inspection uses one panel below a fixed 72px title bar, separated by one full-width divider. Keep Activity and saved Requests visible with inspection off, including when another device is active. Current DNS queries appear while active. Use headings and spacing between sections, without a rule per section or DNS row. The title names the only Inspection switch; keep the setup gear at its left in every state. QR code, certificate guide and global retention settings live in the setup dialog. Disable scroll anchoring on the panel and reserve the document scrollbar gutter to prevent horizontal movement. Activity's range controls wrap on phones and identify the selected range with a shared secondary button and aria-pressed. Requests uses the same controls for Saved and Live while active. Saved history is the default, with a wrapping search and clear action above plain rows; long URLs wrap and each row has a separate 44px download target. A saved row opens the shared dialog for request/response headers and bounded, scrollable body previews. Show binary/truncated content as text status with full native download access. Clear opens a separate confirmation dialog. Live retains the embedded mitmproxy viewer at its existing height. Keep device request storage, router-wide request storage and age retention in one auxiliary line; retention fields explicitly name the router total and preserve units on phones. DNS uses the shared table without a visible header, with Time, Record, Type and right-aligned Answer columns, and without a switch of its own: the panel's switch already opened it. Its search icon reveals a compact filter in the section heading, opening to the left of that icon with a 200ms width/opacity transition that honors reduced motion. The switch stays pinned to the right edge, so opening the filter adds controls to its left instead of moving it. Keep long records and answers readable.

List rows have a minimum height of 64px. On phones, trailing values reflow below the title instead of disappearing. Technical values and important descriptions must wrap or have an accessible path to their complete value. A secondary action is a sibling via ListRow's action prop, outside the row link/button. For Button rendered as a Link, set nativeButton={false}.

Dialogs use a restrained scrim, a 480px default maximum width and 16/24px padding. Long forms must scroll within the viewport and retain a reachable close and submit action. Empty states use a normal surface, a short explanation and a relevant next action where one exists.

Responsive behavior and motion

Overview has four desktop cards: Status, Traffic, Latency and Quality. Clicking the Latency heading links to /latency; omit an add icon. Map and Quality chart content use half the normal card side and bottom gutters (6px on phones, 8px on larger screens), while headings retain their normal inset. Desktop cards target 4:3 proportions with a 240px minimum height and grow for disclosures or extra probes. Use one column on phones, two from 640px and four from 1280px so values and units remain on one line. Traffic's title-right map icon toggles its statistics and embedded map views. Keep both mounted as the front and back of one card to preserve height and map continuity. Rotate the whole card 180 degrees around its vertical axis over 600ms, with 1200px perspective and hidden backfaces. Each face has its own title and toggle so the map appears on the back of the card. Reduced motion switches faces immediately. Make the inactive face inert and hidden to assistive technology. Do not add a Map details row; clicking the map links to /map. The Quality heading and radar link to /quality; omit a separate Test button on the card. Retain measured scores without age-based fading or hiding. Network quality uses a five-axis radar with theme-aware primary fill and border grid lines. It occupies one card at every breakpoint. Only measured, current axes have points; missing/stale axes show dashes and prevent a filled polygon, except Wireless, which defaults to 80 for display. Omit the title-right total and below-plot scope caption. /latency, /quality and /map are normal detail pages inside AppShell, with its header, footer, content width and gutters. All three keep Overview selected in desktop and mobile navigation. Use PageHeading for their visible h1; they have no fullscreen dialog or floating close control. The page header names the view, dates the snapshot and carries the run action with the one line naming the included bandwidth test. A four-column summary then sits beside an eight-column category panel on desktop and stacks in that order on phones. The summary holds the score ring, the display grade, the count of scored categories and a measured-coverage bar, with the transfer panel beneath it leading with the download and upload rates as metric values; the score itself stays in foreground colour while only the ring arc takes the grade hue, so a run of Fair categories does not paint the page as a field of warnings. Categories are hairlined rows of one panel: a 16px semibold heading, the 0–100 score in a fixed right-aligned column, an action slot that stays reserved when a category has no rerun control, and a bar whose track is 160px in every row so fills compare down the list. Each row states its evidence in its own units beside the bar — throughput, median and variation, response counts, reachable services — and repeats no state word from row to row. Expanding a row indents its tests to the category title, and each test shows its own medians with its score landing in the category score column. A service probe is one test item because one run of six fresh connections produces its timing, stability and access measurements; its rerun control updates that service everywhere. Unimplemented items stay listed without a rerun control. Scoring formulas, per-service samples and NAT observations sit in collapsed Measurement details disclosures, so raw evidence never pushes the result below the fold. Keep long errors and addresses wrapping inside the view. Accessible chart descriptions identify partial and missing measurements. Uptime is the first plain disclosure row in Status, above system health. Both rows use aligned 16px Lucide CircleCheck icons in success color when healthy. Uptime opens a dialog with CPU, memory and root disk used/total values. Map has no information icon, direction legend or top-ten summary. The grayscale preview fills Traffic's remaining content area. /map contains a pastel country map (muted colors in dark mode) in a bounded responsive panel below the page heading, with pan/zoom. Keep direction labels, status, credit and other text outside the map. The local detailed map reveals province/state boundaries, their names and major cities on zoom, stopping at regional detail (zoom 6). State names and capital/world-city names begin at zoom 3; other major cities appear at zooms 4–5. Country fill indices are stable and checked against neighboring countries, with separate light/dark palettes. Keep administrative labels neutral and secondary to traffic; traffic carries no GeoIP text labels. Pan, pinch, scroll and double-click zoom stand alone, so place no zoom or whole-world reset buttons over the map. Resizing must preserve the current map view. Links and bookmarks open each detail page directly, and the Overview navigation returns to the overview. On phones each card uses the full column. Its local MapLibre map draws one amber arc per remote location at a single weight — about 1px where the world is fitted into a few hundred pixels, 2px at the world view of the detailed map — and the arcs thin further as the map zooms in, so a regional view is not buried under globe-width ribbons and a small map is not buried under a bundle of them. An arc stays at full weight while its location is in the window and fades out when the location leaves; nothing periodic touches it. Card preview and detailed map show the same rotation: only a few arcs hold a highlight at a time, each a short blurred warm stroke that travels out and back along the line, four seconds each way, with a feathered tail and faded ends, so the light never lands at the hub or on a destination. It carries direction and stops for reduced motion. Keep highlight phases stable across ranking updates and fade arriving/departing arcs over a fixed 450ms eased curve, which always completes. When a snapshot brings or drops several locations at once, give each one a slot in a window that ends before the next snapshot and jitter it inside that slot, so the batch reads as an irregular sequence rather than a step or a metronome; a lone change still fades immediately, and the whole batch has settled by the time the next poll lands. Reduced motion drops the highlight, the stagger and interpolation; hidden tabs pause updates. Arcs use valid returned coordinates without country-center fallbacks; omit locations without coordinates. Draw flows between different locations even within one country. The details dialog supplies city/country, rates and ip.sb attribution without crowding the map.

Overview group headers navigate directly to group details at every screen size; do not expand or focus named groups in place. Device list rows reserve space for up to three 24px service icons with 4px gaps. Use only the space needed by the device's services; additional icons scroll horizontally. Keep the trailing activity column at 48px so service icons sit close to rates and last-seen values without taking space from device names. A device row's trailing value is when it was last heard — an elapsed time, a dash for a device that answered nothing, or never seen — never an online or offline state, which only a dialed-in peer has evidence for.

Network-map device ordering samples current traffic ranks every five seconds. Pause reordering while the pointer is over the map, keyboard focus is inside it, or a touch is active. Resume at the next scheduled update rather than immediately on leaving. Rates and counters keep their normal live refresh; do not smooth them. New devices appear after existing rows until the next reorder; removed devices disappear immediately. Groups retain their name order.

The band above the router holds the only thing outside it: the devices dialed in over WireGuard, one card each, drawn side by side and joined to the router by their own line. A dial-in card is a device node, drawn in the band: the peer's own picture from the same picker a device uses, its label over its tunnel address, and the state in the same narrow figure column a device row keeps for its rate or its last-heard time, with the endpoint and totals on hover. The way in is a 14px badge on the corner of the peer's picture: the WireGuard mark at full brand colour on the same white disc a protocol gets on the Access page, with a 2px ring in the card's colour so it separates from the device tile underneath. A badge on the picture is not a picture in place of the machine, and it costs the card no width; the method also stays in the tooltip ("over wg0"). Connected is a filled 8px success dot whose word lives in the accessible name and the card's title; the other three states (an elapsed time, Never connected, Status unavailable) stay words, since an absence of evidence must not be a status light. It carries no rate, which is why the band's lines stay the thin ones. Never mark an absent peer as a fault. WireGuard off, or a tunnel with no peers, puts no band there at all: the map starts at the router, and with no groups either it is one box. Observed default routes are not cards on the map. A next hop is one line of Link's status — address, interface, family — and drawing each one was a row of boxes above the router that said less than that line while pushing every group a third of a screen down. The device a next hop names is a device on this network, so it is drawn in its group like any other, not lifted out of it. A way out that has stopped answering is red where it can be acted on: the uplink card under Gateway, which also names the interface the next hop does answer on, and a network chip on the router when the gateway exit behind it is down.

Firewall uses one vertical Sankey with three visual rows: external semantic categories above, one virtual OLR / Firewall node in the middle, and trusted/LAN and router-local semantic categories below. Both sides flow toward OLR. These positions distinguish origins, not successive processing stages. Keep the semantic category and packet count on each outer node; omit repeated source and Allowed/Blocked labels. Color conveys the decision, with full text in tooltips. Use one measured packet scale and semantic receive/transmit and success/warning colors. Reserve label space for small nonzero paths without inflating their widths. Provide an accessible tooltip details; narrow screens scroll inside the diagram without causing page-wide overflow. Adapt to available width and wrap labels. When the chart must scroll, start at its leading edge; never automatically center it and hide the first category.

Page navigation resets document scroll to the top before paint. Hash links retain their section-target behavior; query-only changes preserve the current scroll.

Desktop section navigation begins at 1024px. Below that, show all five sections in a five-column bottom navigation; do not require horizontal scrolling. The bottom bar marks the current section with text-primary on an icon and label alone: it has no room for the desktop pill, and a fill behind a 20px icon reads as a pressed button rather than as a location. Account for the device safe area and bottom navigation when laying out content and the footer. At 375px, keep labels, statuses, addresses and action buttons usable. Monitoring statistics use two columns on phones.

The footer is one line at every width: it centres its row and thins the gap to 12px below 360px rather than wrapping. On desktop it bottom-aligns its text and icons with 12px bottom padding, keeping the visible content close to the viewport edge. Its items run in one order — copyright, Credits, version, then the three controls — with one visible 16px gap: each control spends 8px of side padding on a 44px-high hit target, so the footer cancels that padding rather than letting the controls sit in visibly wider intervals than the text. Below 640px the copyright keeps the year alone and drops the product name, which the header already carries; the version stays at every width, because the footer is the only place that reports it. The repository link is GitHub's mark alone and the theme control a single icon; clicking the theme cycles auto, light and dark, and both name themselves in their accessible label and tooltip. Both are 14px, the row's one icon size: an icon's class is its optical size, so artwork with no inset of its own brings that inset with it instead of the call site asking for a smaller box. The language control shows only the language in use, in its native writing (English / 中文): footer text size and weight, no icon, no separate "Language" label, and no filled hover background, so it reads as footer text rather than as a button, with visible keyboard focus. Like the theme control, it reports the state it is in, and its accessible label and tooltip name the language a click switches to. Place the same control below the sign-in and initial-setup forms. Language changes preserve layout, current navigation and in-progress form values.

Use 150–200ms color/opacity transitions. Motion should explain a state change; no ambient animation except observed world traffic and the current device-activity block's traffic indicator. Breathe faster as combined live download/upload increases, with a logarithmic 4s–1.4s cycle capped at 100 MiB/s. Use opacity 1 → 0.45 over 55% of the cycle, rest dim for 10%, then return to full opacity over 35%. Each changing segment uses cubic-bezier(0.37, 0, 0.63, 1), with zero endpoint slopes for gentle reversals. Keep the cell size and palette; no glow or scale animation. Keep a fixed animation timeline and ease playback speed toward each new target with a 350ms exponential time constant (about one second to settle), preserving the current phase. When idle or unavailable, finish the current cycle and pause at full opacity; resume from that phase when traffic returns. Idle or unavailable rates stay steady; historical cells retain their traffic fills. Honor prefers-reduced-motion in the global stylesheet.

Page coverage and review checklist

Review Overview; device and group details; Gateway and interface details; exits, usage and unmanaged settings; every DNS and DHCP detail/settings page; native Firewall; Access and SOCKS5, remote and WireGuard; Advanced with its Caddy, port forwarding, external filtering, DDNS, IPTV, administrator access and all five diagnostic pages; Credits; not-found; token/password sign-in; initial setup and first-run states. Legacy URLs should still redirect to the appropriate current page.

For every iteration:

  • Check 375px, 768px and 1440px layouts, light and dark themes.
  • Check long device names, IPv6 addresses, empty collections and populated data.
  • Verify keyboard focus, a single clear page title and semantic navigation.
  • Verify loading, unavailable and error states cannot be mistaken for healthy data.
  • Open affected dialogs, verify scroll/close/submit access and avoid nested buttons.
  • Keep current value, units and action visible on mobile; avoid page-wide overflow.
  • Run web lint, build and tests; run the repository's Go checks.
  • Capture screenshots of affected pages and states for review.

The stylesheet and shared components are the implementation source of truth. Update this guide alongside deliberate changes to these contracts.

docs.title: Wireless
docs.summary: The top-level Wireless section shows one access point from the network equipment inventory: its radios, the findings that follow from the current reading, and the clients associated right now. It is a monitoring surface, not a configuration editor. A channel change interrupts every client, so it belongs behind the same preview-and-recovery contract as the rest of the router rather than beside the charts.
docs.html:
Status: implemented. Read-only for one managed access point, plus an explicit per-band neighbour scan.

What the page is

The top-level Wireless section shows one access point from the network equipment inventory: its radios, the findings that follow from the current reading, and the clients associated right now. It is a monitoring surface, not a configuration editor. A channel change interrupts every client, so it belongs behind the same preview-and-recovery contract as the rest of the router rather than beside the charts.

Adding the access point

The page can add and edit its own inventory entry. Its empty state and header offer the equipment dialog for the management origin, username and password; removing an entry only forgets it here and never touches the access point. The same dialog and the same list live on the device page (/devices), which is the canonical inventory; this page keeps its own controls because an access point is usually onboarded at the moment somebody is looking at its radios. A stored password is returned masked and is never rendered again, which is why editing an address does not require retyping it. docs/network-equipment.md describes the credential rules and what a backup carries.

Where the data comes from

The browser reads the equipment inventory and then one device snapshot:

GET    /api/devices/config
PUT    /api/devices/{id}             inventory entry only, never the device
DELETE /api/devices/{id}      
GET    /api/devices/{id}/snapshot
POST   /api/devices/{id}/scan   {"radio_id": "radio1"}

The daemon talks to the access point. The browser never reaches it directly and holds no access-point credential. internal/devices owns the adapter, the snapshot contract and the per-section collection status; the page treats every reading as dated evidence, never as current truth.

On the tested Beam WRT build, netifd's network.wireless object and hostapd's get_status/get_clients are not granted to the management session. The adapter therefore falls back to LuCI's luci-rpc.getWirelessDevices and iwinfo.assoclist, which the same session may read. Utilization, MFP/WMM and airtime stay absent on that firmware and the page renders them as “—”, not as zero.

radio_id is the ID the snapshot reports — on this firmware radio0 and radio1. The adapter resolves it to that radio's AP interface (phy0-ap0, phy1-ap0) before asking iwinfo, and also accepts the interface name itself.

The scan is a separate request on purpose. iwinfo.scan is granted on that firmware and takes roughly four seconds per radio, while the radio is off its own channel and every client on that band waits. iwinfo.survey, which would report per-channel busy time directly, is denied. So the snapshot never scans, the page never polls a scan, and a person asks for one band at a time. The request is not published as an MCP tool for the same reason: an agent must not stall the Wi-Fi to fill in a diagram.

What it shows

AreaContent
RadiosSSID, BSSID, band, the standard the radio runs and the newer one it could run, security, roaming options, runtime channel, actual and configured width, transmit power, country, noise, clients, utilization
Findingsconfigured-versus-actual width, clients at or below -75 dBm, utilization at or above 60%
Clientssignal and SNR, directional rates with their own standard, MCS and width, expected throughput, retries and failures, idle and connected time, bytes and packets, airtime, MFP and WMM
Channelson request, one band's scan: every BSS heard with its primary channel, width, signal and security, a strip counting BSS per channel, and how many overlap the radio's own channel

The badge names the standard the radio is running, not the newest one its driver advertises, because that is the question the card answers; when the two differ the card also says what the radio could run. A client's row names the newer of its two directions, which can be older than the radio's; the expanded row splits the directions apart, because one can be older than the other. Roaming is what the access point offers devices that move between access points — fast transition, neighbour reports and client steering — and each is drawn with a dot rather than a word, so "off" and "not reported" stay distinguishable.

Client names come from the clients module when that MAC is known. Otherwise the page says “Private address” for a locally administered address, or shows the MAC. A dash means the access point did not report the value.

Deliberate limits

  • A scan is an action, not a reading. It interrupts the band for a few seconds, so the page asks first, offers it per band, and keeps the answer as a dated sample. Absence of a scan is not absence of neighbours.
  • Occupancy is counted, not measured. Without iwinfo survey the strip counts BSS per primary channel; overlap is inferred from channel, width and signal, not from measured airtime. A strong neighbour on an overlapping channel is evidence of competition, not proof of the cause of a slow client.
  • No hostapd-only counters when the firmware does not expose them. Utilization, MFP/WMM and airtime disappear rather than being substituted.
  • No writes to the access point. Editing the inventory entry is a configuration change on this router, not a change on the device. Disconnect, steering and channel changes remain operations with their own capability checks and confirmations. The snapshot can report that client.disconnect is supported; the page does not yet offer it.
  • Roaming is offered, not proven. 802.11r/802.11k/802.11v are read from the access point's own configuration. Nothing here follows a client from one BSS to another, so the page never claims a handover happened, only that the access point says it is available.
  • No history. A reading is a point in time. Trend lines need a sampler and a retention decision; none is implied by this page.

Verification

The snapshot shape was exercised against a Xiaomi BE7000 running Beam WRT 1.5.6 (OpenWrt 25.12.6): two radios, three associations, the 2.4 GHz width fallback, and the LuCI/iwinfo fallback above. A live scan of the 5 GHz radio heard 25 BSS in about four seconds and a 2.4 GHz scan heard 100 in about four more; survey answered “Access denied”. Adapter fixtures remain synthetic and cover the same protocol shapes.

docs.title: World traffic
docs.summary: Overview's Traffic card flips to a MapLibre preview with a bundled Natural Earth 1:110m country map (public domain). Opening /map loads a separate, fingerprinted local GeoJSON asset with 1:50m countries and simplified global 1:10m first-order administrative boundaries, label points and major cities. State/province boundaries appear from zoom 2; their names and capital/world-city names start at zoom 3. Million-plus cities appear from zoom 4 and the remaining major cities from zoom 5, with collision handling and population priority. Administrative label thresholds are brought forward for this regional view rather than copied from a street basemap; integer thresholds match MapLibre's symbol layout evaluation. Zoom stops at 6: this is an administrative traffic map, without roads or buildings. /map is a regular Overview detail page with the shared header, page heading and footer. The map occupies a bounded responsive panel without text overlays or a close control. Links and bookmarks open the page directly. Pan, pinch, scroll and double-click zoom stand alone. Resizing preserves the chosen map view. MapLibre renders labels with local system fonts; there are no external map, font, sprite or tile requests, including on first use. The asset ships inside OLR and uses the existing immutable asset cache.

Opening /map loads a separate, fingerprinted local GeoJSON asset with 1:50m countries and simplified global 1:10m first-order administrative boundaries, label points and major cities. State/province boundaries appear from zoom 2; their names and capital/world-city names start at zoom 3. Million-plus cities appear from zoom 4 and the remaining major cities from zoom 5, with collision handling and population priority. Administrative label thresholds are brought forward for this regional view rather than copied from a street basemap; integer thresholds match MapLibre's symbol layout evaluation. Zoom stops at 6: this is an administrative traffic map, without roads or buildings. /map is a regular Overview detail page with the shared header, page heading and footer. The map occupies a bounded responsive panel without text overlays or a close control. Links and bookmarks open the page directly. Pan, pinch, scroll and double-click zoom stand alone. Resizing preserves the chosen map view. MapLibre renders labels with local system fonts; there are no external map, font, sprite or tile requests, including on first use. The asset ships inside OLR and uses the existing immutable asset cache.

Only the top forty IPs are located using cached ip.sb city lookups; unknown locations remain in the ranking and its coverage denominator. Coordinates are approximate IP locations, not physical device positions. Arcs use only valid returned coordinates, without GeoIP city, region or country labels or country-center fallbacks. IPs without coordinates remain in the ranking but are not plotted. Administrative label points are representative, not IP locations.

The detailed dataset is generated by web/scripts/build-region-map.mjs from Natural Earth v5.1.2's ne_50m_admin_0_countries.geojson, ne_10m_admin_1_states_provinces_lines.geojson, ne_10m_admin_1_states_provinces.geojson, and ne_10m_populated_places_simple.geojson. Cities are limited to Natural Earth scale ranks 0–5 plus national capitals. Pass a directory containing those files to the script. Geometry is simplified at 0.02 degrees and rounded to three decimal places, unused properties and province polygons are discarded, and internal boundary segments are grouped by country. Regeneration is an explicit maintenance step; normal builds and runtime never download data. See the source dataset and public-domain terms.

Country fills use MapLibre's demo palette in light mode and muted equivalents in dark mode. Each country has a stable palette index generated from the country adjacency graph, preferring Natural Earth's MAPCOLOR8 assignment. Shared vertices in both source and simplified geometry determine adjacency, including corner contacts. Deterministic saturation-degree coloring resolves conflicts and regeneration verifies all detected neighbors have different indices. Dataset order and traffic volume do not affect country colors.

The daemon samples IPv4/IPv6 conntrack counters every two seconds, shared across browsers. It retains counter differences over up to thirty seconds in memory, aggregates by remote IP, and selects forty by combined upload and download. Ranking has deterministic IP tie-breaking. Rates are bytes/second over the available window; the first sample is a baseline. Coverage is the top forty's share of all observed eligible remote-IP traffic, not a share of the separate nftables interface/device totals.

Blue indicates download and teal upload in the details list. The map itself uses one amber hue for every arc, deliberately outside the teal-green-blue country palette, so colour marks traffic as a category. Every arc carries one weight — 2px where the map fits the world into a laptop or a large window, about 1px where it fits into a few hundred pixels, as the card preview and a phone's detail map do — and keeps that weight for as long as its location reports traffic in the sampled window; an arc fades out only when the location leaves the window — no eligible bytes in the last thirty seconds, or pushed below the top forty. A line that dimmed while its flow continued would claim that a connection had ended, which the sampler cannot know: it differences conntrack counters every two seconds, keeps thirty seconds of deltas, and reports a rate per remote IP. It observes no connection start or end, so appearance and disappearance mean "in the window" and "out of it", not "opened" and "closed". Width carries no volume either; the ranked rates live in the details dialog, and the map stays a presence and direction picture. A blurred amber halo sits under each arc; because arcs composite per feature, the halo accumulates where they bunch up — around the router and along busy corridors — and concentration reads as light. Every arc stays translucent so overlaps build up instead of replacing each other, and width is one value per map that thins with zoom: 2px at the world view of a large map, 1px once the same world has to fit into a few hundred pixels. Neither a country-sized view nor a card preview is covered by ribbons meant for a globe. A highlight rides a few arcs at a time, not all of them: the light is a short stretch of the path drawn as two blurred strokes with a tail-to-head gradient, pale warm light rather than white so it lifts the amber without becoming a second hue. It travels out and back in four seconds each way and fades near both ends, so the light never lands at the hub or on a destination. The number of concurrent lights is a quarter of the plotted arcs, from one to five; a turn lasts about six seconds, a location that has just appeared goes to the front of the queue, and the rest are ordered by fewest turns and longest wait, so every arc is served within a minute. Each arc keeps its own phase, so concurrent lights sit at different points along their lines. Both views draw the same rotation; the card preview has room for a soft streak where a bead used to be a speck. Reduced motion drops the highlight and interpolation. The UI polls every two seconds and keeps each IP's highlight phase independent of ranking. Paths fade in and out over a fixed 450ms eased curve, so a fade always finishes. A snapshot can add or drop several locations at once, so those fades are spread across a window that closes before the next snapshot: each location owns a slot in the window and starts at a random point inside it, which keeps the gaps irregular instead of a metronome. The window is capped at 1.35 seconds (the two second poll minus the fade and a margin), so even a full batch has settled before the next one arrives, and a lone change still starts at once. The staggering is presentation only: a location is in or out of the window at the moment its snapshot says so, and every fade is the same length either way. Visual updates render at up to 30fps, and hidden tabs pause them. The highlight stays within amber and warm light, so amber is the only hue the map adds. There are no endpoint dots: the arcs carry the whole reading, and the hub is where they converge. This interpolation visualizes sampled activity; it is not a packet trace. Different returned locations within one country can have an arc; a location at the router's own coordinates gets no arc. The details dialog exposes IPs and both rates, unavailable states, sample duration and GeoIP attribution.

Gateway traffic counting enables net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_acct=1 through the normal apply plan. This affects newly created connections; older entries may lack counters until they expire. Turning counting off stops this sampler and clears its window, but does not disable the shared kernel facility used by remote access. No connection metadata is persisted by this sampler.

Measurements include router-originated and forwarded connections with one local endpoint and one public remote endpoint. Private, link-local and CGNAT destinations are excluded. Conntrack original/reply counters are translated according to endpoint ownership, including inbound connections. Short-lived connections that disappear between samples, final bytes of expired flows, and traffic bypassing kernel accounting can be missed. VPN endpoints are displayed as observed; inner destinations are not inferred.

Large connection tables still cost a full netlink dump, parsing and memory per sample. Measure this on target hardware before reducing the interval. The map's top-ten coverage does not claim exact whole-router accounting.
